item.title: The eco-tourism projects turning fishermen and poachers into environmental guardians
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Project Hiu was featured on Condé Nast Traveller's Bright Ideas in Travel 2026. For a documentary project on the shark fishing industry, Australian filmmaker Madison Stewart traveled to Indonesia. The country catches more sharks than anywhere else in the world, accounting for over 12 per cent of the global supply. There, Stewart came into contact not only with animals in need of conservation, but the shark fishermen too. They hailed from the small communities of Tanjung Luar and Gili Maringkik in East Lombok, and would spend weeks away from their families to hunt fish – endangered and otherwise. Even though the practice is strictly regulated in Indonesia, Stewart learned that some fishers will break federal regulations (such as laws protecting threatened species like whale sharks) when faced with the lack of alternative income options. Project Hiu gives these fishermen a choice. Founded in 2018 by Stewart, this nonprofit – named after the Bahasa Indonesia word for ‘shark’ – hires fishermen and their boats to instead work in tourist activities like snorkelling with blacktip reef sharks in coral forests, and sailing day trips around East Lombok. The Project’s ranks now include about 80 fishermen manning 15 boats who also support the tagging and research of their erstwhile prey (their work has led to the recent world-first tagging of 10 tiger sharks in Indonesian waters). For Stewart, the goal is to get at the heart of conflicts in nature conservation: “I hope this work inspires others to look beyond simply telling people to stop fishing and instead address why they fish in the first place.” Too often, environmental advocates insist on the elimination of poaching, logging and other harmful activities while remaining wholly unfamiliar with the factors at play that lead to predation, neglect, and abuse of nature. Initiatives like Project Hiu demonstrate the importance of repurposing the skills and knowledge of those who relied on hunting wildlife into protection efforts, while offering alternate economic opportunities through tourism and conservation. Such stories happen on the individual and organisational level. In the Philippines, Ruben Gianan is a veteran ranger at Masungi Georeserve, a member of The Long Run, a global network of nature-positive lodges and travel companies. Once a logger in the Rizal province, Gianan now uses his intimate knowledge of the terrain as a master navigator of this limestone ecosystem. Over in Raja Ampat, Indonesia, Misool Resort thrives on what was once a shark-finning camp, and the beach where hunters used to kill their catch is today a terrace where divers sip their morning coffees. The Misool Foundation manages ranger patrols staffed largely by locals who once worked alongside the dynamite-blasters. As a result, shark numbers inside this reserve have doubled since 2012. In Tanzania, local guide Anderson Mgesi grew up in a village in the Iringa region, where bushmeat fed his family. When the government expanded the park in the late 1990s and early 2000s, hundreds of villagers – including Mgesi's family – were forcibly evicted from their ancestral lands. Hunting wildlife is technically illegal in what became Ruaha National Park, but it was, as he puts it, “one of the few dependable ways to make ends meet.” When his grandfather was mauled by a leopard caught in a trap set for an impala, however, Mgesi began to feel that the dangers of hunting wildlife outweighed its benefits for humans. This led him to seek financial sponsorship to study at Mkuyu Wildlife School, which eventually led him to the opportunity to become a guide at Usangu Expedition Camp, part of safari company Asilia Africa. While the complexities around working within a park that his ancestors had been removed from remain, Mgesi now supports much of his extended family with the steady wage. As Mgesi tells it, “Conservation's future lies in neighbouring communities benefiting directly from tourism, and in educating children while they're young about the career possibilities in hospitality.” Shinta Mani Wild, in collaboration with the conservation non-profit Wildlife Alliance, trains and employs former snare-setters in Cambodia's Cardamom Mountains to intercept illegal logging and the poaching of Malayan sun bears, pangolins, clouded leopards, and pileated gibbons in a critical wildlife corridor. To date, the Wildlife Alliance in this region has removed about 350,000 traps, contributing to an uptick in the numbers of these vulnerable and endangered animals. The camp's new general manager, Jacky Collett-Stevens, recently relocated to the property from Rwanda, where she had worked on a string of successful projects focused on community engagement within wildlife conservation. “In Rwanda, people have seen that protecting their extraordinary mountain gorillas brings tangible, lasting value to their families and their country,” says Collett-Stevens. As Stewart of Project Hiu puts it: "When communities are given genuine alternatives, fair pay and opportunities, the impact reaches far beyond conservation – from retiring fishing boats to us being able to send two former shark fishermen to university. They are the villains in everyone’s story, but they are the heroes in ours."

item.title: San Francisco airport flyers can soon clear security in wine country
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
San Francisco airport flyers can soon clear security in wine country Landline coaches are coming to San Francisco International Airport (SFO). The airport transportation provider that offers bus connections inside security at a growing number of airports will launch its first West Coast route on Nov. 17: SFO to Charles M. Schulz-Sonoma County Airport (STS) in Northern California's wine country. "People love traveling. What they don't love is everything it takes to get to the airport," David Sunde, founder and CEO of Landline, said in a statement. "'Straight to Gate' connects [STS] to SFO's global network, so trips to anywhere in the world can start close to home." Landline will operate the new service under its own brand, initially with eight daily round trips. Travelers can book tickets on the company's website, with adult fares of $55 one-way and children under 15 free; the rides are not eligible for airline loyalty points. The offering is similar to Landline's new remote terminal service in the Boston suburb of Framingham, Massachusetts. Travelers will check in and drop their bags at the STS terminal, clear security and then board a bus bound for SFO. Journeys are expected to take a little over two hours, depending on traffic. Buses arrive at Gate A3 in the International Terminal at SFO, where travelers can proceed to their connecting flights without needing to reclear security. And as is standard practice for Landline, travelers can check luggage at STS, where it will be automatically transferred to their connecting flight at SFO. The company is partnering with Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, JetBlue Airways and United Airlines with additional partners planned for the future. Returning travelers collect their luggage at SFO and then board the Landline coach to STS at the baggage claim curb. All Landline buses are configured with 2-1 seating and equipped with high-speed Starlink connectivity. Landline's new SFO-STS service is the latest for the company, which launched seven years ago with the idea that lower-cost buses could replace short regional flights. Its first partnership was with Sun Country Airlines and followed in later years by Air Canada, American and United. Initial offerings were white-labeled services — similar to an American Eagle or United Express flight, but with buses — painted in the airline partner's colors. Its service has since evolved into a mix of independent and airline-affiliated operations. The company debuted airside-to-airside buses, or ones that operate entirely inside security between two airports, with American at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) in 2023. Today, Landline offers both independent and airline-branded services. That includes its own remote terminal and a Transportation Security Administration checkpoint in Framingham, part of a collaboration with Massport, which runs Boston's Logan International Airport (BOS). "Our team has really learned how to take the best from all the networks we've built and make it even better for the person sitting in the seat," Sunde said in an interview. Landline has "doubled" in size in 2026, he added, citing expanded offerings with Air Canada, the new Logan Express service with Massport and now the new SFO coaches that will debut in November. The growth comes as travelers embrace Landline's services. The company now offers 19 daily round trips between Northern Colorado Regional Airport (FNL) in Fort Collins, Colorado and Denver International Airport (DEN), a route that operates outside security and debuted with just four round trips in 2021. And, at BOS, what began as a three-month trial with Massport of postsecurity coaches from the Framingham terminal was extended through March 2027, less than 30 days after launch. Landline staff said in late June that buses frequently departed for BOS full, and the parking lot was at capacity. "Most of our customers are coming from their car," Sunde said of the company's recent expansion. Landline's new SFO-STS route may just be the beginning for the company in the Golden State. If all goes well, Sunde said Monterey Regional Airport (MRY) on the coast and Stockton Metropolitan Airport (SCK) in the Central Valley may be next for SFO connections. Modesto City-County Airport (MOD) and Sacramento International Airport (SMF) could come in the future. All of these potential future Landline routes from SFO are either current or former air routes. United operates up to four flights a day from SFO to both MRY and SMF, according to schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. SFO to STS operated until 2022, MOD until 2014 and SCK until 1993. Replacing flights with buses on the remaining routes could help alleviate SFO's notorious flight congestion, especially in bad weather. It could also offer travelers an alternative to driving. First, however, Landline is working with SFO to secure a more central gate in the terminal complex, Sunde said. Gate A3 is convenient for any airline in Terminal 1 — Alaska, American, Hawaiian and JetBlue — but not United in Terminal 3. "We're successful in markets when we convince people not to drive themselves," he said. "We think that the combination of an airside arrival, bag transfer to multiple major carriers and a comfortable seat with high-speed Wi-Fi is hard to beat." Related reading:

item.title: ‘A winning combination of culture and nature’: exploring Germany’s green heart by bus
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Itâs early morning in Erfurt, the capital of Germanyâs Thuringia region, and Domplatz is abuzz with local growers setting out crates of vegetables and flowers beneath the soaring medieval cathedral towers. This 14th- and 15th-century engineering wonder holds the Gloriosa, the worldâs largest medieval free-swinging bell, cast in 1497 and weighing 12 tonnes. Though the city and surrounding landscape are notably flat, its skyline is pierced by soaring church towers and steeples, the atmospheric old town hardly changed over the centuries. Thuringia â often called the âgreen heart of Germanyâ â lies in the centre of the country, between Hesse, Saxony and Bavaria. Itâs famous for its dense forests, intellectual heritage and hearty cuisine, and Iâm here for four days to explore using public transport. Leaving Frankfurt behind, my three-hour coach journey rolls through rising forested highlands before descending into the wide, agricultural basin that cradles Erfurt. After checking out Domplatzâs morning market, itâs just a short walk to one of the townâs other famous sights, the 120-metre-long KrÃ¤merbrÃ¼cke â a 14th-century bridge lined with colourful half-timbered houses. Erfurt was once at the crossroads of two major trade routes, and the wealth that built its impressive churches and merchantsâ houses came partly from waid, or woad, a plant cultivated in the surrounding fields and processed for its blue dye. I stroll past the craft shops (some still sell the dye) to Petersberg Citadel, one of the largest and best-preserved fortresses in Europe, with a maze of underground tunnels. This is also the city where the Protestant Reformation took root â Martin Luther studied here and was a monk in the Augustinian monastery (you can join a guided tour or even stay overnight). Dinner is in a suitably historic setting; Wirtshaus Christoffel, in the Haus zur weiÃen Lilie (House of the White Lily), dates back to the 12th century (the house-brewed beer and beef roulade with Thuringian dumplings are delicious). Next morning, I head to Egapark (a seven-minute bus ride or a 30-minute walk from town). Spread across 36 hectares (89 acres), it was created for the 1961 international horticultural exhibition. The old Cyriaksburg fortress houses the German Horticultural Museum, which traces the history of gardening, while displays range from landscapes of cacti and succulents to tropical planting. The city of Weimar, a 30-minute bus journey away, is next on my list. The birthplace of the artistic Bauhaus movement, and where Germanyâs first democratic constitution was adopted, itâs full of interesting historic sites and design gems. I visit the Bauhaus museum, with its ceramics, textiles, metalwork and painting, and wander around town, passing the former art school buildings that now house the Bauhaus-UniversitÃ¤t. The next morning, I swap culture for chilling and take another bus to Bad Langensalza, a spa town of 10 parks and themed gardens, 40 miles (64km) away. My guide, Markus Fromm, explains that people come here to âcure, to relax, to refreshâ. Sulphur springs were discovered here in 1811, and today, the Friederiken Therme is the townâs main thermal spa, offering natural sulphur, brine and drinking mineral waters, alongside indoor and outdoor pools, saunas and treatments. Traces of the older spa history remain around the town: at FriederikenschlÃ¶sschen, an 18th-century summer residence, a fountain still runs with sulphur water that has been used for healing since 1812. But itâs the townâs gardens that really win me over. I wander FriederikenschlÃ¶sschenâs restored baroque garden and visit the Klagetor, a gate tower dating from about 1365, where the old town gives way to the Japanese garden, Kofuku no Niwa (Garden of Happiness), with its koi ponds, clipped azaleas and sculpted pines. For nature on an even grander scale, I take a bus to Hainich national park, 10 minutes away (you can easily rent a bike/e-bike and follow cycling paths to get there too). Spanning 7,500 hectares, Hainich offers more than 75 miles of signposted walking trails through its beech forests, part of a Unesco world heritage site. The wider Hainich is Germanyâs largest unbroken deciduous woodland area. âParts of this landscape have been left entirely untouched for decades, abandoned to their own devices without a shred of human meddling,â says park director RÃ¼diger Biehl. Before hitting the trail, I stop at the parkâs restaurant, Forsthaus Thiemsburg, for a regional lunch â roast pork in black beer and Thuringian dumplings, washed down with a cold KÃ¶stritzer pilsner. Then, into the trees. Deep in the beeches, the sun sporadically breaks through the branches and the leaves crunch loudly under my boots. Up in the canopy, itâs mostly just the birds making noise â chaffinches and wood warblers chatter, interrupted by the occasional sharp rattle of a middle spotted woodpecker drilling into a trunk. The Baumkronenpfad, a wooden walkway through the treetops, rises to a 44-metre observation tower. Here, the canopy of an oak that is estimated to be 350 years old is almost at eye level. Itâs a spectacular view, but the forestâs real engine is down below. Deadwood is left to decay where it falls, providing habitat for rare wood-boring insects and endangered Bechsteinâs bats. Back in Erfurt that evening, I catch the final symphony concert of the season at Theaterplatz. Itâs a reminder of the winning combination of culture and nature that Iâve enjoyed over my four days in Thuringia. I had come looking for a less familiar corner of Germany and found a region that offers plenty of variety â and all accessible with a few short bus rides. The trip was provided by the German National Tourist Board. Dorint Hotel am Dom in Erfurt has doubles from Â£85. For journey planning, VMT has information on buses, trains and trams across central Thuringia, as well as a free app with live departure updates

item.title: A lakeside idyll: laid-back cycling and autumn hikes on Italy’s Lake Iseo
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Rust red and burnt sienna speckle the green mountain rising from Lake Iseo. Golden autumn sunlight shimmers on the water. Monte Isola, Italyâs largest lake island, is a peak of sheer cliffs and dense forest, dotted with old fishing hamlets and hillside villages, each as pretty as the terraced villas of Lake Como and Garda, but with far fewer visitors. I arrive at the small port town of Peschiera Maraglio â where striped wooden boats jut from the water like the gondolas of Venice â on a ferry from Sulzano, a five-minute hop across the water. âOnly three people on the island are allowed to own a car: the priest, the doctor and the mayor,â says Chiara, my tour guide from Brescia. Residents can zip up and down the steep island roads on mopeds, and a small fleet of van-sized buses trundle around throughout the day, but nearly all cars are forbidden and visitors have to explore on foot or bike. Even bikes are banned from boats at the weekend. Not that it matters: the harbour front is lined with bike rentals (from â¬4 an hour for a standard bike). Iâm normally a nervous cyclist, but car-free roads raise my confidence. Plus, most other visitors have the telltale front-wheel wobble of novice riders. This isnât the place for Lycra and personal bests; the smooth-as-silk, quiet roads are for slow pedalling, and neck swivelling to take in another gorgeous view of Lake Iseo. The circular lakeside route winds past olive groves tumbling to the shore. I thought Iâd need base layers and gloves this far into autumn, but Iâm in shorts and a T-shirt and already working up a sweat in 24C sunshine. I pedal through the lakeside hamlet of Sensole in the islandâs south-west and stop in Menzino, just along the shore. Thereâs a cafe-bar catering to cyclists, so I fuel up with an espresso con lake view. The view from the western side of the island is somewhat marred by a huge concrete factory on the mainland, so I keep my head down on the pedal to Siviano, the islandâs capital. The shambling streets are sleepy; the stacked skyline of orange, lemon and magnolia villas is punctuated by the looming facade of Santi Faustino e Giovita church and a medieval stone tower. Monte Isola has been inhabited since the Roman era. Venetian rule in the 15th and 16th centuries left the main towns resembling those on Garda and Como: hillside terraces of wooden-shuttered pastel villas. In the late 18th century, Monte Isola found its main industry: net making. At Retificio La Rete Srl, a small shop and net factory at Sivianoâs port, fishing nets have been handwoven for centuries, along with nets for basketball hoops, football goals, shopping bags and hammocks. At the northern tip of the island, I get the best views of Lake Iseoâs craggiest mountains. The south of the lake is chalk-white bell towers against gently undulating hills, draped in franciacorta vineyards. The north is where jagged peaks scrape the sky, plummeting to the emerald-green lake water. Just off the shore, a speck of an island (Isola di Loreto) is topped with a grand, castle-like building, which Chiara says is privately owned. A flotilla of kayakers from Marone make their way towards the private dock, slipping across the glass-still water. In Carzano, I pause to admire thepink-and-white facade of San Giovanni Battista church, before cycling along the more functional stretch of road along the eastern shore. The traffic-free spell is broken by an old Fiat Punto, apologetically crawling along the road. Maybe the driver is the doctor or priest. I complete my circle back in Peschiera Maraglio, where a late lunch of lake fish awaits at La Foresta restaurant. To begin, pickled tench so vinegary it makes my mouth water and a chub carpaccio that tastes like fresh lake water; followed by the island staple of dried, salted sardinas on grilled polenta. âSardina is not a sardine; itâs actually a type of shad fish,â Chiara explains. âIn the middle ages, when Monte Isola had to pay tax to Venice, they didnât understand how money worked, so they paid in salted sardinas instead.â As the last ferries leave for the evening, it feels as if I have Peschiera Maraglio to myself. Accommodation is private holiday apartments or restaurants with rooms. At Decio, a modern bistro dominates the ground floor, with a handful of sleek bedrooms above. The glass front shows off an uninterrupted lake view and the room is bathed in orange light at sunset. I spend the evening perched on a stool outside LâIsola dei Sapori, a no-frills alfresco spot where sparkling franciacorta wine is perfectly chilled, and snacks of local salami, olives and fish dishes combine for a light dinner. The next day, I forgo my bike and lace up my hiking boots. The steep trail to the top of the island begins with the enclosed cobbled streets of Peschiera Maraglio and wends into thick chestnut forest. I pocket a particularly beefy conker, unable to resist the childhood urge for a blinder. My legs start to burn against the gradient â the trail is 450 metres of climbing. Rocks and twisting roots burst through the forest path and thereâs a sheer drop to one side, but the glimpses of Lake Iseo between the trees are worth every wheeze. After an hour, the trees thin out and I emerge at Santuario della Madonna della Ceriola. The striking white sanctuary was built in the 13th century, on the remains of a pagan temple and early Christian chapels. A vast golden altar and detailed frescoes adorn the interior, but itâs the panoramic view outside that really makes the hike worthwhile. The ferry to Sulzano is a toy boat, leaving a white tail of wake. From up high, I see that autumn colours are already creeping into the forest. I wipe the sweat from my eyes. This view is only going to get prettier as the season evolves, and the prize conkers are yet to fall. The trip was arranged by Visit Brescia. Bike rental starts at â¬4 an hour. The ferry from Sulzano to Monte Isola is â¬2.60 each way. Trains run from Brescia to Sulzano from â¬4.10. Rooms at Decio start at â¬90 B&B

item.title: The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses Trevor Warmedahl has spent years documenting rare and traditional cheesemaking methods, and believes that "cheese is an edible manifestation of a place". Trevor Warmedahl was working as a commercial cheesemaker in Seattle when he realised he was using milk that came from animals he never saw. So, he quit his job and set off on what has become a global odyssey to discover places that still make cheese the old-fashioned way. In 2019 he arrived in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and lived alone in a yurt with a dog as his companion. He soon discovered that dairy was sacred there: the women flicked milk into the air before cheesemaking, a gesture of respect called a milk libation. He visited homes where whey bubbled over central hearths and fresh, unripened byaslag cheese covered tables. After hiking to shrines, he noticed people offered dairy products as a symbol of purity. As summer unfolded and city-dwellers migrated to the Mongolian steppe to farm, Warmedahl itched to join. He jumped on a Soviet-era coal-powered sleeper train for a rickety overnight ride across the Gobi Desert. On the journey back to Ulaanbaatar, he met a local who invited him to stay with her herder family on the Zavkhan grassland. Warmedahl spent that summer waking before dawn to milk yaks, chasing livestock up the valley on horses, listening to shepherds' folk songs at sunset and cooking milk into dehydrated, sweet-and-sour curds called aaruul. The experience inspired him to seek out other places preserving rare cheesemaking traditions before they disappeared. During the past six years, Warmedahl has hitched, hiked and driven through more than 20 countries, documenting traditional cheesemaking and pastoral lifestyles, and offering workshops on natural dairy processing. After recently completing a 193km (120-mile) cheese trek across the Peaks of the Balkans Trail, he shared with the BBC what cheesemaking reveals about a place. Ancestral cheeses in Georgia have no analogues – I call them "fossil cheeses" because they were almost lost but are making a comeback as part of a broader post-Soviet cultural revival. My pinnacle moment happened in Tusheti, a mountain region bordering Russia near the tourist village of Omalo. I showed up with vague directions to the shepherds' summer camp, which was deep in the valley. That's a theme: the cheeses I find are always far out, made by hermit types sticking to the old ways out of sheer stubbornness. It was drop-dead gorgeous, just me and my backpack. The valley ends on an abrupt cliff, with deteriorating medieval stone towers. Shepherds build their camps from the decay. I saw how these guys milked sheep by hand with wooden pails, rustic-style. It's a feta-like cheese called Tushuri guda, aged in inside-out sheepskins. At the end of the season, I walked about 130km (81 miles) back down the valley with them and 300 sheep. The herd has done this for generations – they know where to go. The shepherds just coordinated, and it created this crazy lawless feeling with dogs barking and me, chasing stray sheep down ravines. At night we'd build a campfire and drink, and even with the language barrier, we'd relate through food. Sometimes language isn't needed. In cheesemaking, if two hearts want to connect, they'll find a way. How is cheese and cheesemaking a reflection of a community's history and culture? Cheese is a sensory experience and embodies larger ideas about how we live. It represents how meaningful human cultures can be. At its best, cheese reflects this complex relationship between humans, landscapes, microbial life and livestock at a time [when] we've become so separate from how food is made. And the cultural element holds the constellation together. The cheeses I highlight represent an older mentality, with a sense of stewardship over the places we live and farm. So, a little bit more of the wildness of nature slips into the product. [Cheese is] an edible manifestation of place, of cultural history transformed into delicious food. Why is cheesemaking especially important today? The diversity and range of cheese is infinite. When animals eat, they transform grass and entire landscapes into milk that becomes cheese, and animals can graze [almost] anywhere. So, it's a lifestyle that can move in response to climate uncertainty and desertification – real challenges today. The cheeses I focus on – natural farmstead cheeses [made exclusively with milk from a farmer's own animals] – reflect deep, ethical relationships between people and livestock and highlight the incredible diversity of heritage livestock. With industrialisation, that diversity is vanishing at an alarming rate. So pastoral cheesemaking strikes me as profoundly sustainable. What can so-called "exotic cheeses" that challenge us reveal about a place? There's this greyish-brown cheese from Norway, gammelost, [covered in] moulds like fruit rot. It tastes like a musty cellar with bold, mouth-numbing spiciness. It wasn't for me. But deliciousness is cultural. It's taught. So, I always say: don't try something once, try it 10 times. Uncomfortable foods open doors. But be sure to eat them because you're interested in the culture, not because they're freaky to you. One of the easiest ways to express interest in a culture is to say: feed me what you eat. When people realise you're genuine, the relationship deepens and you begin to understand their history through food. Funky cheeses become cultural emblems because of how obscure and special they are. You set out on your global cheese journey without a real plan. What did this approach add to your experience? Back then [in 2019], I was hopping on a whim from one volunteer gig to the next, drawn to remote places where people worked to protect and revitalise traditional cheeses. Workaway on farms, or staying for a while at guesthouses where cheese is made, are still amazing ways to go beyond tourism to see how people really live. Cheese gives you access to a global community, like at [the Slow Food Cheese Festival in] Bra, Italy. But anything you can do to find that deeper experience – food, handicrafts – is worth it, even if you can't always plan in advance. If your heart is in the right place and you jump fully into adventure when it calls, the details will almost always work themselves out. What advice would you give fellow travellers about how to best experience unique cheeses abroad? Find the cheese shop or cheesemonger that has the most local tilt and ask them which cheesemakers you can and should visit. Organising it yourself is cheaper. But there are also paid tours where you can experience a range of cheeses in a short period and really get to know a place. Just make sure that the cost actually supports local producers – that's what I call responsible "lacto-culinary" tourism. How can other travellers seek out responsible agrotourism experiences? Look for local cheesemakers and guides. It's also important to not expect farmers to sanitise things. It's normal to go to a farm and see broken-down equipment and mud. When we romanticise tradition, it encourages locals to put themselves in a museum. But tools [and] tradition have always evolved. More like this: We need to be open to the fact that it's not all grandmas spinning wool on wheels outside stone cottages. Then it becomes kind of a show, and we're pushing farmers to become something they're not for tourists. What places have exciting, overlooked, or under-the-radar cheeses? Where are you keen to travel next? Hands down, Turkey. It's a universe of cheese that doesn't get enough attention. Tulum peyniri is emblematic of pastoral lifestyles and the extreme sacrifice at the root of dairying and – I'd argue – life. That's because it's aged mainly in furry goatskins, so it looks insane because it can take on animal shapes. Somehow, I didn't think it would be delicious. How good can goatskin-aged cheese be, right? It was phenomenal. I was blown away by deep flavours and textures I'd never seen in cheese before. Turkish cheese needs to be talked about alongside Western Europe. More remote places have just as many fascinating cheeses to preserve and celebrate. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. If you liked this story, – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Tipping on a cruise: What to know about cruise ship gratuities
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Tipping on a cruise: What to know about cruise ship gratuities How much should you tip on a cruise? It's a question that trips up many first-time cruisers because some cruise lines tack daily service fees onto passenger bills. However, many travelers still hand out additional cash gratuities, either as a matter of course or to recognize exemplary service. The extra cost of the automatic gratuity charges can be a shock to first-timers. On some lines, these charges run as high as $25 per day. And unlike the typical service or resort fee at a land resort, automatic gratuity charges on cruise ships are per person, not per room. On some big lines, such as Royal Caribbean, it's not uncommon for a family of four staying in a single cabin to see more than $70 a day in service fees added to their bills. On a typical seven-night cruise, that's around $500 in fees. And that's before you add in any additional tips you wish to give to your room service provider or favorite bartender or automatic gratuities tacked on to bar, restaurant and spa bills. Still, not all lines have service fees that high, and some don't charge them at all. And, in many cases, the service charges are adjustable. Tipping on a cruise does not have to be complicated, but you need to understand the big picture to budget for your vacation appropriately. Read on to learn all about cruise ship tipping culture and how much you'll need to tip on your next cruise, based on which cruise line you're sailing. Tipping on a cruise ship: The big picture Most of the largest cruise lines automatically add some type of service or gratuity fee onto passenger bills. Lines with such automatic charges include both giants of the cruise business, Royal Caribbean and Carnival Cruise Line, as well as the next three largest lines: MSC Cruises, Norwegian Cruise Line and Princess Cruises. That said, the total number of lines with a service fee has been shrinking over the years. Many smaller and higher-end cruise operators are folding tips and gratuities into their base fares. For example, Oceania Cruises eliminated its automatic gratuity fee in 2025 and now includes gratuities paid to shipboard staff in its base fare. Other lines that now cover gratuities in their fares include Azamara, Ponant Explorations, Explora Journeys, Regent Seven Seas Cruises, Scenic Luxury Cruises & Tours, Seabourn, SeaDream Yacht Club, Silversea Cruises and Virgin Voyages. For lines that do have them, service and gratuity charges are touted as a convenient alternative to cash tipping on cruise ships — something that was once common. One of the biggest misconceptions about cruise gratuities is that they go only to the cabin steward or dining room waiter you see every day. In reality, the money collected is pooled and shared among a wide range of crew members. Depending on the cruise line, this can include cabin attendants, dining room servers, assistant waiters, housekeeping staff and other behind-the-scenes workers who help keep the ship running. In that sense, the current system is more equitable than the old cash-tipping system, which favored certain workers. Still, some critics see the charges as a sneaky way for cruise lines to make their fares appear lower than they really are. In this line of thinking, lines with these charges are essentially breaking out a good chunk of onboard labor costs as a separate line item on your bill. Exactly how gratuity pools are distributed varies by line, and cruise operators generally don't disclose detailed formulas. At many lines, you can pay your service charges before sailing (at the same time you pay your cruise fare). Alternatively, you can have the charges added to your room bill on board. The big advantage to paying cruise tips in advance is that you lock in the current rate. If your line raises the rate between the time you pay and the time you sail, you won't pay more. Some people also like to pay their service charges in advance for budgeting purposes. It'll be one less thing on your final bill at the end of the cruise. If you prefer to pay for tips once you're on board your cruise, you'll generally find that the gratuities automatically appear on your bill. You don't have to do anything. You are also not expected to leave additional cruise tips for your room attendant or waiters. That's the whole point of the service charge. Similarly, if you're on a higher-end ship that lists gratuities as being included in the fare, that means just what it says. You don't have to tip on these cruises because the line is already paying gratuities to the staff on your behalf. Additional cash gifts are not expected. Still, some people do leave a little extra for crew members who go above and beyond. Others tip their room service or waitstaff at their favorite bar, either early on (in hopes of better service) or at the end (to thank them for enhancing the vacation experience). How much to tip extra on a cruise is entirely up to you because it is not required. If you want to, you can often adjust the charges (up or down) at the guest relations desk on board. If you are adjusting a gratuity charge downward, expect to be asked about the reasons behind the adjustment. The guest relations staff will want to know if you've experienced particular service issues. Some cruise operators make it relatively easy to adjust gratuities, while others place restrictions on reductions or removals. If you prepaid gratuities before your cruise, you may have fewer options for changing the amount once you're on board. Automatic gratuities generally are distributed among a broad range of crew members, including some workers whom passengers rarely encounter. For that reason, many experienced cruisers view gratuity adjustments as something to reserve for situations involving genuine service issues rather than as a routine way to lower vacation costs. If you dislike tipping on cruise ships but can't afford to sail on an all-inclusive line, look for promotions when cruise lines with service charges throw in free gratuities as a booking incentive. Additionally, several major lines in the past couple of years have begun offering bundle pricing to customers who pay for cruise tips, Wi-Fi charges and an onboard drink package all at once in advance of sailing, potentially at a discount. Princess, for example, has added a Princess Plus plan as a booking option. It gives passengers prepaid gratuities (which Princess calls "crew appreciation" fees), a single-device Wi-Fi plan and a basic beverage package for a single bundled price of $65 per person, per day (or $70 per person, per day on Sphere Class ships like Sun Princess and Star Princess) if you book it in advance of sailing. Princess also has an upgraded Princess Premier bundle option that includes gratuities with even more items, such as unlimited dining at specialty restaurants, for a single price of $100 per person, per day if you book it in advance of sailing. Don't worry: When lines offer such deals, it doesn't mean the crew will receive fewer tips the week you cruise. The lines offering these deals say they'll pay the crew a standard gratuity on your behalf. Daily service charges are not the only cruise tips you will pay on board. Many cruise lines will tack an automatic gratuity charge onto the bill for extra-fee drinks, restaurant meals and spa treatments. The included tip amount varies by cruise line but is typically 15% to 20% of the bill. Be warned that the receipt often includes a line for an additional gratuity, even when one is automatically added. This can trick many cruisers into tipping twice. Never feel pressured to add an extra tip when you've already paid one. Note that if you purchase a dining or beverage package, most cruise lines will charge you gratuities based on a percentage of the package price. If you get one of these packages for "free" as a booking perk, you might still be required to pay the gratuities on the theoretical value of this perk. Cruisers should also bring cash to tip the porters who bring their bags onto the ship ($2 per bag is standard these days), as well as tour guides in port ($5 to $10 per person for half-day tours, $10 to $20 for full-day excursions and $2 for nonguide drivers). Piano bar regulars know that a cash tip increases the pianist's likelihood of choosing and performing their song request. When tipping in cash, stick with small bills. Singles, fives and tens are easiest for crew members to use and are widely accepted even on cruises that visit non-U.S. ports. Some cruisers tip their room steward or favorite bartender early in the sailing, hoping to get better service throughout the trip. Others wait until the end to reward good service. Either approach is fine. Guest services can usually provide an envelope if you don't have one handy. How much should you tip on each cruise line? If you're wondering how much you should tip on the specific cruise line you're considering or have already booked, below is a line-by-line look at policies of automatic gratuity charges (also called service charges or crew appreciation charges at some lines). The rates listed are per person, per day. They were accurate as of the publishing of this story. Remember that all additional tipping is at your discretion. Any amount is fine and will be appreciated by the hard-working crew. - Automatic gratuity charge: None. - Details: Gratuities for the crew are included in the fare. One area of exception is an 18% gratuity added to bills for spa and salon services. - Automatic gratuity charge: $17 to $19 per person, per day. - Details: Carnival Cruise Line's recommended daily gratuities are $17 USD per person, per day for standard cabins and $19 per person, per day for suite accommodations. Children under the age of 2 are exempt from these charges. A 20% service charge is added to beverage purchases and to specialty dining reservation fees, including Chef's Table and Bonsai Teppanyaki, as well as à la carte charges at Bonsai Sushi, Emeril's Bistro, Guy's Pig & Anchor Smokehouse | Brewhouse, and Seafood Shack. Carnival also adds a 20% service charge to Steakhouse selections and Bonsai Sushi boats ordered from the Main Dining Room dinner menu, Emeril's Bistro selections, and fresh-pressed juices ordered on Seaday Brunch and breakfast menus. - Automatic gratuity charge: $19.50 to $24.50 per person, per day. - Details: Passengers in most cabins pay $19.50. Passengers in Concierge Class and AquaClass cabins pay a higher rate of $20.50. Passengers in The Retreat suites pay $24.50. Note that Celebrity now charges these fees even for passengers who book the line's higher-priced All Included fares. Until recently, these fares included gratuity charges. Additionally, a 20% gratuity is added to beverage packages, specialty dining and dining packages and when a passenger orders drinks or purchases a minibar item. A 20% gratuity will also be added for spa and salon services. - Details: Gratuities for crew and bar staff are included in the fare. - Automatic gratuity charge: $18 to $19 per person, per day. - Details: Passengers in most cabins pay $18. Passengers in Grill Class suites pay $19. Additionally, an 18% gratuity is added to bar, wine and salon bills. - Details: While Disney doesn't automatically add a gratuity charge, it suggests that passengers staying in most cabins pay $16 per day in total when tipping dining staff and room attendants. The suggested amount for passengers staying in concierge cabins and suites is $27.25. Passengers can prepay the amount in advance or on board. Also, an 18% gratuity is added to bar, beverage, wine and deck service bills and to spa service bills. - Automatic gratuity charge: $18 to $20 per person, per day. - Details: Passengers in most cabins pay $18 for what the line now calls a crew appreciation charge. Passengers staying in suites pay $20. Additionally, a 20% gratuity is added to bar bills and dining room wine purchases and an 18% gratuity to spa and salon services. - Details: Gratuities are included in the fare for passengers on National Geographic Explorer, National Geographic Endurance, National Geographic Resolution and National Geographic Orion. On other ships, gratuities are at the passenger's discretion. - Automatic gratuity charge: About $14.10 (12 euros) to $16 (around 15 euros). - Details: Gratuity charges are $17 on voyages to and from the U.S., except for sailings priced in euros, which have a gratuity charge of 12 euros ($14.10 at current exchange rates). Sailings in Europe also include a 12-euro gratuity charge. Sailings around South America are the highest at $19, while sailings to South Africa are $17. Gratuities for children between 2 and 11 are half the adult rate on most cruises. Gratuities are not charged for children younger than 2. - Automatic service charge: $20 to $25 per person, per day. - Details: Passengers in most cabins pay $20. Those in suites or The Haven pay $25. Passengers younger than 3 are exempt from the charges. Additionally, a 20% gratuity is added to bills at bars, extra-charge specialty restaurants and ship spas. Cruises to Hawaii will also pay a 4.275% prepaid service charge called a general excise tax. - Details: As of January 2025, passengers on Oceania ships no longer have to pay automatic gratuity fees. Gratuity fees of up to $25 per person, per day have been folded into a new "Your World Included" bundle of extra-charge items that all passengers will get for free. - Details: Gratuities are included in the fare. - Details: Gratuities are included in the fare. However, passengers can give more at their discretion; Ponant recommends 10 to 12 euros (about $12 to $14) per passenger, per day. - Details: Princess includes gratuities in the fare for all passengers who purchase one of its inclusive Princess Plus or Princess Premier packages. For passengers not sailing on a Princess Plus or Princess Premier fare, Princess adds an automatic service gratuity of $18 to $20 per person, per day to final bills, depending on your cabin category. Also, a 20% gratuity is added to bills at bars, specialty dining, dining room wine accounts and spas. - Details: Gratuities are included in the fare, except for the spa, which adds an 18% gratuity. - Automatic gratuity charge: $18.50 to $21 per person, per day. - Details: Passengers staying in most cabins, including junior suites, pay $18.50 per day. Passengers in higher-level suites pay $21. Additionally, an 18% gratuity is added to bills at bars, minibars, room service and specialty dining and 20% at salons and spas. - Details: Gratuities are included in the fare, except for beauty salon services and spa treatments. - Details: The line recommends that passengers pay 8 euros (about $9 at current exchange rates) per day in gratuities, but the payment is at the passenger's discretion. A 15% gratuity is added for bar purchases. - Details: UnCruise recommends that passengers pay $45 per person, per day in gratuities, but the payment is at the passenger's discretion. - Automatic gratuity charge: $20 per person, per day. - Details: Passengers pay a $20 gratuity for all cabin types. Also, a 15% gratuity is added to bar bills. - Automatic gratuity charge: $22 per person, per day - Details: As of October 2025, passengers on Virgin ships will need to pay $22 in gratuities for all cabin types. All other gratuities are included in the fare. - Automatic gratuity charge: $16 per person, per day. - Details: Passengers pay a "hotel service charge" of $16 for all cabin types. Additionally, an 18% gratuity is added to bar, beverage, wine and deck service bills. Alternatively, Windstar cruisers can upgrade their bookings with an all-in package that includes unlimited beverages, Wi-Fi and the hotel service charge for $99 per person, per day. item.title: Exclusive: Silicon Valley is getting a new high-tech hotel with AI assistants and a rooftop beehive
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Exclusive: Silicon Valley is getting a new high-tech hotel with AI assistants and a rooftop beehive Sunnyvale, California — the beating heart of Silicon Valley — is getting a new social-forward hotel that's sure to be one of the tech hub's new social centers. M Social Hotel Sunnyvale, part of Millennium Hotels and Resorts, is now taking reservations for stays in December forward. "M Social Hotel Sunnyvale brings together the energy of Silicon Valley and the ease of California living," Jakub Skyvara, the hotel's general manager, told TPG. Once open, the hotel will offer 263 guest rooms and suites with a modern aesthetic and playful touches, providing a "residential counterbalance" to "support both productivity and relaxation for business travelers, extended stays, and leisure guests alike," according to a statement about the property. The hotel will also offer plenty of public areas for getting work done, making new connections or simply kicking back and taking it easy. "Guests can gather over live-fire cooking and shareable dishes at Beast & Butterflies, linger in our courtyard or come together for an event in the Quantum Ballroom, with its dramatic LED video wall," Skyvara told TPG. At Beast & Butterflies, modern Californian fare is on the menu, including ingredients from local farms and partnerships with nearby wineries and breweries. Or if you'd rather just grab a drink and lounge, ctrl+B(ar) serves up coffee, cocktails and those same local beverages in a connected, social setting. This M Social Hotel is all about social connections, yes, but it's also big on tech connections and has a "connected smart-building ecosystem designed to enhance convenience, efficiency, and sustainability," according to the statement. That means mobile room keys, self-service check-in kiosks, robotic service assistants and even an in-room artificial intelligence assistant. "Our philosophy is simple," Skyvara said, "technology should remove friction; people should create memories. We want the stay to feel effortless and the welcome to feel personal, whether you're checking in for a week or joining us for dinner." The property also offers an abundance of conference, meeting and event spaces, perfect for groups looking to get together in the world's most important tech hub. "There's an international outlook here, alongside a strong local sense of community," Skyvara said about Sunnyvale, who suggests that spending time outside, especially on a bike, is a great way to explore the city "beyond the company campuses." But that's not all: "There's also a detail I love: our rooftop beehive. In a place known for technology, it's a reminder that nature and connection have a place here, too." For points and miles enthusiasts, the free MyMillennium loyalty program allows guests to earn and burn points for stays, dining credits and more. M Social Hotel Sunnyvale joins a growing number of locations, including Singapore, Paris, multiple New York locations and more. "Expanding the brand's global collection, M Social Hotel Sunnyvale marks M Social's first presence on the West Coast, carrying its distinctive spirit to the heart of Silicon Valley," Skyvara said. M Social Hotel Sunnyvale opens in mid-December with cash rates starting as low as $239 per night. Related reading:

item.title: A cruisetour vs. a cruise-only sailing in Alaska — which is best for you?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
A cruisetour vs. a cruise-only sailing in Alaska — which is best for you? The state of Alaska is vast: It encompasses 365 million acres and is more than twice the size of Texas. With just 17,000 miles of public roads, much of Alaska is remote and reachable only by ship or plane, making a cruise one of the best and easiest ways to visit The Great Land. However, if you want to explore more of the state's extraordinary beauty, including its rugged wilderness areas such as Denali National Park & Preserve or Fairbanks, the city known as the "Golden Heart of Alaska," consider a cruisetour, a combined sea-and-land vacation. The advantages of cruise-only itineraries There are several reasons a cruise-only trip may be the right fit for you. Most Alaska cruises are shorter than cruisetours, typically lasting seven nights. If you add one additional night in town before the cruise (as a buffer should travel plans go awry), you can still make the trip in just a little more than a week. Additionally, many ships sail round-trip from major cities like Seattle or Vancouver, British Columbia, so airfare and transfers should be easier, and less expensive, to book since you'll be arriving and departing from the same place. A cruise-only itinerary will also be the least expensive option since you can find seven-night Alaska voyages priced as low as $500 to $600 per person, double occupancy. (Cruise fares depend on several factors, including the cruise line, the ship's age, the stateroom category and location, what's included in the fare, the itinerary and the sailing date.) Another plus is that you'll only need to pack and unpack once if you're only taking a cruise. You won't have to haul your luggage between hotels and other modes of transportation, such as buses, trains and planes. If you're thinking a cruise-only vacation is right for you, there are a few popular seven-night Alaska cruise routes that you can take to visit the south-central region of Alaska. Norwegian Cruise Line's "7-Day Alaska Round-trip Seattle: Juneau, Ketchikan & Victoria" itinerary includes stops in the coastal towns of Juneau, Skagway and Ketchikan (Ward Cove) in Alaska; Victoria, British Columbia; and scenic cruising in magical Glacier Bay National Park & Preserve. A number of other lines also offer Seattle departures, including Princess Cruises, Holland America Line, Cunard Line, MSC Cruises, Royal Caribbean International and Virgin Voyages. A seven-night, round-trip "7-Night Alaska Dawes Glacier" voyage with Celebrity Cruises from Vancouver traverses the scenic Inside Passage and the Endicott Arm fjord (home to Dawes Glacier). It calls on the ports of Icy Strait Point, Skagway, Juneau and Ketchikan in Alaska. Several other lines offer round-trip itineraries from Vancouver, including Princess Cruises, Holland America Line, Azamara Cruises and Disney Cruise Line. You can also book a weeklong, one-way voyage, either heading southbound or northbound along the coast. Several larger and smaller lines offer such itineraries. If you prefer a larger ship, Royal Caribbean offers sailings from either Seward, Alaska, or Vancouver that include two days of scenic cruising in Hubbard Glacier and the Inside Passage, as well as visits to the ports of Juneau, Skagway, Icy Strait Point and Ketchikan. For a smaller luxury ship, Regent Seven Seas Cruises offers one-way sailings from Whittier, Alaska, to Vancouver (or the reverse itinerary). These voyages vary depending on the dates, with some cruising the Hubbard Glacier and the Inside Passage, making calls on Icy Strait Point (Hoonah), Juneau, Skagway and the small town of Klawock in Alaska. Longer cruise-only voyages, some with lesser-known ports Since you've traveled so far to visit Alaska, you might want to book a longer voyage to see more of this great state. Extended itineraries, especially on smaller and expedition-style ships, often call on remote and lesser-visited destinations. Silversea's 14-day, round-trip sailing from Vancouver includes stops in some of the more familiar Alaska port towns, such as Ketchikan, , Skagway, Sitka, Seward (Anchorage) and Juneau, as well as less frequented Valdez, Haines and Klawock. You'll also find voyages with a few lines that stop in the small towns of Wrangell on the Inside Passage (this will be a stop on Silversea's 10-night cruise beginning July 5, 2027) and Homer on the Kenai Peninsula. If you're interested in a more immersive Alaska experience — and a sailing on a much smaller ship (approximately 36 to 86 guests) — consider booking your bucket-list trip with UnCruise Adventures. The company offers unique itineraries in wilderness areas, featuring wildlife viewing and active exploration in skiffs and kayaks right from the ship. Its sailings typically are seven-nights or longer. National Geographic-Lindblad Expeditions also features smaller ships, immersive itineraries, active exploration and lesser-known destinations such as Baranof or Chichagof Island in Alaska and Prince Rupert in British Columbia. For a small ship option that's not expedition-style, American Cruise Lines offers eight- to 15-night cruise-only itineraries that also include unique ports of call, such as Petersburg and Metlakatla in Alaska. From the town of Petersburg, you can take a jet boat tour to see LeConte Glacier. And in Metlakatla, located on the Annette Islands, visit a museum to learn about the Tsimshian people who comprise the only Indian Reserve in Alaska. Their ships in Alaska accommodate between 130 and 170 guests. While prices are typically higher for longer voyages (especially on smaller luxury and expedition ships), you can find some base fares under $1,000 per person (double occupancy) for 10-night sailings with a few of the larger cruise lines. These longer Alaska voyages are ideal for travelers who are retired or semi-retired, work remotely or have extended vacation time. Cruisetours — exploring Alaska by sea and ashore For the ultimate vacation to Alaska, consider a cruisetour. A combined sea-and-land vacation booked as a single trip, a cruisetour offers the best of both experiences: sailing along Alaska's picturesque coastline and exploring its boundless wilderness in the interior. Many large cruise lines offer cruisetours, including Holland America, Princess, Norwegian, Celebrity and Royal Caribbean, as well as smaller lines like Azamara Cruises and American Cruise Lines. Others, such as Oceania Cruises and Silversea, offer cruise extensions with fully escorted precruise or postcruise land tours. These add-on extensions may include a visit to Denali, a rail journey through the Canadian Rockies aboard the Rocky Mountaineer or two nights in Anchorage, where you can fly into a remote location for a guided bear-viewing encounter. However, they're not complete package programs like the cruisetours. What's included with a cruisetour? Depending on the itinerary, your cruise may be at the beginning or end of the trip, with the rest of the time spent ashore. There are many variables and options with cruisetours. Most of them begin or end with a seven-night cruise, followed by several days or a week or longer traveling between hotels and destinations, with various tours and sightseeing options along the way. Some of the land portions are escorted, while others can be done on your own. These trips can last as long as 19 days, and they typically include transportation by deluxe motorcoach and a glass-domed railroad car with the Alaska Railroad. Some land tours may also include flights. Hotels and travel between destinations are usually included in the price. However, meals and some featured land excursions — such as an Arctic air adventure or northern lights viewing tour from Fairbanks — will be an additional cost. One example of a cruisetour that you can take with two weeks of time, Princess' 13-day "Denali Explorer" cruisetour from Vancouver to Fairbanks. After the cruise, you disembark in Whittier and spend an evening in Anchorage before boarding the railcar for the Direct-to-the-Wilderness service for a two-night stay at the Mount McKinley Princess Wilderness Lodge, followed by two nights at the Denali Princess Wilderness Lodge. Both properties are just outside the entrance to Denali. While there, you can visit the park with a tour in search of Denali's "Big Five": brown (or grizzly) bears, moose, wolves, Dall sheep and caribou. Other optional excursions include a sled dog experience, a flightseeing or helicopter tour, fly-fishing for Arctic grayling and an evening covered wagon ride complete with an Alaskan feast. The last stop on your Alaska adventure is Fairbanks, where you'll have an included tour on the Chena River aboard a sternwheeler steamboat, then pan for gold and enjoy a hearty miner's lunch at Gold Dredge 8. You'll also find cruisetours with Princess that include overnight stays at their Copper River Princess Wilderness Lodge. This lodge offers access to remote Wrangell—St. Elias National Park & Preserve (the largest national park in the U.S.) and the Kenai Princess Wilderness Lodge, the gateway to adventures in Kenai Fjords National Park. Norwegian offers a "12-day Denali Alyeska — Southbound Cruise Tour," which features a five-day land portion before the seven-night cruise. This trip begins in Anchorage and includes the Alaska Railroad domed railcar to Denali and a motorcoach ride to Girdwood, home to the beautiful Alyeska Resort, nestled at the foot of the Chugach Mountains. After an overnight in Girdwood, you'll head to Whittier to begin your cruise. Boutique line, Azamara Cruises' 14-night "Alaska Explorer Cruisetour: Denali, Talkeetna, Riverboat & Rail," features a 10-night itinerary departing from Vancouver, followed by a 4-night land tour that begins in Whittier and ends in Fairbanks. Guests onboard for the exciting adventure will visit the Alaska Native Heritage Center in Anchorage, explore Denali National Park, take a jet boat tour in Talkeetna and board a Deluxe Domed Railcar for the journey from Denali to Fairbanks. Cruisetours to Alaska are once-in-a-lifetime vacations for many travelers, with prices typically higher than cruise-only fares. However, you can find lower prices in the off- and shoulder seasons, as well as online deals and promotions, starting at less than $1,500 per person, double occupancy. The nearly month-long ultimate Alaska cruise If you want to head as far north as Nome, Alaska, then cross the Arctic Circle and visit Kodiak Island — home to the world's second-largest bears (next to polar bears) — and do it all while on a ship (no land portion included), book the "28-day Legendary Alaska Arctic Circle Solstice" cruise with Holland America. This bucket-list trip sets sail round-trip from Seattle and includes many days of scenic cruising, 12 ports of call and the smaller towns of Valdez, Haines, Wrangell and Dutch Harbor in Alaska's Aleutian Islands.

item.title: The perfect coastal New England road trip itinerary — and how to earn Hilton Honors points at every stop along the way
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The perfect coastal New England road trip itinerary — and how to earn Hilton Honors points at every stop along the way Some of my favorite books are set along the New England coast in Boston brownstones and small Maine harbor towns, but I've never actually been there myself. Living in Florida, I didn't realize how doable this road trip is. Boston to Portsmouth is about an hour by car, with another hour to Portland, Maine. So my husband and I packed up our bags and headed out to the Northeast to explore lighthouses, historical sites, local bookstores and of course, lobster rolls. But here's the thing about me: I am always thinking one trip ahead. Even when I'm planning one vacation, I'm always thinking of ways to save toward the next one. That's where the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card comes in. It turns every stop, snack, gas fill-up, meal and souvenir into Hilton Honors™ points for my next dream trip — all for a $150 annual fee (see rates and fees). And right now, new Surpass cardmembers can earn 130,000 Hilton Honors Bonus Points, plus a Free Night Reward after spending $3,000 in purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. Terms apply. Here's how to plan a New England coastal road trip, with tips on how to use the Surpass Card to earn along the way. TPG editor road trip tip: Use the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card to plan and earn Gas, snacks and quick lunch detours also add up: the Surpass card earns 6 points per dollar at U.S. restaurants, U.S. supermarkets and U.S. gas stations, to really make it worth your while on a road trip. The Surpass card includes complimentary National Car Rental® Emerald Club Executive® Status (enrollment in the National Car Rental Emerald Club through your American Express online account required to access Executive status, terms apply), so you can skip the counter when you land. When my flight arrived at Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), I went straight to the Executive area in the parking garage to choose my preferred vehicle. Surpass card editor tip: Automatic Hilton Honors Gold status gives you space-available room upgrades at select properties, daily food and beverage credits at select brands in the U.S. or complimentary continental breakfast at select brands outside of the U.S., an 80% bonus on base points earned during stays, and the fifth night free on standard room stays booked entirely with points. Tucked between downtown and Boston's historic North End, I stayed at Canopy by Hilton Boston Downtown, within walking distance of Faneuil Hall, Quincy Market and TD Garden. The hotel offers complimentary Canopy Bikes for registered guests to easily explore the city, and it's also steps from the T, Boston's subway system, to reach neighborhoods from Beacon Hill to Fenway Park. In general, there are plenty of Hilton properties across budgets to choose from in Boston based on your itinerary and budget, but a few other TPG-recommended properties include: - Pennyweight Hotel Boston, Curio Collection by Hilton While visiting the historic coastal town of Portsmouth, you'll find lots of smaller properties to stay at. I made the Hilton Garden Inn Downtown Portsmouth my home base. Its Market Square location puts shops, restaurants, the waterfront and local galleries all within easy walking distance without overthinking the logistics. Nearby, Hampton Inn & Suites Portsmouth Downtown is another great option, offering a complimentary hot breakfast buffet daily before you set out on any excursions. The Longfellow Hotel is one of Portland's newer properties — an SLH Hotel with 48 boutique rooms. The hotel was designed with pared-back minimalism, custom furniture, even sleep-optimized beds and Loftie alarm clocks. The on-site Astraea Wellness Spa and gym make it easy to reset after several adventure-packed days on the road. Longfellow also offers amenities such as complimentary bicycles and casual dining at the Twinflower Café and the lobby bar, Five of Clubs. You can also find a second SLH property in Portland: The Francis, a restored 1881 Victorian mansion with 15 boutique-style rooms featuring original stained glass, intricate tilework and cast-iron fireplaces. For a room with a view of Casco Bay, the Canopy by Hilton Portland Waterfront is the pick. Surpass card editor tip: The Surpass card earns 12 points per dollar on purchases made directly with hotels and resorts within the Hilton portfolio. Plus, your entire trip works toward a free night reward that you can earn after spending $15,000 on eligible purchases with the card in a calendar year. It's redeemable at over 9,000+ Hilton properties, any night of the week, with no blackout dates. Surpass card editor tip: 6 points per dollar at U.S. restaurants means every meal, from casual coffee to that fancy dinner, is contributing to your Hilton Honors point balance. It isn't easy to narrow down where you should eat in Boston, as there is no shortage of great restaurants, but a few stood out during my time there. For coffee and breakfast, Tatte Bakery and Cafe is the move with several locations around the city. Don't miss the Honey Halva Latte ($6.25) and pistachio croissant ($5.25). And of course, if you're craving lobster rolls, head over to James Hook and Co. There may be a line, but trust me, it's worth the wait. For dinner, head to the North End and visit Ciao Roma for their vodka pasta ($28). Their outdoor patio is in a courtyard across the street, making you feel like you are dining on an Italian side street. On the walk back, make it a point to stop at Modern Pastry to build your own customized cannoli. There are plenty of great eats in Portsmouth, but the restaurant I can't stop thinking about is Cure. You'll want to make a reservation before you leave on your trip. It's a cozy, intimate space that fills up fast. The menu changes seasonally, but order the Steakhouse Board ($55) if it's available and don't skip the crème brûlée ($12) for dessert. In the morning, walk to Elephantine for coffee and the most delicious chocolate almond croissant and breakfast sandwiches you can imagine. We went right when they opened up, and there was already a line, but believe me when I say it is well worth the wait. When asking around for dinner recommendations in Portland, Duckfat came up again and again, so we made it a point to eat there, and I can confirm it lived up to the hype. They're known for their Belgian frites ($9), double-fried in duck fat until they're golden and crispy, and once you've had them cooked that way, you'll never be the same. If you're craving Italian, Via Vecchia hits the spot. The radiatori pasta ($35), made with Calabrian chili-braised pork, San Marzano tomato ragu, Parmigiano Reggiano cream and smoked pancetta, was absolutely heavenly. And when in Maine, you'd be remiss not to get a good old-fashioned lobster roll. Whether you like them hot or cold, Highroller Lobster is nonnegotiable and will serve you a lobster roll flight ($52), and each one can be topped with a different butter or mayo sauce. If taking a day trip to Kennebunkport, beeline it to the town's beloved Clam Shack for a classic cold roll ($31.95). Surpass card editor tip: Earn up to $50 Hilton Statement Credit each quarter for up to $200 per year on purchases made on the Surpass card directly with a property in the Hilton portfolio, including dining, resort charges and even spa services. For museum entrance fees, tours and souvenirs, you're earning 3 points per dollar on all other eligible purchases. Walking the Freedom Trail is a must for any first-time visitor. The 2.5-mile route follows a red-brick path through 17 historic sites, from Boston Common and Paul Revere's House to the USS Constitution. Budget at least half a day to take it at a comfortable pace without feeling rushed. The highlight of my time in the city had to be my visit to the Boston Public Library. Opened in 1848, it was the first free municipal library in the United States. The stunning Renaissance Revival architecture is one of the few places in the U.S. that makes you feel like you've been transported to Europe. My favorite room was Bates Hall, a picturesque yet quiet reading space with a 50-foot barrel-vaulted ceiling and green lamps lining the entire hall. Speaking of books, I decided to commemorate my literary adventure by supporting two independent bookstores in the city: Beacon Hill Book Store in the Beacon Hill neighborhood and Brattle Book Shop in Downtown Crossing. The 10-acre waterfront Prescott Park is home to the beloved Prescott Gardens, which are beautifully maintained and worth a leisurely stroll. History buffs should also make time for the Strawbery Banke Museum, a living history museum spread across 10 acres of restored homes and buildings spanning 300 years of Portsmouth's history. Once you've explored the park, Market Square is where you'll want to spend your time. You can wander shops and go "deck hopping" as the locals call it, moving from one waterfront restaurant or bar deck to another to enjoy cocktails or mocktails, appetizers and scenic views. Before heading directly into Portland, stop in Kennebunkport and Ogunquit for an hour or two and explore the charm of these two port towns, each with streets lined with independent small shops and restaurants. In Ogunquit, walk Marginal Way, a 0.25-mile scenic coastal cliff walk accessible to most fitness levels, then head 20 minutes farther North to Kennebunkport to get some delicious artisanal ice cream at Rococo's for a sweet treat before arriving in Portland. After several days of driving and walking thousands of steps, my first stop in Portland was the Astraea Spa at the Longfellow Hotel. I treated myself to the Astraea signature massage ($245), which included warm Himalayan salt stones and a facial massage to relieve muscle tightness. Once I felt relaxed and refreshed, we ended our last day watching the sunset at the iconic Portland Head Light for some classic New England vibes. This New England road trip finally brought some of the pages of my favorite books to life. And the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card made it easier to pull off than I expected. Complimentary National Car Rental Emerald Club Executive Status meant no waiting at the counter when I landed in Boston, and 6 points per dollar at U.S. gas stations and U.S. supermarkets meant every fill-up and snack run was working toward the next trip. Add in automatic Gold status, the up to $50 back in quarterly Hilton statement credits (which I used toward my Astraea Spa visit) and 12 points per dollar on Hilton hotel stays, and this road trip was helping me earn the whole way through. If a New England road trip has been on your list, there's no better time to start planning — and no better cards to bring along for the ride than one from the Hilton Honors card lineup, including the highest-ever welcome offer on the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card: - Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. Terms apply. - Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card: Earn 130,000 bonus points and a Free Night Reward after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. Terms apply. - Hilton Honors American Express Card: Earn 70,000 bonus points and a Free Night Reward after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. Terms apply. Terms apply to offers and benefits mentioned.

item.title: United ditches flight segments, raises bar for 1K in Premier status shakeup
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
United ditches flight segments, raises bar for 1K in Premier status shakeup United Airlines is making a big change to how its frequent flyers earn elite status. Beginning in 2027, the carrier will stop counting the number of flights its MileagePlus members take when awarding status. Instead, United flyers hoping to become "Premier" will have to focus solely on accumulating Premier Qualifying Points, or "PQPs." That means the path to status on United involves spending as much money as possible — both on flights and on the airline's suite of cobranded credit cards. That's not the only change United announced. On top of shifting how MileagePlus members earn status, the Chicago-based carrier announced it's raising the requirements to reach 1K. Beginning in 2027, members will need an additional 4,000 PQPs (for a total of 32,000) to make top-tier status compared to the current requirements. United revealed those changes in a memo to loyalty members on Tuesday. All told, it's the second significant shake-up to the airline's loyalty program in 2026 — and the biggest structural shift in how it awards elite status in years. Here's what to know and what it means for flying United in 2027. Heading into 2027, United will ditch Premier Qualifying Flights, or "PQFs," as a metric for awarding elite status. Currently, MileagePlus members have two ways they can earn status: - PQPs only: Earn enough PQPs via spending on flights and United's credit cards - PQFs+PQFs: Log enough flights, combined with a lower number of PQPs That second option is set to go away in 2027. Going forward, PQPs will be the only metric United uses to award Premier status. That means it's your spending on flights and on your United card — if you have one — that will make the difference between qualifying, or not, in the new year. In an interview with TPG, United's recently appointed loyalty chief said the changes were meant to simplify the program "We thought it made more sense for them to have one, consistent metric that actually was something that ... they can focus on across the board between their flight activity, their engagement with the airline," Jarad Fisher, United's president of MileagePlus, said. "And, really making it so that we can invest more in the people who are investing in us." How many PQPs will you need to reach Premier status? If you earn status purely off of PQPs, then the number of points you'll need for Silver, Gold and Platinum status won't change in 2027. However, reaching 1K will get harder no matter how you look at it. Here's how the status requirements shake out. (If you're reading this on mobile, scroll right to see how the new requirements compare to the old ones.) These changes will apply to MileagePlus members in the new year as they aim for 2028 status. While United is ditching PQFs as a status metric, MileagePlus members will still need to take at least four United flights in a year to be Premier-eligible. That's a baseline requirement that isn't changing. Flights on United Express regional jets count toward that four-flight requirement, but flights on United's partners do not. Certain MileagePlus members will get a head start on status in 2027. If you have an eligible United credit card, the airline will deposit the equivalent of 5% of PQPs required for your current status level into your account as the new status year begins. - Members who enter 2027 with Premier Silver status will get 300 PQPs. - Gold members will get 600 PQPs. - Platinum members will get 900 PQPs. - 1K members will get 1,600 PQPs. MileagePlus members who open an eligible United credit card by Dec. 31 will also receive the deposit for next year. Who will this change affect most? Depending on how you typically earn status, these changes might be quite significant — or not so much. If you've historically achieved Premier status by just racking up PQPs, not much changes for you in 2027 (unless you're aiming for top-tier 1K, which is getting harder to reach). According to Fisher, PQPs are how a majority of United members earn status today. "It's basically doubling down on the way most people were earning status," he said. The travelers most affected by this change are United flyers who typically log a ton of segments in the year. Those members have historically been able to reach status by combining all those PQFs with a fewer number of PQPs. If you fall into that category, you'll likely have to spend more to hit the same status in 2027. "For those folks, obviously, getting a United card will be a way for them to actually bridge that gap," Fisher said. No more 'segment runs' Also, there's likely no need to criss-cross the country on an end-of-year "segment run" to hit enough PQFs. Logging flight segments will no longer be a key Premier status metric. "As thought about making these changes, we just didn't feel great about that anymore — that was an old relic," Fisher said. "And so we just thought it was time to retire that metric." As for 1K status, that will require more spending across the board to hit United's top published elite tier in the new year. 1K requirements jump from 28,000 PQPs to 32,000. That's an increase of about 14%. If you previously reached 1K through a combination of flight segments and spending, you'll need roughly 45% more PQPs than you did previously. United's MileagePlus members earn 1 PQP per $1 spent with the airline on flights. Meanwhile, a handful of United credit cards can also earn PQPs on everyday purchases: - United℠ Explorer Card (see rates and fees)($0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $150 annual fee) earns 1 PQP per $20 spent, up to a maximum of 1,000 PQPs annually - United Quest℠ Card (see rates and fees) ($350 annual fee) earns 1 PQP per $20 spent, up to a maximum of 18,000 PQPs annually. - United Club℠ Card (see rates and fees)($695 annual fee) earn 1 PQP per $15 spent, up to a maximum of 32,000 PQPs annually.
