United flyers can also earn PQPs on certain upgrades and other "extras" purchased after booking. And certain partner flights are eligible for PQP-earning, though these need to be booked through United (look for a ticket starting with 016). Partner flights not booked through United will earn at a reduced rate. United's changes to earning Premier status come months after the carrier rolled out a larger shift to its MileagePlus program, overhauling how cardholders and noncardholders earn and redeem miles. United is far from the only airline to pivot how it awards status to its loyalty members. Top rivals American Airlines and Delta Air Lines have focused exclusively on dollars spent — on air travel and on credit cards — for years. Related reading:

item.title: Marriott Bonvoy will now let you see where you stand in line for a hotel upgrade
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Marriott Bonvoy will now let you see where you stand in line for a hotel upgrade Following the company's Member Day, Marriott International has announced two interesting updates that Bonvoy loyalists can look out for in the coming months. Among the announcements is an exciting new app feature that will allow elite members to see where they stand in line for a complimentary upgrade — one of the most coveted perks for those with Marriott Bonvoy Gold status and above. Here's what we know. Complimentary Upgrade List feature debuts in the Marriott app In response to member requests for more visibility into the inner workings of complimentary room upgrades, Marriott is beta testing a new feature called the Complimentary Upgrade List in their app. This feature will provide eligible members (those with Gold status and above) with the ability to see their exact position in the upgrade list before they arrive and check in to their hotel. At the moment, the feature is only available for a small subset of hotels, but Marriott says it will expand to over 250 hotels throughout the U.S. and Canada by November. It will certainly be interesting to see just how long these lists become at popular hotels during peak travel periods, how Nightly Upgrade Awards will be prioritized and whether or not the lists will function similarly to airline upgrade lists. A new lounge experience comes to select premium hotels Asia In addition to the new app feature, Marriott announced a new lounge experience dubbed the Marriott Bonvoy Lounge. Debuting in February 2027, the experience will come to 100 premium-level hotels across Asia-Pacific, with 220 more hotels across Greater China joining in early 2027. The participating lounges will offer elevated food and beverage programming, have dedicated associates on-site during peak lounge hours and serve locally-inspired offerings, according to the company's press release. Marriott Bonvoy members will be able to see participating hotels by using the lounge filter on the app and on Marriott.com ( as well as lounge hours and more property-specific details). There is currently limited information on the experience website, with more details to come soon.

item.title: How to earn and use IHG One Rewards free night certificates
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
How to earn and use IHG One Rewards free night certificates The cobranded IHG One Rewards cards offer many valuable perks. But one of the most valuable on the IHG cards with annual fees that are available to U.S. residents is free night certificates. The anniversary free night certificate you get each year as a cardmember perk can often provide enough value to justify paying the card's annual fee. And, as an added bonus, you have the opportunity to earn an additional free night certificate on some IHG credit cards each calendar year when you meet specific spending requirements. So, here's what you should know about IHG free night certificates. IHG One Rewards may occasionally offer promotional free night certificates, but, by far, the most common way to earn IHG free night certificates is through IHG credit cards. Here's a look at the free night certificates you can earn with select U.S.-issued IHG credit cards that are currently available: For cardholders of these cards, IHG deposits an anniversary free night certificate into your account on your card anniversary each year. IHG deposits certificates earned based on card spending within eight weeks of when you qualify. You can top off certificates that you earn from these three IHG cards with points from your IHG account if you wish to redeem for a night that costs more than your certificate's redemption value. However, existing cardholders who opened their accounts before the recent IHG card portfolio revamp will still receive certificates redeemable for a night costing up to 40,000 points through the end of 2026. Existing cardholders will begin getting certificates with the increased redemption value cap starting in 2027. To this point, cardholders of the IHG One Rewards Select Credit Card (which hasn't been open to new applicants for many years) will begin receiving anniversary free night certificates that are eligible for top-off and have a redemption value of up to 50,000 points starting in 2027. The information for the IHG Select has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. How to check the details of your IHG free night certificate If you want to check whether you have any IHG free night certificates or confirm the details of your certificates, log in to your IHG One Rewards account and click on your name in the upper-right-hand corner. Scroll down the page that loads, then check the "Enjoy your rewards" section. Here, you should see a panel with your free nights (if you have any). Click on "Book a Free Night" to check the details of your certificate. A page will load, showing your account's unredeemed free night certificates. You can see the date ranges during which you must book and stay for each certificate. And if you click "View details" for a specific certificate, you'll see its maximum points redemption value and whether you can redeem points for a night at a higher points cost. IHG free night certificates typically require you to redeem and complete your stay within 12 months of issuance; you won't be able to book a stay that's outside of a certificate's eligibility window. How to redeem your IHG free night certificate To redeem an IHG free night certificate, click the blue "Book Free Night" button on the page we just discussed by the certificate's details. Doing so would automatically select the rate associated with that free night certificate in the "Rate Preference" drop-down box on the booking screen. You can also start on the landing page once you've logged in to your account and then select this same rate (if you have a certificate in your account). Enter your search details, and click the orange "Search" button. Your search results will appear, and you'll see the properties you can book with your free night certificate. If you see "FREE per night," you can use your certificate to cover the room rate and applicable taxes for that night. However, you may need to pay amenity or resort fees at some properties. You can top off most free night certificates. As such, if you search with the certificate rate selected and are using a certificate that allows top-offs, you may see some properties that require you to redeem extra points in addition to your certificate. You may also see some properties that list a paid rate. This means the property isn't bookable with your free night certificate on the dates you searched. In this case, you can click "View available dates" to see nights you can book with your free night certificate (potentially with a top-off required if you're using a certificate that allows it). Once you find a property that works for you, click the orange "Select Hotel" button to see the available room types. Then, click "Select" for a specific room type to get to the final booking page, where you can check your reservation details and select (or enter) a payment card to guarantee your reservation. Click "Book for Chase Anniversary Free Night" when you're ready to book your stay. Like when redeeming IHG points, not all room types are available when using your free night certificate. And unfortunately, IHG's booking system won't let you redeem a certificate for one night and use points or cash for other nights on the same reservation. Instead, you'll need to make consecutive reservations for the same room types if you want to stay longer than one night. But keep in mind that IHG's fourth-night-free benefit doesn't apply when using a free night certificate since certificate reservations must be booked separately from points reservations. IHG free night certificates can provide significant value, especially now that certificates issued through select IHG credit cards have higher redemption caps. To maximize your certificates, compare cash rates and points requirements to find a redemption that offers good value. And remember to use your certificates before they expire, as even a modest redemption is better than letting a free night go to waste. The value of an IHG free night certificate depends on the hotel's cash rate and the certificate's redemption cap, which varies by card and issuance date. To maximize its value, look for a night with a high cash rate relative to any points you need to add. IHG free night certificates can be used at eligible IHG properties with standard reward night availability. You'll need to find a night within your certificate's redemption cap or use points to top off an eligible certificate. Most IHG credit card free night certificates allow you to add points from your IHG One Rewards account to book a night that costs more than the certificate's redemption cap. The number of additional points required depends on the hotel's award price. IHG anniversary free night certificates typically expire 12 months after issuance, and you must complete your stay before the expiration date. Nights booked with IHG free night certificates count toward IHG One Rewards elite status qualification and Milestone Rewards. You won't earn points on the room rate, but you can earn points on eligible incidental charges. You can use multiple IHG free night certificates to book consecutive nights, but you'll need to book each certificate as a separate reservation. You can ask the hotel to link your reservations after booking, though. Terms & restrictions apply. See rates & fees.

item.title: Complete guide to earning and redeeming Avianca Lifemiles
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Complete guide to earning and redeeming Avianca Lifemiles While navigating a foreign airline's frequent flyer program may seem daunting, your savings on award travel can be significant. This is particularly true for Colombian airline Avianca and its unique Lifemiles frequent flyer program. Avianca Lifemiles offers useful Star Alliance redemption opportunities and generally does not pass along carrier-imposed fuel surcharges. However, repeated pricing changes and occasional booking glitches mean you should confirm the award you want before transferring points or miles and that the program is generally better suited to intermediate and advanced points and miles enthusiasts. Here's what you need to know about earning and redeeming Avianca Lifemiles, elite status and the program's most useful sweet spots. You can earn Lifemiles by flying Avianca, Star Alliance airlines (such as United Airlines, Lufthansa and Air Canada) and other carriers like Iberia and Gol Airlines. You can also earn on Avianca-coded flights operated by Clic Air, although Clic is not a general stand-alone award partner. On Avianca-operated flights, redeemable earnings are based on eligible spending and the fare type. Current rates are 3 miles per dollar spent on Basic and Light fares, 6 miles per dollar spent on Classic fares, 8 miles per dollar spent on Flex fares and 10 miles per dollar spent on Business fares. Elite members can earn additional bonus miles. Partner airline earnings depend on the operating airline and the fare class, so check the applicable earning chart before deciding where to credit your flight. Cardless offers two Lifemiles-branded credit cards in the U.S.: - Avianca Lifemiles American Express® Elite Card: Earn up to 100,000 bonus miles: 60,000 miles after spending $4,500 in the first 90 days from account opening, plus an additional 40,000 miles after spending $25,000 in the first 365 days from account opening. Earn 3 Lifemiles per dollar spent on Avianca purchases, 2 Lifemiles per dollar spent on dining and non-Avianca travel and 1 Lifemile per dollar spent on all other purchases. Other benefits include a 10% rebate on eligible Star Alliance award redemptions, 500 bonus Lifemiles each month, up to a 25% discount on Avianca award flights and Avianca Silver status, which includes Star Alliance Silver status, for as long as you have the card. This card has an annual fee of $249. - Avianca Lifemiles American Express® Card: Earn 40,000 bonus Lifemiles after spending $3,000 on eligible purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. Earn 2 Lifemiles per dollar spent on Avianca purchases, groceries and restaurants, and 1 Lifemile per dollar spent on all other purchases. Other benefits include Avianca Silver status, which includes Star Alliance Silver status for as long as you have the card. This card has an annual fee of $99. The information for the Avianca Lifemiles American Express Elite Card and the Avianca Lifemiles American Express Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Avianca Lifemiles has a broad range of bank, business and hotel programs offering rewards you can transfer to Lifemiles at the following standard rates: Avianca often offers regular discounts on Lifemiles purchases. In the past, we have seen prices drop as low as 1.2 cents per mile, though the typical sale price ranges from 1.3 to 1.35 cents per mile. These rates are significantly lower than TPG's October 2026 valuation of Lifemiles at 1.6 cents each. While buying points and miles speculatively is generally not recommended, these sales can be a good option if you have a specific redemption in mind. If you frequently travel on paid tickets with Star Alliance carriers, it might be worth considering crediting your miles to Avianca. This may be advisable if you find more value in the Lifemiles program than in other options, such as United MileagePlus and Air Canada Aeroplan. Crediting your miles to Avianca is also beneficial if you don't travel enough to earn elite status but still want to maximize your redemption opportunities. Lifemiles usually expire 12 months after your last accrual. Redeeming does not reset the clock, but earning does. Avianca elite members and eligible cardholders get 24 months, while Lifemiles+ also extends mileage validity. Avianca Lifemiles has five elite tiers. Red Plus through Diamond require both a set number of total qualifying miles and a minimum number of qualifying miles earned from Avianca-operated flights or additional services purchased directly from Avianca. Magno, introduced on June 10, requires at least 110,000 qualifying miles flown with Avianca annually, so it will only suit those who fly Avianca very regularly. Lifemiles offers a paid subscription program called Lifemiles+ (sometimes referred to as Lifemiles+ World). This program is optional for members and offers four membership levels: Lite, Basic, Pro and Max. Lite is complimentary for Avianca Lifemiles American Express Elite Card members, and cardmembers can receive a discount on Basic, Pro and Max memberships. Members receive various benefits based on their membership tier, including monthly bonus miles and additional miles per dollar spent on Avianca-branded American Express cards. A minimum six-month membership is required, so for non-Amex cardmembers, this would be at least a $120 investment. Most importantly, members receive 10% of the mileage cost back on eligible Star Alliance redemptions, so if you are considering a redemption of more than 200,000 miles, perhaps for your family, this could be a wise investment. Lifemiles+ subscriptions must be paid by credit card. As a member of Star Alliance, Avianca allows you to use your Lifemiles for flights on the carrier or any of its partners. Avianca also partners with Gol Airlines and Iberia, providing opportunities to earn and redeem Lifemiles on eligible flights. You can earn Lifemiles on Avianca-coded flights operated by Clic, but remember that Clic is not a stand-alone redemption partner. Lifemiles pricing varies by route and operating airline, and the program has repeatedly changed award prices without notice. The most reliable way to determine the current price is to search your exact itinerary on the Lifemiles website. Redeeming Lifemiles is typically straightforward. You log in to the Lifemiles website and search for your desired award flight. However, it is important to note that while Avianca should technically have access to the same Star Alliance award availability as United MileagePlus and Air Canada Aeroplan, Lifemiles doesn't seem to show as many seats as other programs, and the carrier's information technology is also known to have limitations. This can result in phantom award space, where seats appear online but are not bookable. Conversely, Avianca may not always display available award space in United and Air Canada's loyalty programs. With most airline loyalty programs in 2026, you face a trade-off between low award rates and high fuel surcharges, or between spending more miles to avoid extra costs. However, Lifemiles is one of the few programs that excels in both aspects. It offers competitive rates for Star Alliance awards and does not pass on fuel surcharges to Lifemiles members. As a result, you can expect to pay minimal taxes and fees when redeeming an award ticket. While Lifemiles previously offered some of the lowest award rates of any program, especially in business and first class, various devaluations have made rates higher, though there are still some deals to be found. Given the many carriers that fly between the U.S. and Europe, it's easy to find business-class availability using Lifemiles, especially if you are flexible on your departure and arrival cities and dates. Lifemiles no longer charges a single business-class rate between the U.S. and Europe; however, we have found nonstop flights in business class for just 59,500 miles (or even less with a Lifemiles+ subscription). Longer domestic coach flights within the US The shortest flights, such as within California on United, are priced at an OK but not amazing 10,000 miles one-way in economy. However, longer flights, like those from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to San Francisco International Airport (SFO), are only 15,000 miles in economy each way per person, which is a great price for a flight of around six hours. As expected, award rates from the mainland U.S. to Asia are higher, but we still found one-way flights from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport (TPE) on EVA Air for 41,140 miles and 83,200 miles in economy and business class, respectively. Flights operated by Avianca can be astonishingly cheap with Lifemiles. We found flights under 10,000 miles each way (or less with a Lifemiles+ subscription) from Miami International Airport (MIA) to Bogota's El Dorado International Airport (BOG), which is an incredible price. Although Lifemiles offers appealing award rates, it might not be the right program for you. The program has a reputation for error-prone IT and inconsistent customer service. Lifemiles members often encounter website glitches when redeeming their miles, and the user experience can be frustrating. Additionally, if you reserve an economy award ticket and a business-class seat becomes available, Lifemiles requires you to pay a cancellation fee to redeposit your miles. You can then rebook your flight in business class. While booking with Avianca may save you thousands of miles, canceling your ticket or changing your award could be tedious and costly. Refunds can be requested online through Lifemiles' refund form or through the contact center, and fees may apply. The carrier's call center can be difficult to resolve issues with, especially if you cannot speak Spanish. Avianca Lifemiles is a frequent flyer program that has proven its worth in the award travel world. With its decent redemption rates, lack of fuel surcharges and partnerships with major transferable points and miles programs, Lifemiles offers value and flexibility to its members. While there may be some customer service challenges and quirks to navigate, the benefits outweigh the drawbacks for many travelers, though it is worth comparing award prices with programs such as Air Canada Aeroplan before transferring points. So, take the time to explore Avianca Lifemiles, delve into its sweet spots and unlock the possibilities it presents for your future travels. With a little research, patience and planning, you can make the most of this program as you consider where to transfer your credit card points and miles. Yes for many Star Alliance awards, if you can tolerate the booking quirks. The elite tiers for Avianca Lifemiles are Red Plus, Silver, Gold, Diamond and Magno. Yes, usually after 12 months without accrual, though eligible members receive 24 months. You can transfer your American Express Membership Rewards points, Capital One miles, Bilt Points, Wells Fargo Rewards points and Citi ThankYou Rewards points to your Lifemiles account at a 1:1 ratio. You can redeem Lifemiles for flights on Avianca and Star Alliance airlines, as well as eligible flights operated by Gol Airlines and Iberia. Clic is an earning partner on eligible Avianca-coded flights but is not a stand-alone redemption partner. Terms & restrictions apply. See rates & fees.

item.title: Delta downplays Seattle rivalry with former 'frenemy' Alaska Airlines
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Delta downplays Seattle rivalry with former 'frenemy' Alaska Airlines Delta Air Lines says there's room for two in Seattle, where it shares a hub with hometown carrier Alaska Airlines. "I wouldn't suggest that there's a battle for Seattle," CEO Ed Bastian said, speaking Friday on the airline's earnings call. But make no mistake: Delta and Alaska are competing aggressively for Seattle customers. And "battle" or not, that fight — or whatever you call it — is playing out on an increasingly global stage. Alaska is far and away the biggest carrier at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA). This year, it will operate roughly double the number of flights that Delta will fly from the airport, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. But Delta has a much more robust long-haul international footprint, boasting routes to a host of places Alaska doesn't fly — from Shanghai to Taipei, Barcelona and Amsterdam. That's not surprising, considering Alaska — until the last couple of years — had primarily operated as a domestic airline, with a heavily West Coast network. However, things are changing. Two years after acquiring Hawaiian Airlines and a new fleet of long-haul planes, Alaska is in the midst of a fast global expansion. Next summer, the carrier will add to its fledgling European map with new service to Athens and Paris. By the end of the decade, it expects to serve at least 15 long-haul destinations from Seattle. Alaska is also planning to compete more forcefully on transcontinental service by adding lie-flat suites on key domestic routes. And, it's building a new, state-of-the-art club at SEA. That "Aurora Lounge" will serve as its answer to Delta's upscale facility that opened last year — and won a TPG Award for best new U.S. airline lounge in 2025. Alaska isn't shying away from its long-term goals in the Pacific Northwest. "By 2030, we expect to be the number one international carrier in Seattle," chief commercial officer Andrew Harrison told investors last month. Despite Alaska's international growth in Seattle, Delta is taking a cordial tone; asked about it Friday, Bastian called its Seattle rival's moves "smart." "Seattle's a big and growing market. It's certainly a market that is large enough for us and our principal competitor up there," he said. "We don't have to 'own' every market we fly in. I think you can cohabitate a bit." It's certainly a different tone than the one Delta has struck in Los Angeles. In recent months, the carrier has boldly touted its place as the "number one airline" at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) — a hub it shares with both American Airlines and United Airlines. Now — that's not to say Delta isn't competing forcefully in Seattle. Just in the last week, Delta rolled out special flights discounts clearly targeted at Alaska-based members of its SkyMiles program. And last year, when Alaska announced London and Rome as its first two destinations in mainland Europe, Delta responded by adding its own route to the Eternal City. At the time, Alaska's top network planner Kirsten Amrine told TPG that the carrier had expected moves like that from Delta. "But where we sit is, we're the hometown carrier," she said then. "Over time, as we have a larger international portfolio, we see the opportunity just to win back much of the travel that we've lost to Delta." Not 'frenemies' ... but not a 'battle,' either Looking ahead, Pacific service is a key area both airlines hope to make gains. Alaska executives recently noted they see flights to Asia as the airline's biggest international opportunity. Interestingly, Delta sees the future similarly, thanks to its duo of West Coast hubs — including Seattle. "No. 1 global carrier in Seattle — we're going to keep continuing to build that," chief commercial officer Joe Esposito told me in August. "We've got great launching platforms in the West to expand into Asia." Long-term, consumers win when airlines compete. At SEA, this build-up by Alaska and Delta is producing more routes and better amenities. Time will tell what it means for fares. Either way, it's clear Seattlelites have two major airlines competing for a slice of their wallet. And for that reason, this Pacific Northwest "cohabitation" of two former "frenemies" could ultimately be a good thing for travelers. Just don't call it a "battle." Related reading:

item.title: An introduction to Alaska cruisetours: What are they and why you should book one
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
An introduction to Alaska cruisetours: What are they and why you should book one If you're planning your first big trip to Alaska, you may already have heard of an Alaska cruisetour — an organized trip that combines a cruise with overland touring. In Alaska, unlike in most destinations, cruisetours are a very common thing. Of the 3 million or so vacationers who go to Alaska every year, roughly two-thirds go by cruise ship. And, of those, a significant percentage sign up for an extended trip that includes both cruising and land touring. Those are much higher percentages than you'll find for cruises and cruisetour-type trips in almost any other part of the world. This is not by accident. For reasons I will explain in more detail below, a cruise — and particularly a cruisetour — is the best way to see a broad cross-section of Alaska's most famous attractions in a single, easy-to-arrange trip. Even if you're not the sort of person who normally signs up for a cruise or a land tour when visiting most destinations, you just might want to make a cruisetour the way you see Alaska. At least for your first visit. This guide will explain why a cruisetour of Alaska makes sense for many Alaska-bound vacationers and everything you need to know to plan and book one. What is an Alaska cruisetour? First, let's start with the basics. A cruisetour to Alaska is a trip that combines a cruise along the coast of Alaska with a multiday overland tour into the state's rugged interior. It is both a cruise and a land tour of Alaska — hence the name. Typically, these are trips that combine a seven-night cruise along the southeastern coast of the state (often called Gulf of Alaska sailings) with three to 10 nights of overland touring. The resulting cruisetours thus range in length from 10 to 17 nights. A cruisetour isn't the only way to do a cruise-related vacation to Alaska. You also can sign up for a cruise-only trip to the state, and many cruise-loving vacationers interested in seeing Alaska do just that. All the major cruise lines that operate in Alaska offer cruise-only options, and as I've experienced firsthand over many years of writing about Alaska cruises, they are wonderful trips. Still, for reasons I will explain below, a cruisetour is arguably the best way to get a broad Alaska experience in a single trip. Why choose an Alaska cruisetour? Alaska is a big place with relatively few people, limited infrastructure and lots of hard-to-reach wilderness — all factors that make it difficult to visit as an independent traveler, especially if you want to see a broad cross-section of its most famous sights in a single trip. For instance, one of the most famous places to visit in the state, Glacier Bay National Park and Preserve, isn't reachable by car. You can't drive there. For most people, the only practical way to get deep into Glacier Bay (and see its stunning tidewater glaciers) is on a cruise vessel. The mountain-backed city of Juneau, another top destination in Alaska —and a hub for whale-watching, glacier flights and other bucket-list Alaska experiences — is also inaccessible by car. You can fly there, but for most people, a cruise is the best way to reach it. Other major Alaska destinations are reachable by car, but are so far-flung that arranging a road trip to see several of them in a single trip is impractical. For example, the driving distance between Denali National Park and Preserve, and the popular tourist town of Ketchikan is more than 1,100 miles. You'd need at least 40 hours to make the journey. It is only through a cruisetour that combines travel by ship, rail cars and motorcoaches that seeing all of the above and more in a single trip becomes possible for most people. And it's not just possible — it's easy. On a cruisetour, somebody else has figured out all of the very complicated logistics of getting you around the vastness of Alaska. All you have to do is sit back, relax and enjoy the ride. As mentioned above, even if you're the sort of person who generally stays away from group travel, a cruisetour is still your best bet if you want to see a lot of Alaska. It will get you both to the popular destinations in the southeastern part of the state that are easily accessible by ship (such as Juneau, Ketchikan, the historic mining town Skagway and Glacier Bay) as well as to the iconic destinations in the interior of the state that are best seen via overland touring (such as Denali National Park, Anchorage and Fairbanks). Which companies offer Alaska cruisetours? Six cruise lines account for nearly all cruisetours in Alaska, with regular departures throughout the Alaska tourist season: Additionally, two small cruise lines known for small-ship sailings — Windstar Cruises and Azamara Cruises — offer cruisetours to Alaska on a more sporadic basis. Windstar, for instance, offered cruisetours in 2026 but has none on its schedule for 2027. Of these, by far the biggest Alaska cruisetour operators are Princess and Holland America. The two brands (which are sister companies owned by cruise giant Carnival Corporation) were the pioneers in offering tours to Alaska that combined cruise travel and overland travel. They continue to dominate the market for such trips. Princess, notably, offers a whopping 28 Alaska cruisetour itineraries, each a little different. The next biggest Alaska cruisetour operator, Holland America, offers 19 different cruisetour itineraries. Royal Caribbean, Celebrity and Norwegian are smaller players in the Alaska cruisetour market, with a smaller range of cruisetour itineraries. But they still each have 12, 13 and 9 different cruisetour itineraries, respectively. America Cruise Lines, a small-ship cruise specialist, has two cruisetour itineraries in Alaska. This is all to say that you have a lot of different Alaska cruisetours from which to choose. The good news is that the huge amount of choice means you'll likely find a tour that aligns perfectly with your interests. There are trips where the land portion of the experience focuses almost solely around visiting Denali National Park, but then there are others that add lots of stops at other outdoorsy areas, including lesser-known Wrangell-St. Elias National Park — the biggest national park in the United States. Some cruisetours will bring you to such off-the-beaten-path towns as Homer, Alaska, known as the world capital of halibut fishing. Others bring you to Fairbanks or Anchorage. Some of Holland America's cruisetours will even take you across the border into Canada to the wild and sparsely populated Yukon Territory and its capital, Whitehorse. The bad news is that, because of all these choices, the process of booking an Alaska cruisetour can be confusing for first-timers. Depending on which itinerary you pick, the overall length of the trip, the places you'll visit and the things you'll see can vary greatly. You'll also get a different experience depending on which cruisetour company you pick. Princess, which is the leader in cruisetours to Alaska, for instance, has built up an array of exclusive company-owned infrastructure in the state that you will only experience by booking a Princess trip. These include: - Two custom-built Princess wilderness lodges at Denali National Park that are among the best places to stay in the area - Three more custom-built Princess lodges in other parts of Alaska - A fleet of luxury glass-domed Princess rail cars that provide direct-to-the-wilderness service - A fleet of luxury Princess Tours motorcoaches Holland America also owns a wilderness lodge in Alaska — just one, at Denali National Park — as well as several hotels in other parts of Alaska and the Yukon Territory. It also owns its railcars and motorcoaches. Through their parent company Carnival Corporation, Princess and Holland America even own part of the White Pass and Yukon Route railroad in Skagway — one of the biggest tourist attractions in the state — as well as part of Skagway's historic port and retail operations. Additionally, both Princess and Holland America will help you book day tours out of their Alaska lodges to explore the Alaska wilderness. These excursions include everything from flightseeing tours and whitewater rafting outings to guided hikes, fishing trips and a visit to a copper mine. By contrast, Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Norwegian and American do not own their own lodging in Alaska. Instead, they contract with local hotels to arrange lodging for their cruisetour customers. Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Norwegian and American also don't own railcars or motorcoaches in Alaska; they contract out that portion of their cruisetours to local operators. What's included in an Alaska cruisetour? When you sign up for a cruisetour to Alaska, you're signing up for a vacation where your cruise line will arrange almost every aspect of your trip, both on land and at sea. For starters, there is the cruise portion of the trip. As noted above, every cruisetour in Alaska includes a cruise that is typically a one-way, seven-night sailing along the southeastern coast of Alaska. These trips typically include day stops at popular southeastern Alaska towns such as Juneau, Skagway and Ketchikan, along with one or more visits to a glacier area for glacier viewing. Cruisetours also include nightly lodging during the land portion of the trip and overland transportation around the state, either on motorcoaches or rail cars. Your cruise line can also usually arrange your flights to and from the trip (for an extra charge) and airport transfers. If you're traveling to or from Denali National Park by train as part of a cruisetour, the cost of the tour usually includes transfers to and from the rail depot near Denali and lodging. In the case of cruisetours operated by Princess, the specific lodging included in the tour is often in one of the five custom-built Princess lodges mentioned above; these lodges play a big role in the land portion of most Princess cruisetours. Notably, they serve not just as lodging for the night but as a base for exploring some of the state's best-known attractions. Meals during the land portion of the trip are not included with many cruisetours. That said, some higher-end cruisetours do include them. Excursions while visiting ports on the cruise portion of the trip are typically not included in cruisetour fares. Excursions during the land portion of the trips, including while staying at cruise line-owned lodges, are included in some cruisetours but not all. (More on that below.) Where do Alaska cruisetours begin? Nearly all cruisetours begin in one of three places: Anchorage, Alaska; Fairbanks, Alaska; or Vancouver, British Columbia. You'll also occasionally find cruisetours that start in Seattle —all of which are operated by Norwegian Cruise Line. Cruisetours that begin in Anchorage or Fairbanks start with the overland touring portion of the trip first, followed by the cruise portion of the trip. Cruisetours that begin in Vancouver or Seattle start with the cruise portion first, followed by the overland touring. In both cases, the cruise portion will typically be a one-way, seven-night sailing between either Whittier or Seward in Alaska and either Vancouver or Seattle. That means that when you book flights for your cruisetour, you'll be booking an "open jaw" ticket that brings you into Alaska at the start of the trip and home from Vancouver or Seattle — or vice versa. Note that you can book your own air for these trips (many TPG readers like to use points and miles) or let the cruise lines book flights for you through their add-on air programs. If booking on your own, just be sure that you are booking through the right airport in Alaska. Trips that start in Fairbanks, for instance, are best reached with a flight to Fairbanks International Airport (FAI) versus a flight to Anchorage International Airport (ANC), even though Anchorage is a far bigger airport. This is because transfers between Anchorage and Fairbanks can be time-consuming and expensive. The big exception to all of the above in where the trips begin and end is with the cruisetours offered by American Cruise Lines. The small-ship brand begins all its cruisetours in Fairbanks and ends them all in Juneau, Alaska, where it bases its vessels during the Alaska tourist season. What are the itinerary choices for Alaska cruisetours? As noted above, Princess is the biggest Alaska cruisetour operator, and it offers 28 different cruisetour itineraries. The next five biggest Alaska cruisetour operators offer another 55 itineraries between them. That's a lot of different cruisetour options to sift through when you are planning a trip. But choosing the perfect Alaska cruisetour for you doesn't have to be quite as difficult as it might seem. Depending on how long you want to stay in Alaska and what sort of experience you are seeking, you can narrow down the choices pretty quickly. For starters, is your main goal for the land portion of the trip is to see Denali National Park, Alaska's most famous attraction? For many people, seeing Denali is the main reason to add a few days of land touring to an Alaska cruise. Or, would you rather see a broader cross-section of the state, including places like Fairbanks or lesser-visited natural attractions like Wrangell-St. Elias National Park? You'll also want to ask yourself whether you want a full-service, guided experience when on the land tour portion of the trip, with lots of inclusions (like meals) and excursions. Or would you prefer to do more of the exploring on your own? Depending on your answers to these questions, you can narrow down the list of available cruisetours significantly. Princess, for instance, makes choosing from its array of 28 Alaska cruisetour easy by breaking them down into three broad categories that each appeal to a different type of traveler: - Denali Essentials trips (10-12 days) - Denali Explorer trips (10-15 days) - Denali Escorted (12-17 days) Of those three categories, The Denali Explorer trips are the ones most people take. In addition to a seven-night cruise, the Denali Explorer trips offer a visit to Denali as the core element of the land portion of the experience. But some of the longer ones also include a visit to Wrangell-St. Elias National Park or Kenai Fjords National Park (where you'll stay at Princess lodges). If you're seeking a cruise to Alaska plus a visit to Denali and maybe a bit more, these are the tours for you. The Denali Escorted trips are similar to the Denali Explorer trips but are much more full-service in their design. On the land portion of the Denali Explorer tours, you are on your own for meals and don't have a full-time tour director accompanying you from place to place as your guide. On the land portion of the Denali Escorted trips, by contrast, most meals are included, and you are escorted by a tour director. If you're the type of traveler who likes full-service tours where every little detail of your trip, including where you eat, is arranged by the tour company and there is an always-present tour leader, the Denali Escorted trips are going to be the right choice for you. For travelers on the opposite side of the spectrum — those who like to be more on their own when vacationing — the Denali Essentials itineraries are the trips specifically designed for you. Several of the other major companies with Alaska cruisetours offer a similar array of trips, though with fewer options. But each of them does the trips a little differently when it comes to specific stops, lodging options and transportation. Each of the brands also appeals to a different audience (see chart below). Princess, for instance, often draws couples, retirees and multigenerational families. Holland America, in particular, offers something that no other Alaska cruisetour company does: the chance to cross the border into Canada to see the Yukon Territory. Holland America breaks its Alaska cruisetours down into two groups: The land portion of the Alaska and Denali cruisetours involves two to seven nights of overland touring, including one to three nights at Holland America's lodge at Denali National Park (named, simply enough, the Holland America Denali Lodge). The land portion of the Alaska, Denali and Yukon cruisetours involves six to ten days of overland travel, with two to three nights at Holland America's Denali Lodge and two to three nights in the Yukon Territory. If seeing the Yukon Territory is of interest to you, the latter tours are the way to go. One big piece of news related to Holland America's cruisetour program: The Holland America Denali Lodge just underwent a significant, $70 million renovation and expansion this year that brought 48 remodeled rooms, a new coffee shop and a revamped public house. It'll also be getting a whole new room complex with suites as well as a new restaurant concept for the 2027 season. In addition, for 2027, Holland America has revamped dining offerings during the land portion of its cruisetours with new menus and dishes created in partnership with Ethan Stowell, a Seattle-based chef and restaurateur who serves as the line's culinary ambassador. Passengers booking eligible cruisetours can also book a new inclusive dining package that covers breakfast and dinner at Holland America properties at Denali, Skagway and Dawson City, lunch aboard its glass-domed McKinley Explorer railcars, admission to the Music of Denali dinner theater, and lunch during the Tundra Wilderness Tour at Denali. Royal Caribbean doesn't offer as broad a range of Alaska cruisetours as Princess and Holland America. But like both of those brands, its 12 Alaska cruisetour itineraries include shorter (nine-night) trips where the land portion is mostly focused on seeing Denali National Park, as well as some longer trips (up to 13 nights) that add on more sightseeing. The land portion of Royal Caribbean cruisetours ranges from two to six nights, and all but one include a stay at Denali National Park. Some of the trips include a stay in Anchorage, while five of the 12 itineraries add on a visit to Fairbanks. Half of the trips include a stay in Talkeetna, which is several hours south of Denali National Park and a base for adventure-type outings such as float trips and jet boat rides. Royal Caribbean also includes a stay at one of Alaska's finest resorts, the Alyeska Resort, with three of its cruisetours. Located south of Anchorage in the Chugach Mountains, Alyeska is a high-end retreat with a spa, fine dining, wooded paths and trails that start on the property's grounds; there's even an aerial tram that will take you up 2,300 feet to the summit of Mount Alyeska. While Royal Caribbean doesn't own its own lodging in Alaska, it uses top properties in the state including the Alyeska Resort as well and the Talkeetna Alaskan Lodge, which is celebrated for its panoramic vistas and grand stone fireplace. Other lodging on Royal Caribbean cruisetours include the charmingly rustic Denali Park Village, where buildings are tucked into a forested site along the Nenana River. Celebrity's 13 cruisetour itineraries range from 9 to 13 nights, with all 13 including at least one night at Denali National Park. As with the Alaska cruisetours that Royal Caribbean (a sister company) offers, most include a stay in Anchorage; some also add stays in Fairbanks, Talkeetna, Homer or at the Alyeska Resort. Among the Celebrity cruisetours are two Premium Cruisetour packages that include select meals, upgraded accommodations, and beverages while traveling by rail. Celebrity cruisetours include stays at a similar mix of properties as Royal Caribbean cruisetours. Norwegian Cruise Line Alaska cruisetours Norwegian's nine cruisetour itineraries range from 10 to 13 nights, and all include at least one, and sometimes two, nights at Denali National Park. Like Royal Caribbean and Celebrity, Norwegian's tours usually include stays at one or more of the following places, too: Anchorage, Fairbanks, Talkeetna and the Alyeska Resort. In an unusual twist, some Norwegian cruisetours also include a two-night stay in fishing hub Homer, known for its world-leading halibut catch, to give tour-goers a chance to sign on for an all-day (extra charge) fishing excursion. If you've always dreamed of experiencing halibut fishing, this might be the Alaska cruisetour for you. Another unusual offering from Norwegian is a "Denali Valdez Explorer" cruisetour, which includes a motorcoach journey south along the Richardson Highway to Valdez, the terminus of the Alyeska Pipeline. This trip also includes a day cruise across the pristine waters of glacier-lined Prince William Sound. American Cruise Lines Alaska cruisetours The small-ship cruise specialist offers two cruisetour itineraries in Alaska that are 15 nights and 18 nights, respectively. Both of the itineraries start with six nights of land touring in the interior of Alaska with visits to Fairbanks, Denali National Park, Anchorage and Kenai Fjords National Park, followed by either nine or 12 nights of cruising down the southeast coast of Alaska. The cruisetours that American Cruise Lines offers in Alaska are significantly different than the cruisetours offered by other cruise brands in that the cruise portion of the trips take place on very small vessels. American Cruise Lines specializes in cruises on vessels that have fewer than 100 cabins and are small enough to visit very small, off-the-beaten-path ports in Alaska and elsewhere. Stops during the cruise portion of the line's Alaska cruisetours include the tiny towns of Haines, Petersburg and Wrangell in addition to Juneau as well as Glacier Bay National Park (with some departures including a rare overnight stay in Glacier Bay). The longer sailings add a visit to the town of Sitka. As mentioned above, American Cruise Lines is an outlier among Alaska cruisetour operators in that it begins all of its cruisetours in Fairbanks and ends them all in Juneau, Alaska, which is where its ships are based for the Alaska season. After completing the land portion of your American Cruise Lines cruisetour, you'll take a short flight from Anchorage to Juneau to begin the cruise portion of the trip, with that portion being a roundtrip sailing out of the Juneau. You'll then fly home from Juneau. American Cruise Lines is expanded its presence in Alaska significantly in 2027 with the addition of a third vessel in the region, the 130-passenger American Ranger. It joins the 170-passenger American Constitution and 170-passenger American Constellation in sailing in Alaska from May through September. Azamara offers four-night Alaska land tours that can be tacked onto any cruise the line offers that begins or ends in Alaska. For the 2027 season, there are six such cruises. For cruises that end in Alaska (either at the ports of Whittier or Seward), the four-night add-on land tour will take place after the cruise and bring one night in the Denali National Park area, one night in Talkeetna, Alaska, and two nights in Fairbanks, Alaska. For cruises that begin in Alaska, the four-night add-on land tour will take place before the cruise and bring the same mix of overnights. Azamara also offers five- and six-night land tours into the Canadian Rockies that can be tacked onto Alaska cruises that begin or end in Vancouver, B.C. The tours focus heavily on Canada's majestic Banff National Park and, in some cases, include a two-day train trip through the Canadian Rockies on the Rocky Mountaineer. With some of Azamara's Alaska cruises, you can add both an Alaska land tour and a Canadian Rockies land tour to the trip by scheduling one before the cruise and one after the cruise. When can I do an Alaska cruisetour? The season for cruisetours in Alaska is a relatively short one, lasting from May to September. For the 2027 season, the earliest cruisetours are operated by Celebrity and Princess, respectively, and begin May 7 and May 8. The first Holland America cruisetours start on May 10. Norwegian and Royal Caribbean kick off their cruisetour seasons on May 11 and May 14, respectively, with American Cruise Lines and Azamara getting late starts on June 2 and June 3, respectively. The last cruisetours of the 2027 season begin almost exactly four months later on Sept. 10. What do cruisetours cost? The cost of a cruisetour to Alaska varies widely depending on the type of tour you choose and its length, as well as the type of cabin you want on the cruise portion. For example, the least expensive Princess cruisetour available for 2027 at the time of this guide's publishing was a 10-day Denali Explorer cruisetour that started at $1,399 per person. That's about $140 per day. This is for a trip that includes a seven-night cruise and three nights of overland touring focused on Denali National Park. At the high end of the price range for 2027 Princess cruisetours were the 17-day Denali Escorted tours mentioned above; they started at $4,999 per person or about $294 per day. Note that these starting rates get you the least expensive cabin type for the cruise portion of the trip, which is an "inside cabin" with no windows. The cruisetour cost can be significantly more in some cases if you want a bigger and more amenity-filled cabin on the cruise portion of the trip. For the 10-day Denali Explorer Princess cruisetour mentioned above, for instance, the starting rates for the trip rose to $1,473 per person — or about $147 per day — if you chose a cabin with a window (known as an "ocean-view cabin") on the cruise portion of the trip. The starting rates jumped to $2,024 per person if you chose a cabin with a balcony and $3,599 if you wanted a suite. Generally, cruisetours with fewer inclusions are priced lower than cruisetours with more inclusions. At Princess, for example, the Denali Essentials cruisetours typically cost less than the Denali Explorer tours, as they have fewer inclusions. Keep in mind that, as is typical for cruise-related trips, the pricing for all of these tours is "based on double occupancy." That is, you will only get the prices listed above if there are two people traveling together in the same room, each paying the stated fare. Alaska can be a difficult place to tour, given its huge size and lack of infrastructure, including roads in some areas. But there's an easy way to arrange a trip to Alaska that will include stops at some of its most famous sights: an Alaska cruisetour. Combining a seven-night cruise along the southeast coast of the state with a land tour into the state's rugged interior, a cruisetour can get you to such iconic Alaska attractions as Denali National Park, Glacier Bay National Park and the Juneau Icefields all in one trip. Planning a cruise? Start with these stories:

item.title: Capital One Spark Cash Plus vs. Chase Ink Business Cash: Which fits your business?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Capital One Spark Cash Plus vs. Chase Ink Business Cash: Which fits your business? The Capital One Spark Cash Plus and the Ink Business Cash® Credit Card (see rates and fees) are cash-back business cards, but that's about where their similarities end. For businesses with high spending across many categories, the Spark Cash Plus is a better fit thanks to its unlimited 2% cash back and no preset spending limit. On the other hand, the Ink Business Cash stands out for businesses that can maximize its 5% bonus categories and want to avoid an annual fee. The way they each reward business spending is almost completely different. The Spark Cash Plus prioritizes simplicity, while the Ink Business Cash rewards businesses willing to pay attention to where they spend. Here's how to decide which strategy works better for your business. Capital One Spark Cash Plus vs. Chase Ink Business Cash: At a glance Capital One Spark Cash Plus vs. Chase Ink Business Cash: Welcome bonus The Spark Cash Plus is currently offering $2,000 cash back, earned after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. You'll also earn another $2,000 for every $500,000 you spend during your first year, so really high spenders can keep stacking those bonuses. Since this is cash back, that first bonus is worth $2,000. But if you pair the card with an eligible Capital One miles-earning card, you can convert the cash back to miles. According to TPG's October 2026 valuations, Capital One miles are worth 1.85 cents each, putting 200,000 miles at a theoretical value of $3,700. Compared with the card's past offers, this is a solid one. The highest offer we've seen was worth up to $3,000, but earning the full amount required $50,000 in spending within six months (offer no longer available). TPG considers a $2,000-plus bonus a good time to apply for the Spark Cash Plus. Keep in mind that Capital One says the bonus may not be available to existing or previous Capital One Business cardholders. The Ink Business Cash currently offers $750 cash back, earned after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Compared with past offers, that's fairly typical. However, the card recently offered a best-ever $1,000 after $8,000 in spending within four months (offer no longer available), so this isn't the strongest bonus we've seen. You can also combine those rewards with an eligible Ultimate Rewards card and turn them into transferable points. According to TPG's October 2026 valuations, Ultimate Rewards points are worth 2.05 cents each, putting 75,000 points at a theoretical value of $1,538. Chase has its own application rules and welcome offer restrictions, including the 5/24 rule. The welcome bonus may also not be available if you've previously held the Ink Business Cash or another no-annual-fee Chase for Business card. Winner: Capital One Spark Cash Plus for businesses that can comfortably meet its much higher spending requirement. Capital One Spark Cash Plus vs. Chase Ink Business Cash: Benefits The Spark Cash Plus gets easier to justify as your business spending climbs. Capital One will refund the card's $150 annual fee once you hit $150,000 in annual spending, which makes the fee a lot easier to swallow for the kind of business this card is built for. Its no-preset-spending-limit structure can also help if your expenses swing from month to month. You can't spend whatever you want, but it does give you more flexibility than a traditional fixed credit limit. The Ink Business Cash takes a more traditional approach, with a fixed credit limit and no annual fee. That can work well for businesses with more predictable spending, while the Spark Cash Plus is better suited to businesses that need more room for large or fluctuating expenses. Both options let you add employee cards at no additional fee, making it easier to keep business spending in one place and earn rewards on those purchases, too. The Spark Cash Plus comes out ahead if your business spends internationally since it charges no foreign transaction fees; the Ink Business Cash does. Both cards also come with some useful protections. The Ink Business Cash includes primary auto rental coverage for eligible business rentals, plus purchase and extended warranty protection. The Spark Cash Plus also offers extended warranty coverage* on eligible purchases, along with other card protections. Winner: Tie. The Spark Cash Plus has more useful features for high-spending and internationally-focused businesses, while the Ink Business Cash offers useful protections and no annual fee. *For Capital One products listed on this page, some of the benefits may be provided by Visa® or Mastercard® and may vary by product. See the respective Guide to Benefits for details, as terms and exclusions apply. How to earn and redeem rewards with the Capital One Spark Cash Plus vs. Chase Ink Business Cash For businesses that can take advantage of the Ink Business Cash's 5% categories, it's tough for the Spark Cash Plus to compete. Spend the full $25,000 annual cap at office supply stores and on internet, cable and phone services, and you'll earn $1,250 with the Ink Business Cash. Put that same $25,000 of spending on the Spark Cash Plus and you'll earn $500. Outside the Ink's bonus categories, though, that advantage flips. A $10,000 purchase at the Ink's standard 1% rate earns $100 in rewards. The same purchase earns $200 with the Spark Cash Plus. This is why the amount you spend is less important than where you spend it when comparing these two cards. There's also a useful break-even point: Since the Spark Cash Plus earns 1 percentage point more than the Ink Business Cash on purchases that would earn just 1% with the Ink, $15,000 of that spending generates an extra $150 in rewards — enough to offset the Spark's annual fee. Winner on earning: Ink Business Cash for maximizing its 5% categories; Spark Cash Plus for substantial spending outside those categories. Both cards make cash-back redemptions pretty straightforward. With the Spark Cash Plus, you can redeem your rewards for cash back, statement credits, travel purchases, gift cards and eligible purchases. Your rewards also won't expire as long as the account remains open and in good standing. The Ink Business Cash rewards are technically earned as Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Redemption options include cash back, statement credits, travel through Chase Travel℠, gift cards, Amazon and PayPal purchases and Pay Yourself Back. Your points won't expire as long as the account remains open. If you're only interested in cash back, there isn't much daylight between them: 1 cent earned is basically 1 cent redeemed. Personally, I love the ability to convert Spark cash back into Capital One miles. I've transferred miles to book Avianca LifeMiles awards to Central America, getting considerably more value than I would have by redeeming for cash back. The Ink Business Cash can play a similar role with a Chase setup. TPG partnerships and newsletter editor Emily Thompson likes pairing it with other Ultimate Rewards cards, which lets her take advantage of its strong bonus categories without keeping those rewards boxed in as cash back. For travelers, this is where both cards get much more interesting. If you pair the Spark Cash Plus with an eligible Capital One miles-earning business card, you can convert your cash back into transferable Capital One miles. The Ink Business Cash works much the same way in the Chase ecosystem. On its own, its rewards don't transfer to airline and hotel programs. But you can combine your points with an eligible card such as the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), which can then transfer Ultimate Rewards points to travel partners. So in both cases, pairing the cash-back card with the right companion card can open up much more valuable redemption options. The programs also share several transfer partners, so if you already use one of those programs, the decision may come down to the partners unique to each currency. Winner on transferring: Tie. Both become transferable rewards when paired with the right card, so the stronger option largely depends on which issuer's transfer partners you prefer. Can I have both the Capital One Spark Cash Plus and Chase Ink Business Cash? Yes. These cards come from different issuers, and holding one doesn't prevent you from applying for the other. In fact, carrying both can make quite a bit of sense. Use the Ink Business Cash for 5% back on office supplies, internet, cable and phone services and 2% back at restaurants and gas stations. Then put purchases that would otherwise earn just 1% on the Spark Cash Plus for 2% back instead. If your business doesn't spend heavily enough to justify the Spark Cash Plus and doesn't have much spending in the Ink Business Cash's bonus categories, a no-annual-fee flat-rate business card may be a better fit. Should I get the Capital One Spark Cash Plus or Chase Ink Business Cash? Choose the Spark Cash Plus if your business spends heavily across a wide range of categories. Its unlimited 2% cash-back rate keeps things simple, and if you spend at least $150,000 annually, Capital One refunds the $150 annual fee. Choose the Ink Business Cash if much of your spending falls into its 5% categories, particularly office supplies, phone service, cable and internet. It also makes more sense if you already have an eligible Ultimate Rewards card that lets you convert cash back into transferable points. And if you have enough spending to make both worthwhile, there's no reason this needs to be an either-or decision. The Spark Cash Plus is a strong fit for businesses with high spending across a wide range of categories, thanks to its 2% cash back on purchases and 5% back on eligible bookings through the Capital One Business Travel portal. The Ink Business Cash can be more rewarding if a big share of your expenses falls into its 5% bonus categories, such as office supply stores and internet, cable and phone services, especially since there's no annual fee. If neither spending pattern fits your business particularly well, a simpler no-annual-fee flat-rate card may make more sense. And if you can maximize both, there's a good case for carrying both. To learn more, read our full reviews of the Spark Cash Plus and the Ink Business Cash.

item.title: If a Silent Retreat Is Too Much, Ease Into the Trend With a Silent Dinner
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The awkwardness settled over the room almost immediately, heavy enough to suppress the uncomfortable smile tugging at my cheeks as I looked around from stranger to stranger. I had, after all, signed up for a seat at this 90-minute, five-course meditative meal with 16 people Iâd never met, and had agreed to do it all without sharing a single word. But knowing youâre about to break bread in absolute silence and actually finding yourself seated at a rectangular table that looked vaguely reminiscent of a Game of Thrones feast, with the sounds of forks scraping plates, throats being cleared, the seconds ticking by on the wall clockâand most importantly, nothing elseâare two very different things. While this might sound like torture to some people, all 16 of us had willingly volunteered to participate in Rancho La Puertaâs iconic Silent Dinner, a complimentary event the wellness hotel has been hosting for at least 15 years. And weâre not the only ones intrigued by the idea of adding quiet experiences into our vacations. Hilton's 2026 Trends Report identified âhushpitalityâ as one of the year's emerging travel trends, highlighting a growing desire among travelers to seek out destinations and experiences that help turn down the noise of everyday life and embrace moments of quiet. At the Ranch, that philosophy has long been woven into the guest experience, from onsite labyrinths and silent meditation sessions to sunrise mountain hikes, all free of man-made noise. In our small private indoor dining room in the mountainous countryside of Tecate, Baja California, the absence of noise wasnât simply the backdrop to dinner; it was the main course. Once our guide rang the bell, the rules of the evening were officially in effect. To request something from our waiterâmore butter, a strawâwe had to find other ways to communicate. (When I wanted an extra slice of bread, I raised my arm and mimed slicing a loaf across the palm of my hand; thanks to my incredible thespian skills, the waiter understood.) Some guests closed their eyes throughout the meal. Others ate with their hands. Phones, already highly discouraged outside of your private guest room at the Ranch, were not allowed at the dinner at all. Instead, the various knickknacks sprinkled across our communal table offered a form of entertainment. At one point, I turned to the three-eyed ceramic creature nearest me and swiveled it around so that we were watching each other, the extra company a welcome distraction from fighting my nervous laughter that was desperate to give any explosion of sound to the evening. It wasnât until the third course was whisked away, a delightful black bean soup, that I started to settle into my chair, less interested in whether my neighbor was cringing at the sound of me slurping from my spoon and more attuned to the way my mind started to pleasantly wander. As a mother with a toddler at home in New York, my life is rarely graced with stillness. Usually, I like it that way. However, in this pocket of reprieve, where nobody needed anything from me, nobody could reach me, and I had only the vantage point of my own self for 90 whole, consecutive minutes, part of me started to shift. My shoulders fell away from my ears, I breathed deeper, and the voice in my head went from rattling through my endless to-do list to something closer to reflection. Without my brain sprinting forward, I recounted a favorite line from a book Iâd read last summer that Iâd written down in my Notes app and promptly forgot entirely. A montage of images of my daughterâs childhood sauntered by, and the ending to an article I was working on simply came to me, my writerâs block annihilated so immediately that the moment felt anticlimactic. I wasnât trying to do anything in particular, I just was. And in that was-ness, silence became an opportunity to listen, make connections, and offer surprises. When the bell tolled 90 minutes later, I wasnât the only one to involuntarily jolt from my cocoon of calm. All of us stayed after to share our observations with the group. One of the women said sheâd never smiled at so many people in a room before. An older gentleman said he had pretended like he had been sharing a meal with his late wife, which prompted his neighbor to lean over and give him a hug. Our guide thanked the person next to her who helped interpret her request for salt, the two having worked together to signal the desire to the waiter. Without conversation to fill the space between us, we became more attuned to each otherâand to ourselves. Silence, it turned out, wasnât isolating us; it was offering us a different way to connect. As our evening concluded, nobody rushed to leave. People lingered, trading observations and phone numbers. During the dinner, we had all retreated into our own little worlds, but we left having, somehow, shared one. Other hotels where travelers can embrace the quiet: - Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise: Quiet the noise at Basin, the propertyâs thermal bathing facility, and run, do not walk, to book the transformative Aufguss experience led by the on-site sauna master. Itâs a multisensory sauna experience designed around heat, scent, breath, and ritual. Their guided silent hike around Lake Louise is another highlight. - Olympic Spa Hotel: Go for the Dolomites Sleep Retreat where the absence of noise, reduced light pollution, and pure mountain air are designed to help you improve your natural sleep cycle. - Eremito: At this contemporary hermitage in the Umbrian countryside, there is no Wi-Fi, television, or mobile signal in the rooms. Instead, the experience is built around reading, nature, reflection, andâperhaps most radicallyânothing in particular.

item.title: Getting Lost in Bolivia's Wine Lands, Storied Mines, and Haunting Salt Flats
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
It is never really about the wine tasting. The balance of those subtle notes of blackberry with a finish of vanilla and leather is secondary. Wine is about landscapes and places. It is about culture and stories and the rich cast of characters: impassioned eccentrics and erudite enologists, enthusiastic amateurs and old landed families, their histories as convoluted as soap operas. Bolivian wines may not feature in many global wine shops, but in Bolivia, as is often the case, vineyards lead to some of the most interesting people in the country. I had come to the windswept altiplano in Bolivia's southwest corner, between the eastern and western cordilleras of the Andes. This vast and bleakly beautiful plateau tips away toward snow-capped mountains and empty reaches of sky. There are cactus-strewn badlands and arid highlands of lava flows; there are gulches and canyons with strange rock formations. I wanted to visit PotosÃ, one of the oldest colonial cities in the Americas, and to see the astonishing Salar de Uyuni, where new lodges have transformed the tourist experience of the salt flats. But first I wanted to drop down into the narrow fertile valleys that cut unexpectedly through the altiplano and find the winemakers around the old towns of Tarija and Tupiza, a region that surely made the first conquistadors homesick for Andalusia due to its haunting resemblance to southern Spain. If there is a Wild West feeling to Bolivian towns, with those sleepy squares of flat-fronted buildings where men, their hats tipped over their eyes, doze on chairs tilted back against walls, it may explain the country's appeal to revolutionaries and runaways, to exiles and outlaws. Che Guevara was killed here in the 1960s trying to foment revolution among Bolivian peasants. Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid were drawn here in about 1906 to make use of the superb bank-robbing opportunities and are said to have met their end just up the road from Tupiza in a hail of bullets. North of Tupiza in the Cinti Valley, astride the old smugglers' route from PotosÃ to Buenos Aires, I had lunch at San Pedro, which, having been founded in the 16th century, is one of the region's oldest vineyards. Graceful whitewashed buildings were set around the cobbled courtyards. Bougainvillea tumbled, fountains trickled, staff scurried, cooking fires blazed beneath ancient stone ovens. My guide and I were ushered into the dining room, where a long table was set with silver cutlery, delicate porcelain, and a bewildering array of engraved glasses. A waiter hovered. Dour portraits looked down from the walls, French windows were open to the vineyards below, and in the salon was a piano made on the rue de Rivoli in Paris. Eighty-something Lorgio Jaime Rivera Calabi held court at the head of the table, his eyes swimming in a face like parchment. He was a gracious host, given to long-winded toasts I struggled to follow. At the other end of the table was his 17-year-old daughter, Luciana, the knowledgeable heir to the estate who watched her aged father with a mixture of concern and admiration. Production at San Pedro is now focused on its famous singani, a white grape brandy and the Bolivian national drink. He poured a small glassful and explained its religious significance, how it was not just a drink but a libation. People used it to bless the dead, to pay tribute to gods, to seal an agreement. âMay you be as fortunate in your children as I have been,â he said, raising his glass. The old eyes seemed to fill. Luciana, embarrassed, looked away to the vines of muscatel beyond the French windows. The previous day I had been with GermÃ¡n Villamor, who, tragically, had been less fortunate with his children. His was a more recent arrival in the world of wines. The Tierra Roja estate was created by his son, Cristian, who had struggled with the idea of the family business; Villamor owned the Bolivian equivalent of Hallmark cards. After a course in viticulture in Italy, Cristian had planted a vineyard of Cabernet in the Cinti Valley. Then suddenly, in 2016, he died of an aneurysm at the age of 37. Heartbroken, Villamor sold his business and came to the town of Villa Abecia to continue his son's work. âCristian wasn't interested in making money,â he said as he showed us around the vineyard. âHe wasn't driven by commercial instincts. But he had a passion, and I have come to run the winery to honor him.â He brought in experienced enologists to advise him and planted more vines as well as citrus fruit trees. After a few years his wines began to win prizes. One vintage was bought by Central, a Lima restaurant that's among the best in the world. He told us to always harvest Malbec grapes at night because they will hold their flavors better. And to never prune under a full moon because the cuts will weep. Leading us down the rows of vines with his walking stick, Villamor was like a pilgrim seeking solace for a battered soul. In the midst of the vines, he stopped by a headstone, his son's grave. âEven if you don't see me or feel me, I am by your side,â the inscription read. âWe make a wine called Hummingbird,â said Villamor. âSometimes when I hear the birds hum, I feel it is my son speaking to me, saying he is happy with my work here. My son's death gave me a new life. I want Cristian to be proud of me.â He stretched his arms to encompass the vineyard, the verdant valley, the wide sky. âLife here is beautiful,â he said, smiling. âI am so grateful to him.â I found my soul's solace at the San Francisco de la Horca winery. Its owner, Marcelo Vacaflores RamÃrez, is a slight man in his 60s with a mischievous, elfin air. He showed us around his bodega, full of equipment assembled in another age: oak barrels, huge earthen pots whose clay lent a particular flavor to his wine. The whole place marinated in the rich, musty odor of fermenting grapes. âWe are four generations here,â he said. âI was born here. I am like one of the old cepas de uvaâthe grape vines.â In the courtyard of the house, we sat under the shade of the loggia while RamÃrez talked about the different wines and vintages as if they were personalities, close friends whom he was keen we should know and like. He appeared from the depths of the old house with platters of goat cheese and cured meats. He gleefully opened bottles (the labels handwritten; the corks sealed with beeswax) and poured wine, then more. There was a big Burgundy-style red made from the Negra Criolla grape and a wonderful Muscat of Alexandria white. I began to lose track. We had been traveling for several days, and now we were becalmed in this sylvan paradise, behind a high garden wall, among fragrant lavender bushes and the sound of birdsong. The glasses of wine kept arriving and I felt I never wanted to leave. The afternoon light filtered down through the yellow-flowering jacaranda trees. We tried the singani, treating it with due respect. This was followed by an exquisite cognac-style drink. We rounded off our tasting with an astonishing pomegranate liqueur. I was lifted from my seat reluctantly as the guide helped me into the car. In PotosÃ we stepped from passion to greed. Dating from 1545, PotosÃ owes its existence to a single and singular pyramid-shaped mountain that looms above the city streets. Cerro Rico, or Rich Mountain, was the world's most profitable source of silver. Carried across the ocean in galleons, dodging storms and English pirates (Francis Drake was said to have plundered about $600 million worth of silver in today's money), it made the Spanish monarchs the wealthiest in Europe. It was the silver used to mint Spanish dollars, or pieces of eight, the world's first international currency. It funded wars against the English, the Dutch, and the French. It is thought to have caused rampant inflation across Europe and sparked a global trade in luxury goods such as Chinese porcelain and Indian textiles. In PotosÃ it financed the grandiose palaces and churches that line the narrow streets. Greed is in the very mortar of the buildingsâexaggerated and self-important. In the basement of the colossal Casa Nacional de la Moneda, the national mint, I found the smelting rooms where enslaved Africans worked the furnaces in inhumane temperatures. The guide described how these poor souls never survived longer than six months. Cerro Rico still towers over the rooftops. And silver, tin, and zinc continue to be mined here. In the course of yielding about 66,000 tons of silver, the mountain has also sent an estimated 9 million men to an early grave, the victims of silicosis, toxic gases, mercury poisoning, tunnel collapses, dynamite accidents, and sheer exhaustion. Local guides say that as many as 20,000 men still work in the mine in conditions that have hardly changed since the 16th century. We had arranged to go inside, with a former miner acting as our tour guide. On our way to the mountain, we stopped to buy obligatory gifts for the workers: coca leaves, black cigarettes, a bottle of pure cane alcohol that was 96 percent ABV, and sticks of dynamite. Kitted up in overalls, helmets, and rubber boots, we climbed to an entrance tunnel, above which llama blood had been smeared across the rock face. We followed the guide inside, stooping to avoid banging our heads on the low ceiling. Behind us the circle of daylight at the entrance grew smaller and smaller as we stumbled along the tunnel. Suddenly there was a loud rattling, and the lights of head torches danced upon the walls ahead. We pressed against the tunnel wall as an ore cart clattered past on tracks. Coming up from the bowels of the mountain, two grimy miners, their faces running with sweat, were pushing the cart. Then there was darkness, and we fumbled with our torches to see where we were going. Cerro Rico felt like the depths of hell. I loved it. There was a devil in this hell.
