His name is El TÃo, The Uncle. We found him just beyond the point where the last ray of daylight could be seen. In a side alcove squatted a strange mannequin, covered in coca leaves and colored ribbons, sporting a huge erect phallus and a leering smile. This demonic figure, considered the Lord of the Mountain, presides over the mine. To keep the miners safe, he requires tribute. Bottles were piled by his feet as gifts. I spotted one of San Pedro singani. Packets of cigarettes had been stuffed into his stumpy hands. The sacrificial llama blood smeared above the entrance was a way to assuage his lust for blood that otherwise might only be satisfied by the death of a miner. From PotosÃ we drove west across the high plateau framed by russet hills, past llamas and vicuÃ±as grazing on tough grasses. Aloof and superior, they turned their heads to watch us, pursing their lips and batting long eyelashes. As we rose over the shoulder of a mountain dusted with green shrubs, we looked down from the pass onto a vast plain. Below was a great expanse of white, like a shining sea: the Salar de Uyuni, Bolivia's most famous salt flat. At more than 4,000 square miles, it is less than half the size of New Jersey. It's said that Neil Armstrong could see it from space. The silhouettes of dark mountains stood around its white rim. My base in this moonscape was a new upscale lodge, Jirira, created by high-end Chilean tour operator Explora, which takes clients on La TravesÃa: a bespoke journey between its sharply designed properties. From Jirira, visitors can travel across volcano ranges to the Ramaditas and Chituca lodges in Bolivia, and over the border to Explora Atacama in the Chilean desert. Until now accommodations on our wanderings had been rambling atmospheric estanciasâold-fashioned colonial properties with courtyardsâwith rooms the size of squash courts decorated with charming antiques. Special mention goes to Hotel Museo Cayara, one of the oldest Spanish houses in South America, close to PotosÃ. Built in 1557, it has many portraits of Iberian monarchs, along with muskets, dueling pistols, armor with a dented breast plate, and a library of priceless 17th-century books bound in goatskin, including a daunting 61-volume set of Voltaire. The stories of the house were like a child's book of adventures. Marquises came and went, marriages were arranged, wars raged, silver was discovered. I prowled through the back rooms, hoping to find a cupboard where sacks full of pieces of eight were hidden. Explora Jirira Lodge, however, was on another level. At first glance the building, sitting on a ridge above the flats, seemed to consist of three long shipping containers, curiously suited to this angular landscape. Designed by Chilean architect Max NÃºÃ±ez, the prefabricated modular structures were installed on stilts to have minimal impact and to allow them to be removed and repurposed. Inside, the industrial feel fell away. The interiors have an elegant simplicity, all space and light; the walls are lined with Bolivian wood, the pale furnishings are deep and inviting, the artwork reflects the flora and fauna. There is an open kitchen and two long tables for communal dinners. Designed by Mauricio LÃ³pez and SebastiÃ¡n GimÃ©nez, of hit La Paz restaurant Ancestral, the menus are proudly Bolivian, using the country's fabulous ingredients, cooked and served by locals. The lodge is one of the finest properties in Bolivia. Few places on earth are as astonishing as the Salar de Uyuni. With a fine-gravel-like surface, its far-reaching expanses glitter and sparkle. In the morning I woke to see just beneath my room flocks of flamingos, which live on the mineral marsh on the edge of the salt flats, and waited for them to rise as one and sail away, a wave of pink. We climbed K'ajchi Island, a small volcano that erupted from the seabed when the salt flats were ocean, its slopes teeming with white butterflies and strange cacti on whose flowers giant hummingbirds fed. We drove to the high shoulders of Tunupa volcano, where locals had piled cairns in tribute to the apu, or mountain spirits. Its half-collapsed cone was a riot of mineral color: red iron, yellow sulfur, and white sodium set among protrusions of black basalt. At night, brilliant constellations swarmed across the sky with such clarity I felt they might cascade down across my bed. For much of the year, stretches of the salt flats are covered in a couple of inches of water, creating a canvas of reflections. As I walked out into this mirrored world, the only things that moved were the reflections of the clouds, slowly drifting past, ravelling and unraveling around my feet. Without the usual prompts to assess scale, all sense of perspective was lost. There was no way to measure size or distance. It was a vast and peaceful nothingness. In this white void the stillness and silence were profound. The landscape of the salar, with mountains ghosting around the horizons on their reversed images, became a meditation. It was humbling. It offered the welcome gift of making me feel insignificant. And nothing is quite so good for the soul. Dehouche can arrange an 11-night Bolivian trip covering Santa Cruz de la Sierra, the wine region, PotosÃ, the salt flats, and La Paz, with all-inclusive accommodations and flights, from $17,740 per person. This article appeared in the November 2026 issue of CondÃ© Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: 11 Best All-Inclusives in Mexico for Every Bachelorette Vibe
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
When planning the ultimate bachelorette party, Mexico is an ideal destination for groups seeking equal parts value and indulgence. Thanks to the country's proximity to the US and the warmth of Mexican culture, itâs an easy sell for âI doâ crews, especially when so many all-inclusive resorts in the area offer personal planners to help make organizing your trip a breeze. All the inclusions (food, drinks, activities) and amenities can come at a price, but groups often find it worth itâyou can leave the logistics behind and focus on celebrating. But itâs not all tequila shots and late-night revelry (though thereâs that too, should you want it). In Baja California Sur, luxury stays come with outdoor adventures like golfing, surfing, and snorkeling. Along the Caribbean Sea in Riviera Maya, resorts feature sprawling wellness sanctuaries with spa menus that will leave you feeling rested and restored. And then thereâs the food: think days spent by the pool enjoying margaritas and tacos, followed by festive evenings with celebratory dinners prepared by Michelin-starred chefs. Ready to book the beachy bach of your dreams? Read on to find the best spot for you and your sun-seeking bridal party. These are the top all-inclusive resorts in Mexico for every type of bachelorette trip. - Victor EliasRead Full ReviewRoom count: 349 oceanfront rooms and suites Why we love it: Beachfront, multiple dining options, expansive spaThis resort offers a more refined approach to a bachelorette party in Tulum, with an all-inclusive package that covers dining and premium drinks. Located on a private stretch of Mexicoâs Caribbean coast, the 349-room Conrad Tulum Riviera Maya offers a seaside infinity-edge pool perfect for enjoying afternoon sunbathing and cocktails, plus a sprawling spa facility with hydrotherapy pools for a more relaxed group reset. Its 10 dining venues range from the Japanese izakaya-inspired Kengai to the Mediterranean-forward Maratea, offering your group plenty of options for celebratory dinners without leaving the resort. Location: Tulum Things to do nearby: Cenote swimming at Aktun Chen, walking the ruins at Parque Nacional Tulum, dining at Hartwood restaurant - Read Full ReviewRoom count: 15 luxury tented bungalows Why we love it: Secluded location, beach access, private plunge pools in the suitesFor ultimate luxury and serenity, take your bachelorette party to Naviva, an adults-only boutique retreat in Punta Mita made entirely of luxury tented bungalows. Each suite has a spacious outdoor deck and private plunge pool, and meals are served at Cocina Copal: open-fire cooking, freshly grilled seafood, and spicy margaritas. Between celebrations, the group can recharge with daily activities like sound healing, yoga, and hikingâplus every guest will enjoy a complimentary massage. Location: Punta Mita Things to do nearby: Boating to the Marietas Islands, surfing at La Lancha, exploring Sayulita Why we love it: Arrive by private boat, rooftop infinity pool, bachelorette conciergeSurrounded by crystal-clear water and full of laid-back beach clubs, Isla Mujeres is a picturesque setting for a bachelorette weekend. Arrive at the adults-only Almare by private boat and kick off the celebration with ceviche and lobster papadzules at beachfront restaurant Boga. Spend the next day sipping cocktails by the palm-lined pool, squeeze in hydrotherapy or sound healing at Alma Spa, and head upstairs to the rooftop infinity pool for sweeping views of the Caribbean Sea at sunset. Location: Isla Mujeres Things to do nearby: Swim with whale sharks, hike to Punta Sur and the Temple of Ixchel, bar-hop around Playa Norte and Avenida Hidalgo Read Full ReviewRoom count: 498 rooms and suites Why we love it: Adults-only pool club, rooftop suites with hot tubs, 17 restaurants and barsA stay at SLS Playa Mujeres is just as much about the beach as it is about classic revelry. Spend the day at Twiggy, an adults-only pool club with multiple hot tubs, private cabanas, and a swim-up bar, then move on to craft cocktails at Monkey Bar after dark. For the ultimate bachelorette setup, book a rooftop suite with a hot tub or one of the swim-out rooms along the resortâs winding river pool. Location: Isla Mujeres Things to do nearby: Charter a catamaran from the Playa Mujeres marina, take a day trip to Isla Mujeres Read Full ReviewRoom count: 259 rooms and suites Why we love it: Personal butler service, complimentary hydrotherapy, MoÃ«t & Chandon served by the glassFor a bachelorette thatâs equal parts wellness and indulgence, look no further than Le Blanc Spa Resort CancÃºn. While you enjoy days swimming in the Caribbean Sea and sunbathing by the infinity pool, your butler can unpack your bags, press your outfits, or draw you a post-party bath. For celebratory nights, choose between six restaurantsâfrom French and Italian to Mexican and Japaneseâand enjoy MoÃ«t & Chandon poured by the glass at dinner. Recover the next morning in the hydrotherapy circuit at Aura Spa. Location: CancÃºn Hotel Zone Things to do nearby: Playa Delfines, NichuptÃ© Lagoon, cocktails and dancing in the hotel zone - Courtesy Marquis Los Cabos Resort & Spa Read Full ReviewRoom count: 209 suites and 25 casitas Why we love it: Adults-only, three infinity pools, casitas with private plunge poolsGather your group and book a few of the private casitas at Marquis Los Cabos Resort & Spa, where your rooms will include private plunge pools and views of the Sea of Cortez. Spend the afternoon rotating between three infinity pools, including a magical three-story waterfall pool (perfect for pictures), with margaritas and fish tacos in hand. When youâre not trying to spot whales breaching in the distance, indulge in a zodiac-inspired treatment at Spa Marquis before getting ready for a teppanyaki dinner at Sakke. Location: Los Cabos Things to do nearby: Snorkel at Chileno Bay, surf at Costa Azul, bar-hop in downtown Cabo San Lucas - Courtesy Rancho La Puerta/Â©2009 John Granen Read Full ReviewRoom count: 86 private casitas Why we love it: Daily fitness classes, farm-fresh meals, holistic resetFor the bride who would rather wake up for a sunrise hike than recover from late-night tequila shots, Rancho La Puerta is the ideal resort for an all-out wellness bachelorette. Choose a three- or four-day all-inclusive stay, complete with dozens of daily fitness classes and farm-fresh meals made with Baja seafood and produce sourced from the property's organic garden. Your group can even add holistic therapies like reiki and craniosacral massage to your itinerary to make it extra restorative. Location: Tecate Things to do nearby: Wine tasting in Valle de Guadalupe, hiking Mount Kuuchumaa, visiting downtown Tecate Why we love it: Adults-only, private beach, suites with hot tubs or plunge poolsFor a more intimate, luxurious take on a Los Cabos bachelorette, book a few of the suites at Grand Velas Los Cabos for your group and prepare to be pampered. The resort sits on a private beach, so morning strolls and evening sunsets are especially breathtaking. Then thereâs the abundance of restorative treatments to choose from at SE Spa, and the colorfully tiled infinity pool set before the Sea of Cortez to enjoy. For dinners, donât miss Loto, a Japanese concept led by two-Michelin-starred chef Sidney Schutte. Location: Los Cabos Things to do nearby: San Jose del Caboâs Thursday evening Art Walk, snorkeling at nearby Cabo Pulmo National Marine Reserve, surfing at Nine Palms - The Westin Resort & Spa, Puerto Vallarta Why we love it: Adults-only area, swim-up suites, expansive spaLocated in Marina Vallarta, the Westin puts bachelorette groups close to downtown without sacrificing the tranquility of a beachfront escape. item.title: Why Do Airplane Seats Have to Be Upright for Takeoff and Landing?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
You've finally managed to fall asleep on the plane, reclining your seat ever so slightly, and then you feel a soft tap on your shoulder. "Please return your seat to its fully upright position," the flight attendant says. The abrupt wake-up call may feel like an unnecessary nuisance, but there's an important safety reason why passengers aren't allowed to recline their seats during takeoff and landing. So much so that in the US, the rule is enforced by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), says former flight attendant Lia Ocampo. âKeeping seats upright during takeoff and landing is required for safety,â she tells Traveler. âFlight attendants make an announcement to ensure all seats are upright. They enforce this rule, and passengers must comply.â Hereâs a closer look at the safety requirements behind why your airline seat must be upright for both takeoff and landing. Takeoff and landing are critical phases of flight One confusing part of the regulation is the timing of flight attendantsâ requests. It can feel frustrating when you just want to settle into your seat, recline, and get cozy before pushback. So why must your seat only be upright during takeoff and landing? Although these phases of flight are short and routine, they are among the most accident-prone stages aboard an aircraft. About 20% of fatal accidents occur during takeoff and the planeâs initial climb, and about 47% of them occur during the final descent and landing, according to recent data from Boeing. As such, cabin crew take special precautions during these times to ensure maximum safety for everyone on board. Potential evacuations could go faster with upright seats If an incident does occur during takeoff or landing, itâs possible that hundreds of passengers will need to evacuate the plane in a matter of seconds. âA reclined seat can trap the passenger behind you during an evacuation,â Ocampo explains. âThe passenger behind you has less space to get up and evacuate quickly.â Although leaning your seat back an extra inch or two might not seem like a major safety hurdle, it can make a big difference in an airline cabin that might be smoky and chaotic in the face of an emergency. âAn upright seat allows for quicker evacuations, reducing the time needed to exit the aircraft,â Ocampo says. It leaves room for the brace position in an emergency In the case of a hard landing or other safety incident, flight attendants could instruct passengers to assume the brace position. In the brace position, fliers generally are instructed to bend forward at the waist and stabilize their head with their hands by leaning on the seat in front of them. This helps protect their heads and necks from flailing on harder-than-usual impact. (The positions are usually shown in the safety card in the seatback pocket.) A passenger behind a reclined seat could be prevented from assuming the most ideal brace position in an emergency. âIt can also increase the impact and the risk of injury,â Ocampo notes. Although it might seem irritating to sacrifice extra room in a snug economy seat by putting your seatback upright, cabin crew arenât asking you to do so in order to be a nuisance. âRemember, flight attendants are there to keep you safe, so don't make their job hard by not complying,â Ocampo says. âFollowing these mandated rules makes life easier and safer for everyone on the plane, especially during an emergency.â

item.title: Florence Pugh Calls This Edenic Destination the “Eighth Wonder of the World”
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
âLovely form. Back straight, lean forward,â a voice off camera is directing Florence Pugh as she lifts two Aperol spritzes like heavy weights. âI think you might need to take a sip of the left one to make sure they're even,â the voice suggests. Pughâs laid-back, witty approach to life is part of the reason sheâs so well lovedâthat and, of course, her breathtaking talent, both on screen and off. We caught up with the actor before the release of East of Eden, a Netflix series based on the Steinbeck classic, starring Pugh as Cathy Ames and Christopher Abbott as Adam Trask. In this edition of our Globetrotter series, Pugh debates vacation red flags, remembers her favorite childhood travel memories, and nominates the eighth wonder of the world. Sightseeing or sun lounger? Sun lounger. I love to lie down and feel peaceful and read and just let the sun kiss my skin and swim in the sea and eat amazing food, and then go back to lying back down, and then get back up and eat more amazing food. That's my vacation love language: food, lying down, food, lying down, food. Best place to sun lounge? Probably Greece. I love sun lounging in Greece just because firstly, the people are gorgeous and all of the grannies and the mums that run their whole family in the tavernas just always make my heart feel full. And because of the food. I think Greek cuisine is the best cuisine because it just nails every single element perfectly. Protein, perfect. Vegetables, perfect. Homegrown goods, perfect. Tzatziki, perfect. It's perfect! Whatâs your favorite wonder of the world? Probably the Acropolis. That was such a special experience. We shot there at nighttime on The Little Drummer Girl and no one was up there. So I'll never, ever, ever get that experience ever again in my life because we were alone, just the crew and the cast. And all of the lights were lighting up the pillars and there was this beautiful shot that director Park Chan-wook had me do where I was dancing and the shadows were on the building and the ruins. It was just like it was a âpinch meâ moment all evening. It was the only night shoot that I hadn't cared what time it was just because it was so dreamy to be there. Nominate your eighth wonder of the world. Oh, Arthur's seat in Edinburgh. I love that. I love how you get to look at it from all around the city and then when you climb up there, you just get the most fantastic sense ofâ¦ Well, I've always done it when I'm knackered, and I know that when I've made it to the top, I can breathe and I can have my snacks and I can look at the view, and then I can go down and find a good pint somewhere. It's definitely a very successful feeling when you get to the top. What's your biggest vacation red flag? It's not a [vacation] red flag, it's more of the people that join you on [vacation] red flag... Itâs people that don't understand sun cream and sand, it really bothers me. And I don't know why it really bothers me, but it just does. When you put sun cream on, do not sit in the sand and then be surprised that there's sand stuck to your body. That just really grinds my gears. Describe a vacation disaster. Oh, Christ. A [vacation] disasterâ¦ What about maybe if your room isn't ready and you've arrived and you've got loads of luggage and everybody's grumpy and hungry and you want to get out to the beach but you can't and the hotel doesn't take your bags and you're like, "Ah, that's a bit of a disaster." That has happened to me. Oh, I tell you what is a [vacation] disaster. When you've purposefully woken up early to put the towel on the lounges and then you go and have a little coffee and it's early. It's like seven. And then you go back to your lounger and someone has moved your towel onto the floor so that they can have the lounger. I feel like you should get a red mark on you if you do that. So everybody else is aware that you're the type of person that would move towels so that you can get the lounger. Also, we can share. Let's just talk about sharing. Why budge my stuff? What memories do you have from your childhood vacations? Oh, sunburn. Sunburn on my shoulders and on my thighs. Running around feral, probably usually naked, just wanting to be a part of every adventure. Eating tuna salads as a child when we were in Spain, just having big chunks of albacore tuna with chunky bits of cucumber. I remember that dribbling down my chin and loving that sensation. Forgetting to eat because you're just playing for so many hours in the pool and you're actually shattered and then you finally eat and it's like you forgot to breathe for, I don't know, 10 hours. What else? Oh, going on a boat and then when you go to bed at night, you're waving. I used to love that sensation. I still thought that I'd be on the boat, so I'd close my eyes and fully pretend that I was at the front of the boat. That's a good memory. And fishing, I used to fish a lot with my dad when I was younger, and that was just a really sweet day that Toby, my brother, and my dad and I would do together and then put the fish back in the sea. What is your favorite city? I loved Auckland. I really, really did. I thought that was a very special place. Auckland and maybe Tokyo, just because it's so special and otherworldly and not things that I see every day. So yeah, those two places. Do you collect souvenirs? I do, actually. In the last few years, I've started to collect. When I was younger and I looked at magnets in tourist shops, I always thought, who buys them? I've become that person. I buy magnets. But the rule is you either get a really beautiful, ornate, stunningly created, designed one, or if they don't have those, then you get the tackiest, most disgusting, cheap, yucky one. And so my fridge is this fantastic array of beautiful magnets and awful magnets, and I love itâ¦ My favorite isâ¦ I went to Sri Lanka last year. There's a little bottle magnet of Lion Beer and the liquid moves on the inside and I just thought that was quite cool.

item.title: The Best Things to Do in Laguna Beach, Orange County's Historic Arts Enclave
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Laguna Beach is a place of loreâthatâs especially true for millennials who watched the eponymous reality show that ran for three seasons in the early aughts and reunited earlier this year. Though there is some truth to the luxury lifestyle Laguna Beach exudes in pop culture, the cityâs roots go deeper. Originally, of course, Laguna Beach was inhabited by Indigenous groups who stayed for the lush areaâs natural resources and fostered a culture of music, art, and storytelling. This legacy continued into the early 1900s when outside artists started flocking to the area to live and work in what became an artist colony. Still today, itâs hard to stand on any corner of the city and not see art in some form. Take one look at its rugged coastline, craggy coves, and expansive wilderness, and you might just get the urge to relocate here yourself. These are the best things to do in Laguna Beach, California. John Wayne International Airport (SNA), ranked among the best airports in the country, is a 20-to-30-minute drive away. Especially in the summertime, Laguna Beach is not without traffic and finding a parking spot can sometimes be a challenge. Walking around town is a great option, depending on where you stay, as is taking a rideshare. But the most fun transportation option are the iconic blue and gold Laguna Beach Trolleys, which run year round with an expanded summer schedule and stop at points of interest. Take one look at the coastline and sitting on the beach becomes activity number one. Aliso Beach, Main Beach, and Victoria Beach are all worth your time. But you canât go wrong with any part of Lagunaâs seven miles of coastline, which are all a part of Californiaâs Marine Protected Areas to preserve the diverse rocky intertidal and shallow kelp reefs. To get up close, check out eight different tide pool locations throughout the city. (Pro tip: Go to the cave at Treasure Island.) To get one of the best views, youâll need to put in some physical effort. Climb the two-mile-steep hike up to Top of the World, for expansive views of the ocean and inland Orange County at just about 1,000-feet above sea level. For great views and a stroll without as much of a workout, Heisler Parkâs trails will do just fine. Laguna Beach is more than beaches, even though most places you can still snag a view. Spend part of your day at the Laguna Art Museum, which was founded in 1918 by a group of local artists and sits right on Pacific Coast Highway (please, call it PCH). Home to a diverse collection of California art, they also host events, such as their upcoming annual Art + Nature celebration (November 1-9, 2026). If it is (more than likely) too nice out to spend all day inside, join in on the First Thursdays Art Walk from 6-9 p.m. Enjoy walking around town and pop into some of the 40 odd art galleries that open their doors (often with wine and charcuterie). Festivals are the name of the game in Laguna Beach in the summertime. Attend Pageant of the Masters, which has been going strong since 1932, where volunteer performers re-enact famous pieces of art on stage. Show-goers often bring binoculars with the hopes of catching small movements during their poses. The Sawdust Art Festival, which is wrapping up its 60th season, is an idyllic outdoor art show with art for sale at a variety of price points. Youâll have the chance to speak to the artists, along with watching demos and attending workshops, all while walking in a eucalyptus grove. Book a show at the Laguna Playhouse, which was founded in 1920. This fall, they are putting on the world premier of Wild Child. When it comes to shopping, there are endless options, but be sure to check out Thalia Surf, where you can buy (or just admire) retro surfboards and unique apparel, Gorjana, a jewelry brand that was founded on the floor of a Laguna Beach apartment, and Laguna Beach Books, an independent, women-owned bookstore with great author events. Where to eat (and drink) in Laguna Beach, from tacos to Michelin-star Japanese What better way to start your day than with your toes in the sand and breakfast burrito in your hand? Lost Pier Cafe is literally on Aliso Beach. Bring a towel and get your food and coffee to go sit on the beach and watch the morning skimboarders catch a wave. (See for yourself with this live webcam of the surf.) If youâre on the hunt for a classic beach diner breakfast, Orange Inn and Penguin Cafe have been serving up locals since 1931 and 1942, respectively. For a mid-morning coffee pick me up, you will not be short on options. Try Jedidiah Coffee for a sit on their idyllic patio (youâll feel like you're in your best friend's backyard), Thorne Brothers Coffee, for an interior that will make you want to cozy up with a good book no matter the temperature, or Sur Coffee for coastal vibes and a cold brew that canât be beat. Wigz, which got its namesake because it is located in a former wig shop, is a great choice for lunch, boasting sandwiches on delicious Dutch crunch bread (a San Francisco delicacy that has, thankfully, made its way south). If you donât have the restraint to wait to eat it until you get back to the beach, they have a cozy patio, where they will also serve you a local beer. Tacos and surf culture go together like the sun and the sand. The Taco Stand's Laguna's location might be their most interesting, set in the third-oldest Taco Bell in the world: Order the warm and freshly made chips to start. For a higher-end experience, Rebel Omakase is the only restaurant in Laguna Beach with a Michelin star; here youâll find a pre-fixe menu filled with ceviches and raw shellfish that are all imported across the Pacific from Japan. For the turf, head to Selanne Steak Tavern, located in a historic 1934 home on PCH, for steaks served in a much airier and brighter space than your typical leather-boothed steakhouse. Fun fact, itâs owned by Hockey Hall of Famer and six-time Olympian Teemu Selanne and local businessman Kevin Pratt. For burgers in a more casual space, Ahba is the place to be for a delicious wagyu burger with caramelized onions and a creamy aioliâmake it a double. Keeping it cool, but casual, Truly Pizza recently opened their second location in another quaint little bungalow on PCH. They source their ingredients from local farms in Orange County and were recently ranked the fourth best pizza in the country. Simple, yet absolutely perfect, try the Champion Cheese, or for a more unique pie, the Umami Mushroom, both of which will have a thick, bubbly, long-fermented crust. For a pre- or post-dinner beverage, Laguna Beer Company, founded in 2014 by two natives, has a wide array of style options, along with their own diverse food menu. If youâre more into wine, McClain Wine Cellars, which is one of a small number of Black-owned wineries in the country, offers red and white options sourced from vineyards in the Santa Ynez Valley. Or end your day with some Gelato Paradisoâin the summer, expect to get in line, although itâll be worth the wait. (Try the pistachio gelato with imported nuts from Bronte, Italy.) Laguna Beach is not short on luxury hotels. Montage Laguna Beach offers rooms and suites, along with three bedroom villas that can sleep up to eight people. Youâll enjoy its pristine, mosaic-laden pool with dramatic ocean views and its wide variety of restaurants on site, which draw even non-hotel patrons. Though you should definitely explore everything else Laguna Beach has to offer, if you donât feel like leaving Montage property, no one will blame you. Casa Loma Beach Hotel, which was recently reimagined, is right in walkable downtown Laguna. There are views, of course, and design-focused rooms embracing âCaliforniaâs coastal spirit," along with live music sessions just for hotel guests. (And they offer freshly baked chocolate chip cookies from local bakery Rye Goods.) Hotel Joaquin is a motel, but donât let that word fool you: The once dilapidated building has been restored into a space that takes inspiration from âthe island of St.Barths, the 1950s Southern California beach culture, and the timeless and pristine aesthetic of the Mediterranean coast.â Itâs exactly where you should be staying in a beach town. For those preferring a home away from home, there are plenty of Airbnbâs around such as this Charming Manzanita Red Cottage, built in 1927 by Hollywood film producer Harry Green, or this Ocean View Beach House, with a beautiful patio perfect for year-round alfresco dining. Just have a sweatshirt ready for when the marine layer rolls in.

item.title: The Most Exciting Hotel Openings of Fall 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
There was a time when fall was hospitalityâs quiet seasonâthe quiet lull between summer beach trips and ski season escapades, the time when back to school and back to work meant people largely stayed home. Not anymore. The trend that advisors and insiders seem to be talking about these days is how shoulder season is the new peak season. And this season, some of travelâs most exciting debuts are landing in this exact window: an English country-style inn from the beloved SingleThread team in Healdsburg, California; new boutique options in New Orleans and Savannah, two of the Southâs most popular destinations this time of year; and an effortless YucatÃ¡n long weekend escape, too. If an autumn getaway is in your future, these are the most exciting hotel openings to have top of mind. The Selvedge, A SingleThread InnâHealdsburg, California Where itâs located: Along the Russian River in Healdsburg, the heart of Sonoma County, The Selvedge stands a short stroll from everythingâtasting rooms, restaurants and boutiques. Why weâre excited: It makes sense that the three-Michelin-starred SingleThread team would expand their award-winning vision of hospitality, and the transition from restaurant to inn feels natural. Owners Kyle and Katina Connaughton have transformed the old River Belle Inn by drawing on their years traveling and living in England, and the result makes so much sense for this destination. Think afternoon tea and Sunday roastsâwith killer wine pairings to match. With interiors by AvroKO, this ten-room property features both garden-view and riverside rooms, cozy fireplaces, a two-bedroom suite with its own Miele kitchen, and communal spaces including library, parlor, and coffee bar. Best of all? Your rate includes a full-service breakfast prepared by the restaurantâs culinary team, and dinner in the restaurant is guaranteed for guests of the inn. During harvest season when Healdsburgâs best reservations are that much trickier to secure, that perk alone is worth its weight in gold. The Observatory, A Viceroy ResortâSun Valley, Idaho Where itâs located: In downtown Ketchum, a few minutes away from skiing at Sun Valley Resort. Itâs inside the Central Idaho Dark Sky Reserve, the nationâs first Gold Tier International Dark Sky Reserve, spanning more than 1,400 square miles of protected night skies. Why weâre excited: While other Rocky Mountain towns have become more about the scene than the skiing, Sun Valley has quietly charted its own course, which is exactly why itâs feeling so special this season. The resort has long been a hideaway for billionaires and Hollywood types, but its hospitality scene has lacked a real luxury option until now. The Observatory isÂ one ofÂ Viceroyâs first openings since announcing its comprehensive brand launch two years ago, and it has all the polish you would expect: 73 slick guest rooms, 12 lavish penthouses, a full-service spa, restaurant, cafÃ© and bar. But itâs the rooftop observatory that will be the propertyâs defining feature and clearest embodiment of Viceroyâs new experience-driven ethosâwith programming led by local astronomer and celestial photographer Travis Amick, including stargazing, private sessions and experiences timed to astronomical events such as meteor shower sand planetary alignments. The Observatory will be great for skiing, yes, but it will be great for much more, too. Where itâs located: Overlooking Jackson Square in the heart of Savannahâs Historic District, Recess Hotel & Club is the transformation of the 114-year-old Manger Building, one of the cityâs first skyscrapers, originally built as the Hotel Savannah in 1912. Why weâre excited: Thereâs something in the water when it comes to creativity in Savannah. From the outsize presence of the Savannah College of Art and Design, to its countless oak trees draped dramatically in Spanish moss, itâs a perfect backdrop for cool hotels. Recess is the latest from Left Lane, the hospitality team behind Savannahâs Hotel Bardo. The 221-key property embraces its historic setting with a self-proclaimed ânew old school and retro-futurist design philosophyââa colorful, modern interpretation of the Manger Buildingâs historic bones. Itâs a hotel that doesnât take itself too seriously and stands for the idea that hotels should be social and fun: think cleverly designed bunk rooms, rooftop pool and bar, and âRumpus Roomsâ on each guest floor stocked with mahjong tables and vintage video games. For a fun weekend getaway on the East Coastâemphasis on funâthe aptly named Recess makes a convincing case. The Warbler HotelâNew Orleans, Louisiana Where itâs located: On St. Charles Avenue in New Orleansâ historic Garden District, one of the cityâs loveliest neighborhoods, known for its 19th-century mansions and oak-lined streets. The Warbler sits on a streetcar line and the Mardi Gras parade route. Why weâre excited: The Warbler marks the first hotel from local real estate development firm Verdad, and deep local roots show in every detail. The 58-key, six-story hotel takes its name from the Jazz Age term for a singer, and its design evokes the sleek grandeur of the Streamline Moderne movement. Each aspect of the hotel has been touched by people with deep New Orleans roots. To name a few: the architecture by local firm EskewDumezRipple; the interiors by designer Jamie Bush, who sits on the Deanâs Advisory Council at the Tulane School of Architecture; and the bar by CureCo, the group behind other NOLA favorites including Cure and Cane & Table. One particularly useful feature: a mix of one-, two-, and three-bedroom suite configurations that make this a flexible option for families and groups. Where itâs located: Oyster Estate is in the center of Greenport Village on Long Islandâs North Fork, a five-minute walk from the LIRR station and Shelter Island ferry. This area is popular for its vineyards, farms and breweries, and feels especially alive during harvest season. Why weâre excited: Itâs a full reimagining of the historic Greenporter Hotel, purchased by Blue Flag Capital in late 2022 and transformed over the last year into a 34-room boutique experience. To usher in the premisesâ new era, Blue Flag enlisted Islyn Studioâwho also did Dune House in Florida and The Tusk Bar in New York Cityâto spearhead the design, which swaps stark white walls for warm beige tones, wood finishes and textured ceilings that flow from common areas into the guest rooms. The refreshed courtyard pool acts as the propertyâs social nucleus, as does Fortune Favors, its Asian-inspired restaurant and cocktail bar. Where itâs located: Itâs the anchor of West Palm Beachâs emerging NORA District, which has all sorts of shops, restaurants, bars, galleries, fitness studios, and all the walkable things that can be hard to find in Florida. Why weâre excited: A lot of Floridaâs visitors focus their time on the glitzier Palm Beach across the Intracoastal, but the arrival of The Nora Hotel is a stamp of approval for whatâs happening on this side of the bridge. It also marks the first major collaborative project outside of New York City between award-winning hoteliers Sean MacPherson and BD Hotels, who have shaped New Yorkâs cultural landscape going on 20 years with projects like The Bowery, Hotel Chelsea and The Ludlow Hotel. As such, The Nora brings the sophisticated, moody interiors of Lower Manhattan to the otherwise sun-drenched, Lilly Pulitzer-esque Palm Beach area. The Nora opens this fall with a splashânamely, the Floridian debut of famed Starr Restaurants concept Pastis, a Sisley Spa, as well as a rooftop restaurant, Lillys. The property is debuting as a member of Leading Hotels of the World, ushering in a new era of luxury for the area, and proving that, yes, chic and fabulous things can happen on either side of the Intracoastal. Where itâs located: Itâs set within AMAI, a sprawling hotel development between CancÃºn and Puerto Morelos, located within a mangrove landscape that gradually opens onto the Caribbean. Itâs close enough to CancÃºn International Airport that it can be easily done as a long weekend from the East Coast, but feels like a true getaway. Why weâre excited: Park Hyatt is on something of a Mexico spree, having opened Park Hyatt Cabo del Sol last December and with Park Hyatt Mexico City still to come in the new year, and Riviera Maya is particularly notable as it is the brandâs first all-inclusive resort. But donât mistake this for the all-inclusive experience you think you knowâeverything here is done in true Park Hyatt luxury. All 152 guest rooms overlook the Caribbean, and each guest gets a dedicated Resort Ambassador who serves as a dedicated point of contact throughout your stay. Food is a major focus here, with a chef-led program that spans seven distinct venues. Wellness is another focus, with a beachfront pool, open-air spa garden, and access to El Tinto Golf Course.

item.title: The 50 Best Gifts You Can Buy the Traveler in Your Life
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The best gifts for travelers occupy a particular sweet spot: theyâre personal, but also useful enough to take up some precious carry-on space. The frequent flier in your life probably has much of their travel kit on lock, so they can be a tricky person to shop for. Your gift has to work that much harder: A clever piece of gear they never knew they needed, a skincare fix that makes their next long-haul flight a little more civilized, or a small luxury they may not consider buying for themself. From smart tech to hard-working accessories, Iâve rounded up 50 thoughtful gifts travelers will genuinely want to pack on their next trip. These are the gadgets and gear theyâll appreciate every time, with options to impress every type of journeyer. Whether you decide to upgrade their luggage or help them capture their favorite travel memories with a curiously small camera, these gift ideas have you covered. FAQ: What do you get someone who is always traveling? Frequent travelers are probably well-stocked with the basics, so I'd recommend thinking outside the box. The next time they're filling you in on their travels, make a mental note of any pain points they mentionâif they regularly fly in economy, maybe they could use a foot hammock. If they're heading somewhere for a long-term stay, send them a duplicate of something they love from home but likely left behind, like a warm robe or cozy pair of slippers. What is the best way to gift travel? Gift cards are the easiest option. For the travelers in your life who are keen on staying in a rental, Airbnb gift cards can be purchased in amounts from $25 up to $500, so you can chip in (or cover) their next stay. Calling rideshares while traveling can quickly add up; a gift card to Lyft or Uber helps relieve any back and forth over whether a car is worth it or not, making it a great gift for younger travelers heading out on group trips or gap years. What are the best travel gifts for new travelers? For new and aspiring jet-setters, consider the basics. A nice leather passport holder will be appreciated. If they're heading abroad, a universal travel adapter will come in handy, as will a phone case with a compartment to keep cards, cash, or an ID easily accessible. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Meaghan Kenny.

item.title: The Best Hotels in Napa Valley for a Weekend in Wine Country
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Napa Valley, California, has come a long way since 1839, when American settler George C. Yount planted the first grapevines in the area. More than two centuries later, it's now regarded as one of the most beloved and prestigious wine destinations in the world. Encompassing four regionsâincluding Oakville, Rutherford, and five towns from American Canyon to Calistogaâthe area boasts more than 400 wineries and counting, plus acclaimed restaurants helmed by lauded chefs and a diverse selection of boutique hotels and luxury resorts for solo travelers, families, and couples alike. As a California native who has lived in big cities most of my life (including nearby San Francisco), I swapped city life for a slower pace in Northern Californiaâs Wine Country a few years ago, and I havenât looked back. It's given me plenty of time to get more acquainted with Napa Valley's hotel scene, and I've rounded up my favorite spots in the region I call home below. From an eco-luxe hotel and spa poised on a former family homestead in Yountville to a reconceived 203-room resort with a wellness wing in Napa, read on for the best hotels in Napa Valley for your next trip. Our top picks: - Best for a stay in downtown Napa: Archer Hotel Napa - Best for something transportive: Okaeri Calistoga FAQ: What are the best cities to stay in Napa Valley? As clichÃ© as it sounds, thereâs something for everyone in Napa Valley, as each city has its own distinct personality and scene. Downtown Napa is the bustling main hub, with walkability to tasting rooms and easy freeway access to other areas further north. Calistoga lures wellness seekers with geothermal hot springs and a laid-back vibe, while idyllic Yountville attracts culinary enthusiasts and wine aficionados with its storybook-esque setting. When is the best time to visit Napa Valley? Thereâs no such thing as a âbadâ time to visit Napa Valley. But my personal favorite season here is spring. The weather is ideal, and everything is just greener. A close second is winter. Itâs quieter overall, and chilly evenings and misty (and sometimes frosty) mornings mean cozying up in a comfy robe and slippers. If you prefer the heat, come in summer. Itâs warm and dry. How we choose the best hotels in Napa Valley Every hotel review on this list has been written by a CondÃ© Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.
