item.title: The 8 Most Exciting New Restaurants in India
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The CondÃ© Nast Traveller x District Top Restaurant Awards powered by Visa have been announced, celebrating the 50 best restaurants across India. Eligibility for the list required restaurants to have opened before January 1, 2026, which left some of the year's most exciting new openings just outside the window. This is where they get their due. This year's crop spans the country and refuses to sit still: a Hyderabad bar built around the idea of a village chaupal, a Delhi tasting menu nine years in the making from Gaggan Anand, and a Bengaluru dessert-only degustation born out of a sisters' supper club. There's a pizza workshop obsessed with fermentation science, a cocktail-and-tasting-menu hybrid that runs only on weekends, and a chef's long-awaited return to the city that made him. None of these restaurants qualified for this year's Top 50, but each is already shaping the way we eat and drink, and every one of them deserves an honourable mention. Here are the hottest new restaurants in India this year. Hyderabad's bars have been getting bigger for years, so restaurateur Vickas Passary built Kadamba to go the other way: a warm, intimate space in Hitech City modelled on the idea of a village chaupal, the community hub where everyone already knows your order. The room is anchored by a 30-foot omakase-style bar that puts guests and bartenders at eye level, and mixologist Sujan Shetty's menu runs on nostalgia with a technical edge, from an Aam-Chur with tequila and olives to a Bloody Mary rebuilt with black garlic and raspberry. Chef Jyoti Singh's food travels the country too, pulling from a 2019 backpacking trip through Bihar, Nagaland, Kerala and Assam into dishes like Chena Paturi and a donne mutton pulao. It's the kind of bar Hyderabad's maximalist nightlife hasn't made room for in a whileâ unpretentious, pan-Indian, and built for staying a while. The Kowloon Tiger comes from Ilvika Chandawarkar, second-generation restaurateur at Pune's Malaka Spice Hospitality Group, and her partner Prantik Haldar, previously bar head at The Bombay Canteen. The idea was born on a trip to Hong Kong and Kyoto, where a wrong turn led them to a neighbourhood bar that became their regular spot, and they wanted to build something with the same pull in Baner. The 35-seat room leans into an Asian-alley, speakeasy mood, with a lower-level omakase-style bar where the real energy sits. Rohan Mahabal's food runs through Hong Kong and Japan with a heavy hand for pork, including dandan noodles with a peanut base and a Sichuan-heavy pork sausage chili fry, while Haldar's cocktail list names each drink after a character, from the Earl Grey-and-melon Blue Lantern to the scotch and black sesame Black Myth. MinibÃ© started as a monthly supper club run out of sisters Jenny and Steffi Clinta's apartment, and is now a permanent, 20-seat spot in Indiranagar built around a nine-course dessert tasting menu. Chef Jenny trained through a diploma in Bengaluru, an internship at Restaurant Salicorne in Normandy, and a bootcamp under pastry chef Will Goldfarb in Bali, before shaping it all around memories of growing up in Minnie Bay on the Andaman Islands. The menu, called Sagarika, moves from savoury to sweet, opening with a Marina Bites course of pani puri made from puffed potato and a yellowfin tuna cutlet based on her mother's recipe, and building through a chicken shikampuri kebab and a Mont Blanc reworked with chickoo and cashew. It closes with a Petit Fours course that includes a Kolkata-style potato samosa and a crÃ¨me caramel from the chefs' grandmother. It's rare to find a tasting menu built entirely around dessert, rarer still one this personal. Nila comes from chef Rahul Sharma, a graduate of the Oberoi group's STEP programme whose path runs through two stints with the opening team at Masque, an internship at noma, and a stretch leading the kitchen at Araku, where he met his eventual investor, Ola's Bhavish Aggarwal. Set in a remodelled bungalow in Cambridge Layout, the space leans Japanese-Scandinavian, with rounded archways and a one-wall open kitchen, and the 12-course tasting menu is built around the forests and tribal food traditions of India's northeast, particularly Nagaland. A Black Rice Momo arrives with a glutinous, nutty filling nothing like a usual momo, and a Tree Tomato Custard pairs a Nagaland tamarillo with a cheese broth laced with confit wild garlic. The menu changes every three months, and Sharma promises to keep digging into regions of the country that rarely make it onto a tasting menu at all. rÄga is Gaggan Anand's long-awaited Indian homecoming, run day-to-day in Janpath by chef Rydo Anton, his Jakarta-born right hand, since Anand himself splits his time between the Delhi kitchen, his Bangkok restaurant and a hotel project in Japan. The 22-dish menu runs nearly three hours and is deliberately less intense than Anand's Thailand flagship, with a page of house rules on phone use and smoke breaks handed out before the welcome drink. The highlights carry real weight. A tribute to the Bombay sandwich is a technical showpiece, a cup of chicken dashi with Japanese puffed rice and toasted tea tastes like something worth returning for on a rainy night, and the bhetki paturi builds from mustard to kaffir lime to green chilli in a single, restrained bite. It's vegetarian-forward, the bar is tucked out of sight, and at Rs11,111 a head before taxes, it is one of Delhi's most anticipated and most expensive new tables this year. The Cavity is a nine-seat basement experience tucked beneath Barbet & Pals in GK II, where co-founders Jeet Rana and Chirag Pal pair cocktails built around India's GI-tagged, seasonal ingredients with food from chef Amninder Sandhu, running Fridays through Sundays only. The nine courses move between drink and dish, from a Sundarban honey mead with cotton candy to a Tooyamalli rice cocktail with clarified rasam, whiskey and rice foam, served alongside a Gunpowder Idli filled with pepper crab and caviar. Portions are deliberately small, capped at 240 milliliters of alcohol per person across the whole tasting, so the point is range rather than volume. The standout pairing is the Black Cardamom cocktail, smoky with single malt and mezcal, next to Sandhu's nihari reworked with compressed shank meat. It's a rare instance of a cocktail menu and tasting menu built as equals rather than one serving the other. Yokocho is chef Auroni Mookerjee's return to Kolkata, two years after he left Sienna Calcutta, the restaurant he helped place at number five on this list in 2023. Tucked on Park Street behind a deliberately maze-like entrance, modelled on the back-alley izakayas of Tokyo, the restaurant runs on Mookerjee's bajaar-to-table instincts but stretches them across Asia, with a rotating bank of 25 to 30 banchan made entirely from local market produce, from pickled Malabar spinach seeds to dried shrimp. A Xiao Long Bao built on a slow-cooked chicken broth comes in a bowl handcrafted by Sienna Calcutta, and a pork belly char siu gets a topping of crunchy shrimp shutki in place of fish sauce. The drinks, developed with Pankaj Balachandran of Countertop, include a whisky highball made with water softened in clay pots over days. It's a quieter, more restrained version of a chef who built his name on going big, which might be exactly the point. Pizza No Cap opened on Ulsoor Road in February this year, founded by chefs Rahul Singh and Vichita Kumar alongside Siddharth Nest, whose background in microbiology shapes how the team treats pizza dough, which is cold-fermented for up to 96 hours and adjusted for Bengaluru's climate and the seasons. The 40-seat space is built like an open workshop, with a handmade wood-fired brick oven and counter seating that lets diners watch the whole process, from dough to bake. Start with the Parma & Peru Pizzette, a mini pizza layered with Parma ham and guava jam that chef Vichita based on her own after-school snacking memories, mixing something familiar with something a little more expensive. The Kerala Flex is also worth trying. It's a young, still-evolving menu, but the obsession with getting the dough right is already the kind of thing worth building a reputation on. A version of this story originally appeared in CondÃ© Nast Traveller India.

item.title: 8 Best Boutique Hotels in Philadelphia, From Historic Townhouses to Chic Apartments
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The best boutique hotels in Philadelphia draw on some of the cityâs greatest treasures: its historic architecture, vibrant art scene, and diverse and distinct neighborhoods. Iâve lived in Philly for more than a decade, reporting on the cityâs hospitality and culture, and I love introducing visitors to the places that make my hometown special. While there are plenty of traditional hotels that fit that description, the properties on this list offer a more intimate way to experience the City of Brotherly Love. All have fewer than 100 roomsâsome just a handfulâwith singular design, personalized hospitality, and a true sense of place that reflects both the people behind them and their surrounding communities. The options range from lovingly restored buildings with stories of feminist trailblazers to contemporary suites filled with work by independent artists and makers. Some come with the perks of a private members club; others offer beautifully furnished apartments that make a longer stay appealing. All put you within reach of some of the city's best restaurants, independent shops, cultural gems, and local hangouts. Read on to find my picks of the eight best boutique hotels in Philadelphia. FAQ: What does it mean when a hotel is a boutique hotel? A boutique hotel is typically a smaller hotel, with fewer than 100 rooms, plus distinct design, a keen sense of place, and a more personalized feel. Theyâre often independently owned properties, though they can belong to a larger hotel brand or collection. What is the most luxurious hotel in Philadelphia? It depends on your definition of luxury, but if it includes stunning architecture, fine- dining restaurants, consistently thoughtful service, plush accommodations with epic city skyline views, and a 57th floor infinity pool that you wonât stop gushing about, then itâs the Four Seasons Philadelphia. Where should I avoid staying in Philadelphia? Unless youâre visiting for a concert or sporting event, skip the hotels near the stadiums in deep South Philadelphia. Theyâre less convenient for exploring Center City, Old City, Fishtown, and other popular neighborhoods. How we choose the best hotels in Philadelphia? Every hotel review on this list has been written by a CondÃ© Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

item.title: I Took the UAE's New Train Service From Dubai to Abu Dhabi—Here’s What It's Like
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
For as long as Iâve lived in the UAEâalmost 16 yearsâtrips between Abu Dhabi and Dubai have meant getting in a car and joining the steady stream of traffic heading south, confined behind the wheel for an hour or two, depending on the day's traffic. Itâs a ritual familiar to commuters and sightseers alike. But now, that journey is changing. Etihad Rail has launched its first passenger service between the UAE's two biggest cities, offering a fresh perspectiveâand speedâon a route long confined to the road. Dubai joined the UAEâs national passenger rail network on Wednesday, September 30, when Al Yalayis Station opened beside Jumeirah Golf Estates. On the same day, passenger services extended to Al Dhaid in Sharjah. These two additions mark the second major stage of Etihad Rail's rollout, following on from the Abu Dhabi-Fujairah route, which began operating in June as part of a phased expansion that will bring the 10 announced passenger stations into operation by the end of March 2027. After opening its doors to much fanfare on Wednesday evening, a rumble of excitement is still palpable the following morning as I arrive at Al Yalayisâ vast, glassy facade to test the experience. Hereâs what to expect when you ride Etihad Rail from Dubai to Abu Dhabi. Dubaiâs station is suitably forward-thinking. A dedicated pedestrian bridge will soon connect it directly to Dubai Metroâs Red Line, while Nol integration lets passengers add a day pass for the bus, tram and metro to their rail ticket via a QR code. The interior is expansive, with grand, high ceilings and well-designed, comfortable armchair seating unlike the train-station pews I am used to. Hospitality is woven into the experience from the off, with free Arabic coffee offered to all passengers and a dedicated lounge with complimentary food and drinks for those traveling in Premium class. For those traveling in standard class with Comfort tickets, thereâs a Starbucks, Shot Neighbourhood Coffee, WHSmith and soon-to-open McDonald's, along with a vending machine selling affordable hot meals. Access to the two platforms is via escalators, a lift, or stairs, all well-signed and large enough to accommodate passenger volumes. Purchasing tickets at the station is simple, with easy-to-use touchscreens manned by helpful staff members. After entering a few details, passengers receive both a digital and physical copy of their ticketsâcertainly a perk if youâre keen to collect a piece of inaugural memorabilia. Though prices are higher when purchased in person, starting from Dh60 ($16) for Comfort or Dh130 ($35) for Premium, compared with Dh39 ($10) and Dh129 ($35) when purchased online. Boarding begins at Platform 2, where Etihad Rail staff guide passengers to the correct carriages. Stepping onto the train felt surreal, an experience previously confined to my trips aboard. Carriages are decked out with high-end finishesâincluding charging ports, foldable tables, shutters and free Wi-Fiâmaking it clear youâre in a country where comfort is a valued commodity. The cushioned seats in Comfort offer ample room, while the Premium seats recline, giving passengers even more space to sit back. As the train pulls away from the station, Arabic coffee and chocolates are handed out, later followed by a snack box with two shawarma sandwiches, a cake and a bottle of water, all included in the ticket price. A highlight of Comfort class is the karak (which you have to request from staff). Dreamed up by Emirati chef Maitha Warshaw, the spiced tea is intensely creamy and sweet, and Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan praised its flavor during the trainâs inaugural voyage. While the scenery visible from the train might not be as pretty as the mountainous route from Fujairah, the windows offer an interesting, previously unseen view of the emirate as you journey through industrial zones, farmland, and arid desertscapes. The ride takes one hour and four minutes, averaging 200 kilometres per hour, 150 km/h less than the planned high-speed service that will roll out in the coming months, set to take just 35 minutes to travel between the emirates. As you approach Mohamed bin Zayed City, it's clear youâve reached theÂ capital, with the platform and station bustling with commuters. The stationâs location puts you in the heart of the residential area of the same name, which is close to Dalma Mall and Mussaffah. For those wanting to venture further into the emirate, thereâs a Dh10 ($3) shuttle bus between here and the ADNOC headquarters on Corniche Road West, the ADNEC Centre on Al Khaleej Al Arabi Street, and Reem Mall on Reem Island. For those who are among the first to take advantage of this new way to travel across the UAE, it might feel like a novel experience, but this route will soon become an essential part of everyday life for the many people who make the regular journey between the country's two biggest hubs. And after years spent behind the wheel on Sheikh Zayed Road, it's certainly a welcome change to let someone else steer the way. This article was originally published on CondÃ© Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: 25 Best Beaches in Florida, From South Beach to Amelia Island
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Florida has more than 1,300 miles of coastline, and choosing its best beaches is an exercise in splitting hairsâor, more accurately, grains of sand. Along the Gulf Coast, spectacular stretches of powder-white sand meet waters that can look downright Caribbean, while the Atlantic side counters with cinnamon-hued shores, coral-fringed coves, wave-friendly breaks, and the glamorous beaches of Miami. What makes Floridaâs beaches so compelling is just how different they can be. Some stretch for miles through undeveloped state parks; others come backed by Art Deco architecture, beachfront hotels, and promenades made for people-watching. A few require a ferry or seaplane to reach. Along the way, they serve as gathering grounds for families and fishermen, surfers and sun-worshippers, wildlife lovers and, in some corners of the state, LGBTQ+ travelers looking for a welcoming patch of sand. Whether youâre plotting a laid-back Gulf Coast escape, a road trip through the Keys, or a hotel-hopping weekend along Miami Beach, thereâs a shoreline here for it. From the Panhandle to South Florida and back up the opposite coast, these are the 25 best beaches in Florida, plus our picks for where to stay nearby. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Birmingham, Alabama, Is Called The Magic City For Good Reason
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
âEverything begins and ends with Frank Stitt,â someone declared when I asked what I should do in Birmingham, Alabama. I'd heard this sentiment before, having stopped through the city a handful of times over the last 20 years. Unfailingly, the advice from both locals and fellow travelers insisted on reservations at chef Frank Stitt and his wife Pardis's restaurants, foundational not just in the course of Birmingham's food history but the country's. On my first trip, in 2010, after a fever-dream stint reporting on the Deepwater Horizon oil rig catastrophe off the Louisiana coast, I sat in the cozy clamor of Bottega, the Stitts' classic Italian place, now 38 years in operation. On another trip, accompanying my husband, who was in town for work, I tucked into a feast of luxurious Southern and French food at the now shuttered Highlands Bar & Grill, including a delicately battered soft-shell crab I still dream about paired with a glass of cold Chablis. But I had not yet had the chance to experience Chez Fonfon, the couple's classic French bistro. So, on my first evening in Birmingham this past spring, I found myself in what felt more like Paris or Provence as I sat at the bar of Chez Fonfon. I was transported by butter yellow walls, brass rails, 19th-century French furniture, a glass of CrÃ©mant du Jura, and a dish of boeuf bourguignon. Chez Fonfon sits at the crux of Five Points South, a neighborhood named for five streets that converge in a star shape where streetcars connecting the then suburb of Highland to the city once rumbled. It's legendary in American restaurant lore, one line of DNA related to the expat troupe of AmericansâRichard Olney (with whom Stitt worked), Julia Child, Kermit Lynch, James Baldwinâwho took up in France to translate its spirit into cookbooks, poetry, literature, and art. Stitt points out a photograph of Olney in a hallway near the bathroom, while recalling sharing wine with Lulu Peyraud, the beloved matriarch of the Domaine Tempier wine estate in Provence, among a collage of other French memories. Stitt, who grew up in Cullman, an hour north, the son of a country doctor, reminisces about traveling to eat with his parentsâto New York, Chicago, San Francisco, Miami. But it is the memory of Birmingham's restaurants of another era that tether him: There was Browdy's Jewish deli for bagels and pastrami; Joy Young, a white-tablecloth Chinese restaurant, for Cantonese; and The Club, a private supper club with a dance floor and a live swing band at the crest of Red Mountain that is still going strong. âBirmingham was [one of] the first major cities north of the Gulf Coast and became a magnet for all the best Gulf Coast seafood with Greek and Italian restaurants, Sicilian, Jewish, and Lebanese communities,â he said. He described the geography as a center of natural abundance, which is really an origin story for Birmingham itself. This north-central Alabama city was born in 1871, springing up after the Civil War as the South sought to rebuild a leveled economy with an industrial lifeline. Birmingham came to be called the Magic City for its near-overnight appearance, its growth accelerated by its central location to massive deposits of the three main ingredients used in steel: iron ore threaded through Red Mountain, a ridge that zigzags through the city; limestone from a plethora of nearby quarries; and coal from the Cahaba, Coosa, Plateau, and Warrior fields. This natural history is reflected in the city's grand cloak of Art Deco, neoclassical, and Romanesque architecture, the buildings' faÃ§ades swathed in stone and iron detailing and girded by skeletons of steel. This is a city full of glittering theater marquees and mint midcentury signage, and ringed with rail yards and the scars of an industrial center remade for human scale. Food has played a central role in its rebirth. Twenty-five years ago Stitt, alongside real estate CEO Catherine Sloss Jones, helped establish the Market at Pepper Place in what was previously the Dr. Pepper syrup factory and the adjacent Market Biscuit Building. Today it's a major destination, with 10,000 visitors passing through each Saturday. The afternoon I was there, a crowd of farmers, chefs, and shoppers braided through the rehabilitated complex, lined with permanent businesses like The Son of a Butcher, where local meats shimmer behind a pristine counter, and Back Forty Beer Company, a massive brewery with plenty of outdoor space. The market is one cornerstone of a larger scene that has built an outsized reputation for dining on the foundation of the Stitts' vision and mentorship. This year five restaurants were named James Beard Award semifinalists, a feat for a city of around 196,000. At one of those restaurants, Pizza Grace, located in a downtown cobblestoned arcade, executive chef and co-owner Ryan O'Hara explained, over a perfectly charred fennel and mushroom pie, how he and his wife, Geri-Martha, pastry chef and co-owner, met while working at Bottega. The O'Haras also own locally beloved ice cream joint Big Spoon Creamery, which serves dreamy seasonal flavors like salted honey blackberry and strawberry rhubarb cobbler. Up the street and over a few blocks is Salud Taqueria, from JesÃºs MÃ©ndez and Christina Tellez, which uses fresh-ground masa as a base for its Mexican menu. I had a fluffy, cheese-crusted Sonoran taco alongside a zippy pomegranate agua fresca that made me feel as if I had escaped to a shady spot in the subtropics. At Helen, also downtown in a 1920s-era building, chef Rob McDaniel serves a menu almost entirely cooked over a grill that's inspired by his grandmother's open-fire cooking. The evening I was there, I had satin-soft angel biscuits with whipped cane syrup butter, Benton's ham, roasted winter beets, and Carolina gold middlins, a broken-rice dish with mushrooms and a poached egg. Next door, his restaurant Bayonet serves pristine raw bar dishes in a sleek white-box room; McDaniel was also nominated this year for a James Beard Award. As much as Birmingham has become known for its culinary scene, it's also a crossroads for Southern and international art. At one time the city contained more than 70 theaters, three of whichâthe Lyric, the Carver, and the Alabamaâremain and have been restored with proper grandeur. Its roots in Southern music run deep and broad; big band leader Erskine Hawkins, composer and musician Sun Ra, country legend Emmylou Harris, and trap pioneer Gucci Mane were born here. Today a myriad of arts organizations champion wildly diverse missions. Ground Floor Contemporary is an artist-run collective with studios in a building owned by art-scene stalwart Sara Garden Armstrong. At the Old Bailey Gallery, curator Dan Bailey hosts visiting artists to build the city's relationship with outside talent, while Studio by the Tracks has forged a grassroots space for artists with autism. InToto, a creative arts forum, provides programming for people experiencing economic hardship, and at his African Village in America, an ongoing art installation, Joe Minter brings the living memory of the Black experience into central focus. On a broader level, this spring the Birmingham Museum of Art (BMA) hosted the show âFrench Moderns: Monet to Matisse, 1850â1950,â which has traveled internationally over the past six years. Thanks to the BMA's extensive and exquisite collection of European pieces, the show was doubled in size with paintings by DÃ©gas, Renoir, Rodin, Cassatt, and more. At the Abroms-Engel Institute for the Visual Arts at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, curator John Fields has built a renowned space for visual art, attracting a kaleidoscope of artists and shows over the course of his 12-year tenure. âWe are a tight-knit community, and very supportive of one another,â said Garden Armstrong, a Birmingham native who lived in New York from 1981 to 2017 before moving back full-time to live and work at Ground Floor, now a center for art in a downtown building Armstrong bought in 1979 for $50,000. At that time it was abandoned and cluttered with equipment and debris left behind by a prior tenant. Even 15 years ago it was unthinkable that downtown Birmingham would have the density of businesses present today. Despite the city's stunning bones and central urban spine, old theaters and majestic buildings sat empty for decades, the wind whistling through broken windows and down empty streets. But over the course of the past decade, an influx of entrepreneurs plus a comprehensive plan led by the city and REV Birmingham, a nonprofit focused on revitalization and economic development, has brought the center back to life. At Grounds, a queer- and Black-owned neighborhood cafÃ©, retail, and community space, the collective of owners feature only vendors and creators whose practices are equitable and fair-trade, including local Cala Coffee Roasters and the American zero-waste fashion designer Alabama Chanin. It's one of the businesses that makes Birmingham feel vital, current, pivotal even. âPeople look at Alabama as if we're a radically red state, and that we're closed-minded and that we have no elements of progress,â said Grounds cofounder Tyler Hatcher. âIt's a [place] with a dark and hard history, but if you come to downtown Birmingham, we are full of energy. I would say we're the driving force of the good in Alabama, and you get a taste of all that right downtown.â One afternoon, just on the other side of downtown, I wandered around the remains of Sloss Furnaces, a massive campus of ghostly rust red industrial buildings that house two 400-ton blast furnaces, casting sheds, boilers, and engine rooms that operated from 1882 to 1971, during which time it became one of the largest producers of pig iron in the world. In 1981 Sloss Furnaces was designated a National Historic Landmark, preserved so that guests might experience the history of Birmingham's industrial largesse with tours and metalworking classes but also so that they might understand the foundation upon which the South's economic engine was built. At one point over two thirds of Sloss's entry-level workforce was composed of Black labor, which was socially and hierarchically segregated and, up until 1928, often sourced from nearby prisons. Despite the fact that slavery had been abolished, it was transmuted into a different form, one that America continued to exploit to expand its wealth and industry. In his âLetter From Birmingham Jail,â Martin Luther King Jr. declared the city the most segregated in the United States. Here, in May of 1963, he led the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) alongside Reverend Fred Shuttlesworth into one of the most storied nonviolent protests in modern history, which would result in the eventual desegregation of the city's public institutions. Since those moments Birmingham has occupied a central space in the physical and spiritual lineage of America's Civil Rights Movement. At the Civil Rights Institute, visitors can walk through galleries that simulate the experience of living in a city whose schools, libraries, and businesses were divided by race and what it was like to live through the Birmingham Campaign, a movement pivotal in passing the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Just across 16th Street North is Kelly Ingram Park, an assembly site for the SCLC in 1963 now filled with sculptures that preserve the memory of protesters and its leaders. Kitty-corner from the park is 16th Street Baptist Church, the city's first Black congregation, housed in a thick tan brick building of Romanesque-Byzantine design, which became a center for civil rights meetings. In September of 1963, two weeks after King's âI Have a Dreamâ speech, a bomb killed four little girls attending Sunday school, amplifying the city's racial reckoning. Today the church is a vital site of memory, its famous stained-glass windows, a gift from the people of Wales, filtering the golden sun through its wistful blue and violet spectrum. On my final morning in Birmingham, I sat in musician Chandler Jones's apartment in the Phoenix Lofts, a building populated with creative residents. We drank coffee while looking out over the city through steamy factory glass windows as his menagerie of society finches chirped and chatted. Jones has become known for hosting some of the biggest names in Southern art, including Tara Stallworth Lee, Daniel JosÃ© Carr, Renee Hanan Plata, and William Dooley, at Room 412, his tiny gallery space at the front of his apartment. He told me about the spiritual quality of Birmingham, its spaciousness, the magic that lies in the soil, the concentration of people who choose to be here, and the myth of Vulcan, the Roman god of fire who, from atop a 124-foot sandstone pedestal dreamed up by the Works Progress Administration on Red Mountain, overlooks the city. At 56 feet tall and over 120,000 pounds, it's the largest cast-iron statue in the world. According to local lore, Vulcan has been conducting a love affair with Electra, the bronze Divinity of Light statue gilding the Alabama Power building for the better part of a century, the pair meeting each other for moonlight trysts along their sight line of 18th Street. All at once it began to snow outside, a sweeping whip of fluffy flakes cloaking the city in white, a wild reversal from the sunny, 75-degree spring weather only 24 hours before. As Jones concluded his story about the romance of Vulcan and Electra, my mind wandered to a memory of the warm bustle of Bottega's cafÃ© from nearly 20 years ago, and I wished I'd had the time to bookend my visit here with a final moment at that institution of the Stitts (the city's other mythic couple). I wouldn't make it this time, but I knew when I returned to Birmingham, it would be the first place I'd go. Tucked into the charming center of Mountain Brook, a suburb a few minutes' drive from downtown, Hotel Wildemont, Autograph Collection, has the feel of a warm, woodsy lodge. Elyton Hotel, now a Marriott property, occupies the stunning landmark Beaux Arts Empire Building, which was the tallest building in Alabama when it was built in 1909. Frank and Pardis Stitt's legendary French and Italian restaurants Chez Fonfon and Bottega are true cornerstones of the Birmingham community, with beautifully appointed dining rooms, soulful food, and deeply thoughtful hospitality. Helen, Rob and Emily McDaniel's wood-fire-and-coal-cooking restaurant, is a cozy downtown spot that serves up chicken thighs, angel biscuits, and tomato pie. Last Call Baking is a must-visit for any lover of laminated dough, giant brownie bricks, or chunky cookie energy. Just next door its sibling coffee shop serves perfect cappuccinos and seasonal matcha potions. At Pizza Grace sourdough pies are served with a natural-wine-heavy list in a quaint arcade in the middle of downtown. Don't skip desserts from pastry chef and co-owner Geri-Martha O'Hara, the mind behind beloved ice cream shop Big Spoon Creamery. An institution by any measure, Johnny's Restaurant is part of a family tree of Southern and Greek joints whose jovial cafeteria-style lunches use local ingredients for dishes like spanakopita and fried green tomatoes. Shu Shop, dark and inviting, is an izakaya and ramen spot with a tight list of gyoza, sashimi, and soups, and aromatic, low-ABV drinks. Automatic Seafood & Oysters is an altar to Gulf seafood from the accomplished chef Adam Evans and designer Suzanne Humphries. Its sibling restaurant, Current Charcoal Grill, spotlights Asian and Southern flavors. With two locations, the Golden Age Wine Garden downtown and Golden Age Wine Shop and Bar in the Mountain Brook area, this group has one of the great libraries of natural wine in the US, with bottles that range from obscure to highly collectible. High Dive HiFi Lounge, an all-day vinyl lounge that feels like sitting in someone's Big Sur living room, serves sharply honed drinks, bites in collaboration with renowned Southern chef Sean Brock, and guest-DJ sets; beverage nerds and dilettantes are equally welcome. Birmingham's first serious cocktail spot, The Collins Bar, was a foundational business in the downtown 2nd Avenue corridor when it opened in 2013; with only the bartenders to guide (no drink menu) and solid tots and hot dogs, it's more an excellent neighborhood bar than a highbrow lounge. AdiÃµs, from JesÃºs MÃ©ndez (owner of the tasty Salud Taqueria) and JosÃ© Medina Camacho, is an ode to Mexico City with agave-forward drinks, a living ofrenda meant for the community, and doors thrown open to make it seem like a street party every night. Once a farrier's shop, Bygones Cocktail Bar, centered on a horseshoe bar, has romantic lighting, cocktails executed with joy and delight, and a laissez-faire atmosphere. It's the spot for a low-key date night or even early Sunday evening drinks.

item.title: 13 best hotels in Valencia 2026, Spain's most sought-after city break
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Valencia has been collecting accolades almost as enthusiastically as it has been welcoming new hotels. Voted the world’s best city for expats time and time again, Spain’s third-largest city has become one of the Mediterranean’s most sought-after destinations. And it’s not hard to see why. A nine-kilometre park winds through a former riverbed, cycle lanes connect palm-lined squares to golden beaches and a flourishing food scene has taken the birthplace of paella well beyond its most famous dish. Throw in an architectural landscape that spans Gothic palaces, flamboyant Modernista buildings and Santiago Calatrava’s futuristic City of Arts and Sciences, and there’s plenty to keep visitors looking up between long lunches. The city’s appeal extends to where you lay your head. Historic buildings are finding new life as glamorous five-star stays, from a former telephone exchange overlooking Plaza del Ayuntamiento to an old bank where the vaults have become a spa. Art Deco interiors, rooftop cocktail bars and restaurants championing Valencian produce are increasingly part of the package, while the choice of where to recharge at night extends well beyond the winding streets of the old town. Whether waking up to Mediterranean views at Las Arenas, soaking up the youthful buzz of Ruzafa at adults-only Yours Boutique Hotel or checking into a centuries-old palace with Roman ruins beneath its floors, these are the best hotels in Valencia for making the most of a city that has plenty to celebrate. item.title: 17 best hotels in Crete with jaw-dropping views we'll be sure to check back into in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
There are countless reasons why Crete remains one of the most popular Greek Islands. It's big – the largest of the Greek islands, in fact – which means it’s easy to find areas of seclusion and authenticity as well as historical sites and architectural ruins. For active travellers, the gorgeous hiking trails offer plenty of things to do. Those looking to relax will revel in its beaches, which have proper sand, unlike those found on Santorini or Mykonos. Our tip: venture to the eastern side of the island to find sandy stretches that are void of many people at all. Then there’s the food scene and the chance to explore quiet (or rowdy) tavernas where catch-fresh seafood dominates a simple menu of local delicacies. The hotels here seem to get better every year and span everything from romantic boutique boltholes to some of the best family-friendly hotels in Europe. Villas too, are a popular choice for multigenerational groups looking to soak up the surroundings in the comfort of a private space. Here, we round up the best hotels in Crete, tried and tested by our editors. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Crete: What is the best location to stay in Crete? Crete is the biggest island in Greece and home to some of our favourite Greek island hotels. Those visiting for the first time are spoilt for choice on where to stay. The obvious choice is Chania in the northwest, where hotels such as Domes Zeen Chania cascade down the hillside and overlook the sea, making it the ideal spot to settle for a week soaking up the Cretan sun. But the eastern half of the island is also well worth exploring. Near-deserted beaches and some of the best Airbnbs in Crete spell escapism; go now before it becomes better known. What's the best resort in Crete for families Direct flights from London make Crete a popular choice for families, and the island is home to some of the best family-friendly hotels in Greece, so booking a multigenerational trip is easily done. Domes of Elounda overlooks the UNESCO-protected island of Spinalonga. Book into self-catering facilities that offer the perfect set-up for families with little ones. When is the best time to visit Crete? Traditionally aligned with a European summer, the hottest months in Crete are between June and September. Many hotels close during the winter. Those visiting during shoulder season – April, early May and October – will be rewarded with quieter beaches, a slower pace, and a sense of locality. This is when the tourists disperse and the spotlight is on Crete’s verdant grounds, fresh food and sublime sea. item.title: 12 best hotels in the Algarve, Portugal's prettiest coastal region
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Ah, the Algarve… that light, the long expanses of burnt butter sands, blue waters washing against golden limestone cliffs; the smell of sizzling fresh fish, drizzled with local olive oil and the clack-clacking of storks sitting atop the squat olive trees that border the winding roads. There is a wealth of magic in this region, of hidden beaches where fishermen still mend their nets, small white-washed Portuguese villages where the only sound is that of the sonorous church bell, and vineyards where you can stay to taste the wine from the vines around you, immersing yourself in the terroir. And then there is the lively Algarve, where warm nights are filled with music and cocktails and beach parties, days with surfing or riding. There is something for everyone in this region and below are the best hotels in the Algarve. item.title: 12 best restaurants in Hong Kong: I've been eating here for nearly two decades, here's where to go
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
I've lived in Hong Kong and eaten in Hong Kong restaurants for more than 20 years and written about it for most of that time. Along the way, I started some farmers’ markets (no small thing in a city that imports over 95 per cent of its food) and have eaten enough char siu to fill a red taxi. Even so, I hesitate when friends ask where to eat. Partly, it’s the sheer number of restaurants: there are more than 17,000 for just 7.5 million people, and since most of our kitchens are the size of a wardrobe, eating out is how the city feeds itself – in this town, everyone’s an expert. A six-stool wonton noodle shop is as representative of Hong Kong as a tasting menu that would hold its own in New York or Paris. Having said that, Cantonese cooking is still the backbone and main reason to eat here: restrained, skilful and ingredient-led, judged on whether the fish was swimming an hour ago and the wok was the right level of scorching. But this was a port city long before it was a financial one, and has always made room for whoever and whatever came ashore, from Indian spices to French technique. The restaurants below are the ones I return to and would happily send a first-time visitor. Some need to be booked when you book your plane ticket; others might require you to queue or take a trip to Kowloon – both are usually a good sign. The best Hong Kong restaurants to discover now In Mong Kok, the heart of Kowloon, London Restaurant delivers the quintessential dim sum experience – rickety carts weaving between tables in vast dining rooms across three levels. This heirloom banquet hall feels as alive as ever, fuelled by the chatter of families, the shattering of spring roll wrappers and the billowing steam of freshly steamed buns. It was once fashionable to name grand Chinese restaurants after global capitals (the now-shuttered Washington Restaurant was another), but few have managed to endure. Come for the nostalgia, stay for the har gow (shrimp dumplings). Address: Good Hope Building, 612 Nathan Road, Mong Kok Trained with the likes of Daniel Boulud, homegrown chef Vicky Cheng was among the first to combine French luxury with their Chinese counterparts to brilliant effect – think caviar, dried abalone and durian all in one tasting menu – with that spirit of classical French precision meeting cultural exploration running through every dish. With a sleek open kitchen, it’s one of the city’s most iconic fine-dining experiences, rooted in the local yet globally aware, like Hong Kong itself. For Cheng’s take on modern Chinese cuisine, Wing downstairs also promises an exceptional experience. Address: 30/F, The Wellington, 198 Wellington Street, Central While Hong Kong is mostly about Cantonese food, Yong Fu offers a rare treat from Ningbo, Eastern China – delicate, seafood-driven and intensely seasonal. Rarely outside of the Mainland will you find this sort of food presented at this level: expect meticulous sourcing, from mud crab, marinated and served raw, to river eels and freshwater fish, nuts and greens only known in that region, all prepared with understated precision. This is an elegant detour from the usual fare, and a delectable reminder of the diverse culinary traditions of the country at large. Address: Shop 2, G/F & 1/F, Golden Star Building, 20-22 Lockhart Road, Wan Chai Deceptively simple, unshowy, yet profound, The Chairman is perhaps the very definition of modern Cantonese cuisine. Founder Danny Yip honours tradition while quietly reshaping it – coaxing depth from local clams, flower crab, pigeon and the like. His respect for provenance and seasonality has influenced an entire generation of chefs. The Chairman rewards those who plan ahead – reservations are notoriously hard to secure. Address: 3/F, The Wellington, 198 Wellington Street, Central “Noisy, rude, overrated” states Big JJ’s website – and it’s that swagger that epitomises this raucous hotpot joint’s appeal. Having gained cult status during its original cramped, side-alley incarnation, it recently relocated to more spacious digs in the swanky Prince’s Building – yet its combination of retro dai pai dong (street hawker) vibes with top-drawer ingredients (including locally slaughtered beef and catch-of-the-day seafood), a savvy wine list and up-for-it service, remains as irresistible as ever. Book in advance or expect long lines, whether you’re coming for a hearty rice or noodle dish at lunch, or a full-on Cantopop-soundtracked hotpot feast for dinner. Address: Basement, Prince’s Building, 10 Chater Road, Central In the basement of Jardine House in Central, the city’s CBD, Basehall is home to some of Hong Kong’s best independent and Michelin-recommended names under one sleek roof. It’s a contemporary food hall with polish: air-conditioned comfort, stylish communal tables and everything from Michelin Bib Gourmand Shandong dumpling joint Ah Chun, to sizzling dai pai dong-inspired dishes at Ying Hung Palace, to Cantonese barbecue hotshots Kamcentre, it’s perfect for sampling the city’s huge range without criss-crossing town. There’s even Artifact, a hidden speakeasy, should you want a classy end to the night. Address: LG/F, Jardine House, 1 Connaught Place, Central Duddell’s merges art, design and gastronomy in a way few restaurants do. With classy interiors by star designer André Fu, this bi-level space is filled with rotating contemporary art, a nod to its art world founders. The menu, helmed by celebrated chef Chan Yau-leung, is just as remarkable – elegant, precise and subtly innovative. Especially when the weather gods are amicable, the well-heeled make a beeline for weekend dim sum brunch on the terrace with free-flow tea, cocktails or Champagne. Neighborhood, by Hongkonger David Lai, is an unpretentious spot down a back alley that consistently draws a knowing crowd. Trained in French cuisine, Lai’s philosophy is boundary-agnostic, sourcing impeccable ingredients anywhere from the local wet market to the best farms in Europe. His concise, ever-changing menu is a direct reflection of what is best at the moment, making his discreet restaurant a steadfast favourite among chefs and locals – despite it being Michelin-starred, it still feels like an insider’s secret. Address: 61 Hollywood Road, Central (entrance on Man Hing Lane) “Wok hei” – the distinctive smoky flavour imparted from the “breath of the wok” – is a much-coveted concept in Cantonese cuisine, and it’s found in abundance in Cheong Gor’s greatest hits. Meats, seafood, vegetables, rice and noodles are wok-fried to perfection; fresh, light, crisp and addictive enough to have you fighting over who gets the last bite. Hearty, homey and oh-so-satisfying; since most of us don’t have Chinese grannies effortlessly dishing up these classics at home, this is the next best thing. Address: Room 208, 2/F, Yip Fung Building, 2-18 D’Aguilar Street, Central A rite of passage for visitors and locals alike, who still jostle for a spot at the fast-turning tables at this iconic cha chaan teng (think East-meets-West version of a caff). Come for Hong Kong’s most famous scrambled eggs, silky steamed milk pudding and local-style milk tea, served with a lot of tough love and no frills. Go early in the morning for a less frantic experience reminiscent of the Hong Kong of yore. For a truly one-of-a-kind tasting experience, look no further than Mono. Venezuelan chef-owner Ricardo Chaneton cut his teeth at culinary blockbuster Mirazur and has hit his groove here – a highly personal, totally singular distillation of his Latin-American heritage and European training. With ever-changing seasonal tasting menus, creativity is king and no effort is too great – including elements like house-made cheese, pod-to-bar chocolate and a 20-ingredient mole. Book a kitchen counter seat to watch the magic up close. Indian fine dining might not be your first thought for what to eat during a trip to Hong Kong – but miss out on Leela at your peril. Chef Manav Tuli’s first solo venture following stints at award-winning restaurants in India and London, Leela offers a rich tapestry of diverse regional Indian dishes, cherry-picking inspiration from street snacks to royal recipes alike – plus a “Flavours of Hong Kong” section showcasing the influence that Tuli’s current home has had on his cooking. His take on ham sui gok, a traditional deep-fried dim sum dumpling, is a cross-cultural slam dunk. Address: Shop 301-310, Lee Garden Three, 1 Sunning Road, Causeway Bay

item.title: Ever wondered where Halloween was born? Let us take you back 2,000 years to Ireland's eerie ‘Hell Cave’
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
As Irish folklore tells, a black horse with glowing eyes sprints through the Emerald Isle's raw countryside in the murky night, carrying a terrified countryman who canât escape this ghastly ride. They gallop past eerie sites, which have now become tourist attractions â mystical fairy forts, prehistoric passage tombs, abandoned Royal capitals, and the âhell caveâ where Halloween was born. While Halloween was popularised by the US in the 1900s, the holiday originated 2,000 years ago with Irelandâs pagan festival, Samhain. Now, Ireland is making moves to reclaim the celebrations, branding itself as the world capital of Halloween. An island-wide tourism campaign involving dozens of events, including fire processions, carnival parades, and Europeâs biggest Halloween festival has launched this month, in a bid to bring the holiday back to its original setting. Each event is designed around helping tell the creepy history of Samhain, during which supernatural beings ran riot across Ireland. Inhabited for up 10,000 years, Irelandâs green fields, serene forests and raw coastline echo with riveting folklore. The Irish people respect the Celtic mythology, telling stories of these beings, like the aforementioned Puca horse. Some such tales are mere campfire stories, describing lost cities and invisible islands. Others are grounded in reality, like that of Samhain. Every November 1, on Samhain, Irish pagans would mark the Celtic New Year by chanting alongside bonfires at sacred sites such as Oweynagat hell cave â a supposed portal to Irelandâs mythical underworld, TÃr na nÃg. This subterranean realm bulges with Sidhe fairies, including leprechauns and pucas, which are infamous for supposedly abducting humans after dark. Sidhes are trapped in TÃr na nÃg, which is supposedly separated from the living world by an invisible border. Every now and then, this barrier briefly dissolves. Sidhes emerge from the underworld to either save the Irish people or plunge them into disasters, like the Great Irish Famine, according to mythology. Samhain is the main moment this spirit invasion occurred. During the early versions of this festival, Sidhes would pour out of Oweynagat cave and swarm adjoining Rathcroghan, the capital of Irelandâs ancient kingdom of Connachta. Meanwhile, Samhainâs human attendees prayed for protection from fairies, in between feasting, dancing and trading at Rathcroghan. Now known as Europeâs largest un-excavated royal complex, Rathcroghan allows visitors to wander fields dotted by its 240 archaeological sites, including stone forts and ceremonial mounds. Tourists keen to known how Samhain inspired Halloween can join guided tours of Rathcroghan and Oweynagat, or they may attend the nearby Rathcroghan Visitor Centre, which has a small but informative museum. There they learn that, in the 1800s, Irish immigrants brought Samhain to the US, where it gradually became a kitschy, commercialised festival aimed at children. Which explains why Ireland last year decided to plant its flag on this festival by launching its annual âHome of Halloweenâ programme, says Julie Wakley, head of Great Britain for Tourism Ireland. "Halloween is one of the most widely celebrated festivals globally, yet many people are surprised to discover that its roots trace back to the island of Ireland,â Wakley explains. Home of Halloween involves dozens of events across the entire island of Ireland â festivals, performances, food experiences, walking tours â and is a collaboration between Tourism Ireland and Tourism Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland is home to plenty of spooky places itself â including the Dark Hedges, a lane of overhanging beech trees, often used as a filming location in series such as The Game of Thrones. Puca Festival (October 29 to November 1) in County Meathâs Boyne Valley incorporates heritage tours, live music events, a mythical character parade and a stunning fire procession that mirrors prehistoric Samhain rituals. Northern Irelandâs Derry Halloween (October 28 to November 1) is Europeâs largest Halloween festival, with events focused on storytelling, music, dance, fire shows, and a replica of an ancient Samhain harvest market. Meanwhile, smaller Halloween festivals will unfurl in the cities of Dublin, Limerick, Galway, Longford and Kilkenny. Each of Irelandâs Halloween festivals is slightly different in character. But all have one thing in common: they aim to remind the world that, eons before sinister-looking pumpkins were carved by US kids, this festival was being celebrated by chanting, costumed Irish Pagans illuminated by bonfires. Ireland is reclaiming Halloween. Irelandâs spooky sites to visit for Halloween Some 2,000 years ago, Irish pagans accessed this âhell caveâ through a purpose-built entrance. Now, thereâs only a narrow opening in a tranquil field, 140km west of Dublin. Tourists can peek into its dim interior, or read a nearby sign explaining its extraordinary history. But theyâre not allowed to squeeze inside the cave, for safety reasons. No ticket is required. Grassy mounds rising from farmland contain remains of this Irish Royal capital, some 5,500 years old, which hosted ancient Samhain celebrations. During those rituals, shapeshifting beasts escaped from Irelandâs underworld to haunt Rathcroghanâs 6.5sqkm of forts, earthworks and standing stones. Visitors can access Rathcroghan at any time, for free. But itâs worth booking a 2.5 hour guided tour via nearby Rathcroghan Visitor Centre, for â¬21.20. Rathcroghan Visitor Centre, County Roscommon Located in tiny Tulsk town, 4km east of Rathcroghan, it has a cafÃ©, gift shop, and petite museum. That latter facility, which costs â¬6 to enter, explains Rathcroghanâs ties to Samhain and Irelandâs eerie underworld, and displays ancient artefacts from this site. It is open year-round, Monday to Saturday, from 9.15am to 5pm. Sligoâs mountainous countryside contains more than 100 eerie "passage tombs" up to 5,000 years old, including at scenic Carrowkeel and Carrowmore. It remains unclear whoâs buried inside the majority of these stone tombs, the most spectacular of which is Keshcorran, overlooking majestic countryside. Local lore suggests Keshcorranâs tunnels are connected, underground, to Oweynagat "hell caveâ. Entry is free, at all times, and itâs a moderate 15-minute uphill walk from the carpark. National Leprechaun Museum of Ireland, County Dublin Rather than providing a cartoonish explanation of leprechauns, this museum in downtown Dublin unravels the Irish folklore ofÂ Sidhe fairies. Visitors must join guided tours, which mix eyecatching video displays depicting Irish artefacts and ancient maps, with storytelling about Irelandâs supernatural beings. These 45-minute tours depart every 30 minutes, and cost â¬18 per adult. Cnoc Meadha Fairy Fortress, County Galway A dense, serene forest provides fine protection for Cnoc Meadha, the underground fortress supposedly home to Ireland's Sidhe fairies, who were key characters in Samhain lore. Visitors can take a scenic, 10-minute uphill walk from the carpark to reach this 1,000-year-old site, the legendary headquarters of the King of the Sidhes, Finvarra. During ancient Samhain celebrations, bonfires glowed so intensely atop this 3,000-year-old ceremonial site that it was named Tlachtga, after a Celtic goddess of the sun. Now commonly called the Hill of Ward, it sits on private farmland in County Meath. But tourists can access it by joining one of the daily 90-minute Hill of Ward guided tours between October 29 and November 1, for â¬27.50 per adult. Blood stained the Hill of Ward during prehistoric Samhain rituals, which saw animals sacrificed to Pagan demons. This prehistoric Royal burial site, in emerald fields 18km east of Tlachtga, is now a heritage attraction, with free access to visitors seven days a week.

item.title: Cancelled trains, unexpected fog and rough seas: This is what it's like tracking wildlife on the Scilly Isles
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
28 miles off the southern coast of Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly are made up of more than 100 islands. Just five of them are inhabited, with a population of around 2,200, but all boast breathtaking white-sand beaches, a tropical microclimate and a vast array of wildlife that draws in 100,000 visitors each summer. I've dreamt of visiting these remote isles for years, so when I finally got offered a work assignment to photograph the famous Isles of Scilly puffins, I jumped at the opportunity. Little did I know that I'd spend 24 hours trying to reach the islands – a journey that featured unexpected fog, cancelled helicopters and a wild goose (puffin?) chase to find the elusive birds. A journey starting in London and ending off the Cornish coast took just as long as one to the other side of the world, all to see the little seabirds. I visited at the beginning of June – peak puffin season, I'll have you know – to see the colony which returns to the Isles mid-April to breed. One hundred pairs of puffins return annually to the same breeding spot where they will raise one chick (endearingly called a ‘puffling’) until the end of July, when it is big enough to take flight and off they go back to sea. I set off from London on a six-hour train journey to Penzance, with my Fuji camera and lenses in tow, packed and excited to seek out the black-and-white sea bird. Once in Penzance, after a long train delay, I was told my helicopter over to the Scilly Isles was cancelled due to unexpected fog – something I didn’t expect to hear during one of the hottest UK summers on record. It meant I was to spend the night on the mainland and have just one night in the Scilly Isles – not ideal when you're tracking wildlife. I had my fingers crossed for a flight the next morning. A day later, I was booked on a flight at 3pm and my journey to the puffins was closing in. Helicopter flights from Penzance to either St Marys or Tresco take just 20 minutes. If the weather's right, its a scenic flight over the craggy Cornish coast and the English Channel to approach the bright green islands floating in crystal-clear seas – I couldn't believe the sights after such a grey, foggy 24 hours on the mainland. On arrival, I was quickly whisked away by my tour guide in a buggy (the main mode of transport on the islands) to a little port on Tresco, where I boarded a small boat bound for the rocky outcrop where the puffins and their pufflings live. As fate would have it, the sea was very rough that day due to the storm the night before so we couldn’t get as close as we'd hoped to the rocks where the birds nest and burrow. It also meant the puffins, which frequently sit on the calm waters, were nowhere to be seen. Turns out, they didn’t want to get thrown around on the waves – and I couldn't blame them. We spent 15 minutes being thrown around ourselves on the choppy open sea, spotting the occasional bird diving for food and then darting back to the warmth of their rocks to feed their little ones. Other black-and-white sea birds such as guillemots and razorbills threw me off from my search, but the guides helped point out the few puffins swooping down, identifiable by their bright orange beaks. Back on land, we went after a few sightings. Unfortunately it just wasn't the day for it. So, did I travel over 24 hours to see five puffins? Yes, I did. Nature and weather make a truly unpredictable pair, but I did come away with some helpful learnings. It's hard to know exactly what to expect on these remote isles, where weather chops and changes so quickly. Next time, I'll be sure to plan longer time to give myself the best possible chance of seeing the wildlife I'm seeking, ideally on a clear and calm day. Timings and boat routes are very flexible and work around weather conditions, plus the skipper will do their best to navigate based on spottings. I did get to enjoy spotting other marine wildlife – and there are seals, porpoises and wales to be seen if you're lucky! On dry land, I made the most of my time on the islands pottering around Tresco gardens, walking along the sandy shoreline and admiring the unique flora and fauna growing undisturbed. It’s obvious why people return here every year. While puffins are not considered rare, there are only a few colonies in the UK which gather on specific rocky coastlines. A few other popular locations to spot them are Skomer in Pembrokeshire, where you can walk amongst their burrows, the Farne Islands in Northumberland and Isle of May, Firth of Forth. It's a truly beautiful place, home to incredible wildlife and rugged, unpredictable landscapes that are well-worth the long journey.

item.title: 11 best UK Christmas breaks: the places full of festive magic, as chosen by our editors
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
UK Christmas breaks are world-famous for a reason. As an Italian who grew up Catholic (and a December Sagittarius), I take Christmas very seriously, and since moving to the UK and marrying an Englishman, I've learnt to love a good, cosy and indulgent British Christmas. As far as cities are concerned, nothing beats London for Christmas spirit and decorations – no, not even Paris. I love walking beneath the twinkling lights on Regent Street, catching a show in the West End, risking my life on skates at Somerset House and retreating into a warm pub for an early dinner. The only places that are possibly better than London at Christmas are nestled in the British countryside. After all, there are few better places to ring in the New Year than Scotland during Hogmanay, while the frost and Christmas spirit somehow manage to make the Cotswolds even more magical. Here, we’ve rounded up our favourite UK Christmas breaks, from the idyllic Scottish Highlands to some of England’s prettiest country towns. This quintessentially English region is picture-perfect in any season, but there’s something particularly magical about the Cotswolds at Christmas. The windows of the honey-hued houses glow from candlelight, pubs are jam-packed with locals huddling up by crackling fires and, if you’re lucky, snow covers the rolling hills like a fluffy quilt. Windswept walks along the Cotswold Way are a must, stopping off in small villages en route to refuel at cute cafés or visit independent stores for a spot of last-minute present shopping. Where to stay: For the ultimate winter retreat, Thyme is the place to be. Set on the Southrop Manor Estate, with its manicured gardens and farmhouse aesthetic, it’s the perfect place to hole up for a decadent festive break. This year, the hotel is hosting a packed programme of festive events, from mince-pie making and Christmas cookery classes to cocktail masterclasses and Bach by Candlelight. For more inspiration, check out our edit of the very best hotels in the Cotswolds. It doesn’t get much more Christmassy than London in December. The city centre is a treasure trove of festive magic – stroll along Regent Street to see the twinkling angels hovering overhead before popping into some of the shops decked out for the season. There are plenty of wintry activities to choose from, from maze-like markets selling everything from steaming hot chocolate and mulled wine to stocking fillers, to ice skating and festive shows – including A Christmas Carol at The Old Vic Theatre and The Snowman at the Peacock Theatre. For something a little different, head to Christmas at Kew, which returns with new light installations for 2026 as well as its first adults-only evenings. Where to stay: A stay at The Ned is bound to boost festive cheer. Inside, glittering décor adorns every corner, from one of the biggest Christmas trees in town to live music throughout the festive season. This year, Gareth Malone and his choir will perform Christmas carols on three Sundays in December, while festive afternoon tea and Christmas Day dining are also on offer. Those looking to make a proper Christmas getaway of it can book a two-night stay from Christmas Eve, including a festive feast on Christmas Day. In the summer, you’d be hard pressed to find a corner of Cornwall that isn’t already rammed with people. But come winter, this beautiful county is a wonderland of misty moors and blustery beaches that are yours for the taking. Wrap up warm and pack a bag full of snacks and a thermos filled with steaming tea, and spend days hiking stretches of the South West Coast Path and sandy beaches before cosying up by the fire. For a dose of Christmas spirit, head to Mousehole, where thousands of colourful lights illuminate the harbour and surrounding village throughout the festive season. Where to stay: For a romantic Christmas getaway, book The Scarlet Hotel, an adults-only retreat overlooking Mawgan Porth beach. Its four-night Christmas break kicks off with mulled wine and mince pies before taking in live music on Christmas Eve, a four-course Christmas Day lunch and a Boxing Day sea dip. In between, retreat to the spa or warm up in one of the hotel’s clifftop hot tubs overlooking the sea. Not to sound too bah-humbug, but a Christmas spent in the middle of nowhere with no one to bother you but the lowing cows and swooping birds of prey sounds pretty idyllic to me. The Scottish Highlands are the place to be for those in need of a serious end-of-year reset – pack up the car with all your thickest jumpers and woolliest socks (and the rest of your family if need be), and head for the hills. Opening up the curtains to views of misty moors, pristine beaches and Munros galore is bound to make for a Christmas morning unlike any other. For something a little more festive, head to the Cairngorms, where you can visit Britain’s only free-ranging herd of reindeer and, on selected dates in the run-up to Christmas, see some of them at the Cairngorm Reindeer Centre’s festive paddocks. Where to stay: There are plenty of storybook cottages and cosy lodges to book if a Scottish Airbnb is what you’re looking for, but Killiehuntly is one of the very best places in the Highlands to book for a festive escape. Set within the Cairngorms National Park, the farmhouse dates back to 1850 and has just four bedrooms, making it an intimate base for a Christmas break spent truly getting your fix of the great outdoors. There’s nothing quite like Christmas by the sea. Kent’s seaside towns can be packed with tourists in the summer months, but the coast is particularly beautiful in the festive season. Brisk walks along the beach (and Christmas morning dips for those brave enough) are enough to blow the cobwebs away – check out our guide to Kent’s best beaches. Warm up at one of the area’s best restaurants – Deal is home to some particularly lovely places to eat. Where to stay: Updown Farmhouse is a restaurant with rooms not too far from Deal – think modern farmhouse, with cosy corners and rustic touches alongside splashes of bold colour, contemporary art and excellent food. At Christmas, the farmhouse goes all out, with four Christmas trees – including a 21-foot centrepiece – and a packed festive calendar. This year, expect mulled wine and mince pies, carols, wreath-making workshops and a candlelit Winter Solstice Supper, as well as a special festive dining menu throughout December. With its cobbled streets, medieval buildings and cosy pubs, York feels like it was made for Christmas. Come December, the historic centre is taken over by twinkling lights and wooden chalets, with York Christmas Market filling Parliament Street and St Sampson’s Square with more than 80 per cent Yorkshire-based traders selling gifts, crafts and plenty of festive food and drink. Browse the stalls before exploring the independent shops along the Shambles, warming up with a mulled wine or escaping the cold in one of the city’s centuries-old pubs. Where to stay: Just outside the city centre, Middlethorpe Hall goes all in on a traditional country-house Christmas. Its three-night Christmas House Party includes afternoon tea on Christmas Eve, carols and Champagne around the open fire, a four-course Christmas Day lunch and a black-tie dinner on Boxing Day. Guests can even head into the city for midnight mass at York Minster before returning to port and mince pies. Few cities look quite as good dressed up for Christmas as Bath. Every winter, wooden chalets pop up between the honey-coloured Georgian buildings surrounding Bath Abbey, transforming the centre into one of the prettiest Christmas markets in the country. In 2026, 250 traders will take over the city streets, alongside live music, street performers and plenty of festive food and drink. Once you’ve ticked off your Christmas shopping, escape the cold with a soak in the thermal waters at Thermae Bath Spa or settle in for a long lunch at one of the city’s excellent restaurants. Where to stay: It’s hard to beat The Royal Crescent Hotel & Spa for a suitably indulgent Christmas getaway. Set inside Bath’s most famous Georgian crescent, the hotel has a spa and beautiful secluded gardens, while its festive programme includes seasonal dining and live music. Its Christmas package for 2026 has already sold out, but a limited number of bed-and-breakfast stays are still available over Christmas. Edinburgh knows how to do winter properly. From mid-November, the Scottish capital turns into a festive playground, with Christmas markets, fairground rides and seasonal entertainment spread across Princes Street Gardens and George Street, all overlooked by Edinburgh Castle. Spend the afternoon browsing the market with something hot in hand before heading into the Old Town for dinner, then stick around after Christmas if you can: few places do New Year’s Eve quite like Edinburgh during Hogmanay. I have been three times over the last decade, and I can't wait to go back. Where to stay: For something suitably atmospheric, book one of the theatrical suites at The Witchery, tucked beside the gates of Edinburgh Castle at the top of the Royal Mile. Its candlelit dining rooms feel particularly made for dark December evenings, with a festive menu celebrating Scottish classics and a seasonal afternoon tea for anyone in need of a break from Christmas shopping. There are Christmas markets, and then there is the one at Winchester Cathedral. Inspired by traditional German markets, more than 100 wooden chalets fill the cathedral grounds each winter, selling everything from handmade decorations and homeware to artisan food and Christmas gifts. The 2026 market runs from 20 November to 22 December, but don’t spend the entire day shopping: step inside the cathedral for one of its Advent services or carol concerts before finding a cosy pub for dinner. Where to stay: Hotel du Vin Winchester occupies a handsome Georgian building in the heart of the city, making it an easy base for wandering between the cathedral, market and shops. Two-, three- and four-night Christmas packages are available for 2026, with Christmas Eve dinner, breakfast and a four-course Christmas Day lunch included, while longer stays also come with dinner on Boxing Day. If your dream Christmas involves muddy boots, roaring fires and very little reason to leave the countryside, head to the Lake District. Winter strips away much of the region’s summer crowds, leaving misty lakes, snow-dusted fells and walking trails that feel wonderfully peaceful at this time of year. Spend crisp mornings wandering along the shores of Windermere before retreating somewhere warm for an afternoon spent eating, drinking and doing very little at all. Where to stay: Set in 20 acres of gardens and woodland overlooking Windermere, Cragwood Country House Hotel offers the sort of old-fashioned Christmas break that requires almost no planning once you arrive. Its three-night 2026 package includes cream tea on Christmas Eve, a traditional four-course Christmas Day lunch, roaring log fires, festive entertainment and even a Boxing Day cruise across Lake Windermere. I might be biased after spending many weekends here over the years, but Stamford is one of England’s prettiest towns at any time of year – and particularly lovely at Christmas. Its honey-coloured stone buildings, independent shops and cosy pubs already provide most of the ingredients for a festive short break, while the annual one-day Christmas Market brings more than 100 stalls, live entertainment and festive activities to the town centre. Just outside town, Burghley House hosts its own Christmas Fair, with around 200 stalls filling its courtyards and grounds with gifts, decorations, mulled wine and festive food. Where to stay: The George of Stamford sits right in the centre of town, in a historic coaching inn that feels particularly suited to a winter weekend away. Spend the day browsing Stamford’s independent shops or wandering around Burghley before retreating to the hotel for dinner and a drink.

item.title: The best festivals in Europe to book for 2027
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
I tend to avoid festivals in the UK as I do not see myself standing under the rain, not taking a hot shower for four days and sleeping in a tent – sorry Glastonbury fans. Thankfully, Europe has a vast choice of festivals catering to every musical taste, but also every kind of setting. The best festivals in Europe are a particularly eclectic bunch. There are sun-soaked events that have long drawn the biggest names in commercial music, such as Hungary’s Sziget and Primavera Sound in Barcelona and Porto, attracting music-loving hordes from around the world. Fans of EDM, drum and bass and cutting-edge techno are particularly well catered for, with Croatia becoming quite the festival hub in recent years; long-running Hideout Festival has been joined by more recent additions to the summer calendar such as Terminal V Croatia. But it’s not all about frozen cocktails on sun-kissed beaches, with festivalgoers heading to the French Alps for Snowboxx Festival, which combines chalet stays, skiing and live music each March. And if Bad Bunny helped you develop a passion for Latin sounds, you are in luck as one of Europe's biggest celebrations of Latin and Afro-Cuban music is held in a small town in southwestern France. Whatever type of music does it for you, whatever budget you’re working with, there’s sure to be something among Europe’s best festivals to warrant a hedonistic escape you’ll never forget. Best for: immersive stages and electronic music Tickets: Not yet on sale. Visitors can currently pre-register for updates on the official website. If Mysteryland confirms anything, it’s that the Dutch know how to pull out all the stops come festival season. Returning in 2027 after taking a year off, the electronic music festival is one of the Netherlands' longest-running, bringing together DJs playing everything from house and techno to trance. Sets take place among the ponds, lakes and grassy hills of the former Floriade site in Haarlemmermeer, just outside Amsterdam, with elaborate stages and installations transforming the grounds into a temporary fairytale landscape. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, and tickets aren't on sale just yet, but festivalgoers can pre-register on the official website to be among the first to hear about the next edition. Best for: big-name headliners and a city break Tickets: Already on sale. Five-day passes are currently advertised from €349 (£295), plus a €23 (£19) handling fee. There are also discounted passes for under-21s. Sziget's line-up is usually so packed with big names that it's often tricky to decipher who precisely the headliner is. Previous editions have welcomed everyone from Kylie Minogue and Halsey to Charli XCX and Chappell Roan, with a mix of pop, rock, indie and electronic music spread across multiple stages. But there's much more to Sziget than the music. Taking over Óbuda Island in the middle of the Danube, the five-day festival also features art installations, theatre, circus performances and workshops, while Budapest's famous ruin bars, thermal baths and cultural attractions are within easy reach. Festivalgoers can camp on the island or make a proper city break of it by staying in the Hungarian capital. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, but five-day passes are already on sale from €349 (£295), plus booking fees. Tickets: Early bird allocation sold out; check the official website for further releases. Expect no holds barred on the production front at Terminal V Croatia when it takes over The Garden Resort in Tisno next July. The five-day festival brings together international DJs playing everything from techno and house to trance and hard dance, with cutting-edge light displays and powerful sound systems keeping the crowds dancing well into the early hours. It's an oddly picturesque setting for an electronic festival that packs this much of a punch, with four open-air stages dotted around the resort, including beachside dancefloors overlooking the glistening Adriatic Sea. Away from the main stages, festivalgoers can join boat parties along the Croatian coast or keep the night going at the legendary open-air Barbarella's Discotheque, where afterparties continue until sunrise. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, and tickets for boat parties and certain afterparties are sold separately. Best for: house music by the Mediterranean Tickets: Not yet on sale; check the official website for presale announcements. Brunch Electronik Festival is hailed as the ‘biggest brunch of the year’, although you won't find many eggs Benedict being served on its dancefloors. Instead, expect three days of house, techno and electronic music from international DJs and emerging local talent, all against the backdrop of Barcelona's Mediterranean coastline. The festival has previously taken over several locations across the city, but its main home is Parc del Fòrum, a sprawling open-air venue overlooking the sea. As well as the music, Brunch Electronik puts an emphasis on community, sustainability and inclusivity, with initiatives ranging from waste reduction to supporting local organisations. And with Barcelona's beaches, restaurants and nightlife on your doorstep, it's an easy excuse to turn a festival weekend into a longer city break. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced. Best for: pop stars and affordable tickets Tickets: 2027 details yet to be announced SummerDaze Festival transforms the dazzling Mediterranean island of Malta into a playground for music lovers each August, bringing some of the biggest names in pop and dance music to its sun-soaked shores. Previous editions have welcomed everyone from Central Cee and Bob Sinclar to Calvin Harris and Lewis Capaldi, who headlined the two main events in 2026. Unlike some of Europe's pricier music festivals, SummerDaze is also surprisingly affordable, with tickets for the 2026 concerts costing just €10 each.
