The festival's latest edition took place at the Ta' Qali Concert Area, a large open-air venue in the heart of the island, leaving plenty of opportunities to spend your days exploring Malta's beaches, historic towns and waterfront restaurants before heading to the concerts in the evening. Dates, artists and tickets for 2027 are yet to be announced. Tickets: Not yet on sale; ticket information expected in December 2026. Tomorrowland is like Disneyland for EDM enthusiasts. Each summer, the Belgian town of Boom (fittingly) becomes a vibrant utopia where some of the biggest names in electronic music entertain crowds throughout the day and late into the night across two weekends. The festival revolves around a spectacular Mainstage that looks like something out of a fairytale, with elaborate designs, dazzling light shows and production that puts some of Europe's most impressive castles to shame. Beyond the Mainstage, dozens of other dance floors cater to everything from house and techno to trance and harder electronic sounds. Those wanting the full experience can stay at DreamVille, the festival's dedicated camping village, or book one of its travel and accommodation packages. Tickets are famously hard to come by, so it's worth keeping an eye on the official website for pre-registration and sale announcements. Tickets: On sale. There are few better places to spend a summer weekend dancing than the French Riviera, and Les Plages Électroniques makes the most of its enviable location. Taking over the beach and terraces surrounding Cannes' famous Palais des Festivals, the three-day event brings together some of the biggest names in electronic music, with a mix of house, techno and EDM playing across several stages. Previous editions have welcomed the likes of Tiësto, Booba and DJ Snake, but what really sets this festival apart is its location: you can dance with your feet in the sand, overlooking the shimmering Mediterranean Sea as the sun goes down. And with Cannes' restaurants, bars and beaches on your doorstep, it's the perfect excuse to turn a festival weekend into a longer holiday on the French Riviera. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, but tickets are already on sale. Tickets: Dropping November 2026. The tranquil Croatian island of Pag is renowned for a remarkably eclectic range of things: cheese, its moonlike landscape, picturesque bays – and one of Europe's leading electronic music festivals. Each summer, Hideout takes over Zrće Beach, where festivalgoers dance through scorching afternoons, balmy evenings and into the early hours to a soundtrack of house, techno, drum and bass and other electronic sounds. Previous editions have welcomed the likes of Ben Hemsley, Hybrid Minds and Dimension, but it's the setting that really makes this festival special. Expect five open-air beachfront venues, poolside parties and boat trips along the Adriatic, with some sets continuing until sunrise. Forget wiggly tent poles and repair patches – visitors can book accommodation in nearby Novalja, with shuttle buses running to and from the festival. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, and festivalgoers can register on the official website for ticket updates. Tickets: Early allocations sold out; next release on 29 October 2026 While many of the best festivals in Europe are held on breathtaking beaches and in sprawling parks, Snowboxx is a rather different affair. Taking over the car-free ski resort of Avoriaz in the French Alps, the week-long festival combines days on the slopes with live music, DJ sets and raucous après-ski parties. Previous editions have welcomed the likes of Pendulum, The Blessed Madonna and Groove Armada, with performances taking place everywhere from a huge open-air stage surrounded by snow-capped peaks to the legendary slopeside La Folie Douce. There are all the high-altitude shenanigans you can shake a ski pole at, too, from bottomless brunches and mountain parties to some of the best skiing and snowboarding in France. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, but tickets are already selling fast, with accommodation packages and discounted lift passes available through the festival. Best for: indie, rock and alternative music Tickets: 2027 details yet to be announced; waiting list open. With its mix of indie, rock, pop and electronic music, MEO Kalorama is one of the best European festivals for those who like a little bit of everything. Previous editions have welcomed everyone from Massive Attack and LCD Soundsystem to Robbie Williams, Deftones and Turnstile, with international stars and emerging artists taking to the stages at Lisbon's Parque da Bela Vista. The sprawling green space is just a short journey from the Portuguese capital's historic neighbourhoods, restaurants and nightlife, making it easy to combine a few days of live music with a proper city break. Beyond the performances, the festival also puts an emphasis on art, sustainability and local gastronomy. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, but festivalgoers can sign up for ticket updates on the official website. Best for: techno in an industrial setting Tickets: Early allocations sold out; join the waiting list for further releases. The Italian city of Turin is best known for its art galleries, historic attractions and culinary heritage, as well as its legendary shroud. But summer brings with it a very different vibe, as some of the world's leading DJs and producers descend on Parco Dora for Kappa FuturFestival. Taking place in a former industrial complex, where towering steel structures and old factory buildings provide a dramatic backdrop, the three-day festival has become a major fixture on Europe's electronic music calendar. Previous editions have welcomed the likes of Skrillex, Carl Cox and Honey Dijon, with house and techno taking centre stage. For the ultimate festival experience, look out for the Art & Techno package, which combines VIP access with luxury accommodation, fine dining and private tours of Turin's art galleries and collections. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, but visitors can join the official waiting list for upcoming ticket releases. Best for: underground beats on the coast Tickets: Register on the official website for ticket updates Launched in 2025, Adriatic Sound Festival is one of the newer additions to Europe's electronic music calendar, bringing some of the world's leading DJs to the Italian seaside town of Fano. Taking over the city's airport, the three-day event combines house and techno with some seriously impressive stage designs inspired by the area's Roman and industrial heritage. Previous editions have welcomed the likes of Armand Van Helden, Sven Väth and Stephan Bodzin, with performances taking place across two striking stages: a 360-degree Roman-inspired amphitheatre and an open-air techno arena framed by old aircraft hangars. And with the Adriatic coast just a short distance away, there's plenty of opportunity to combine late-night dancing with lazy afternoons on the beach. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, but festivalgoers can register for ticket updates on the official website. Tickets: Not released yet. Register on the official website for 2027 updates. Croatia has established itself as one of Europe's leading destinations for electronic music, and Sonus has played a big part in putting the country's festival scene on the map. Since launching in 2013, the event has attracted some of the biggest names in underground house and techno, with previous line-ups featuring the likes of Adam Beyer, Seth Troxler, Richie Hawtin and Sven Väth. For more than a decade, the festival took over the open-air clubs of Pag Island's Zrće Beach, where marathon DJ sets, boat parties and dancing until sunrise became part of its appeal. After cancelling its 2026 edition, Sonus is planning a comeback in 2027 at a new location in Croatia. The dates, venue and line-up are yet to be announced, but festivalgoers can register for updates on the official website. Tickets: Four-day passes sold out; official resale available. If the name doesn't give it away, a quick scan of Hellfest's website is enough to decipher who this festival in Clisson, western France, attracts. Expect black T-shirts emblazoned with the logos of the world's best-known heavy metal and rock bands, enormous sculptures and a festival site that looks like something out of a post-apocalyptic fantasy. It's quite literally meant to be hell on earth, but the community feel and friendly faces bring a lighter air to the proceedings. The 2027 edition marks the festival's 20th anniversary, with more than 300 bands expected to perform across 10 stages, covering everything from heavy metal and hard rock to punk and hardcore. The line-up is yet to be announced, but four-day passes have already sold out, with tickets available through the festival's official resale platform. Tickets: On sale, from £225 for a five-day pass. If drum and bass and beach holidays are your vibe, why not combine them at Hospitality on the Beach? Taking over The Garden Resort in the Croatian coastal town of Tisno, the festival brings together some of the genre's biggest names, with previous editions welcoming the likes of Netsky, Hybrid Minds and Camo & Krooked. Expect everything from liquid drum and bass and jungle to jump-up and neurofunk across five stages, with boat parties on the Adriatic and afterparties at the legendary Barbarella's Discotheque keeping the music going into the early hours. And with several days of raving by the sea, there's plenty of time to break away for some R&R, swim in the crystal-clear waters or explore the charming town of Tisno. The 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, but tickets are already on sale, with accommodation and boat parties booked separately. Best for: indie favourites and major headliners Headliners: Phoebe Bridgers, Massive Attack, Robyn, Caroline Polachek, Turnstile and Skrillex Tickets: On sale from €295 (£249) plus fees for the standard fan-sale pass. Few European music festivals have quite the same reputation for bringing together some of the biggest names in indie, alternative rock, pop and electronic music as Primavera Sound. Taking over Barcelona's waterfront Parc del Fòrum each summer, the festival has previously welcomed everyone from Charli XCX and Chappell Roan to Sabrina Carpenter, and its 25th edition in 2027 promises another stellar line-up, with Phoebe Bridgers, Massive Attack, Robyn and Turnstile among the confirmed acts. There's no camping here, so festivalgoers can spend their days exploring Barcelona's beaches, restaurants and cultural attractions before heading to the stages in the afternoon and evening. For those who prefer a slightly more laid-back atmosphere, Primavera Sound also has a sister festival in Porto, taking place a week later in the city's leafy Parque da Cidade, with four-day passes already on sale. Headliners: Tame Impala, Caroline Polachek, Kacey Musgraves, Patti Smith Quartet and more announced acts Thanks to a stellar roster of acts arriving from across the globe, Roskilde is one of the hottest tickets in Denmark each summer. Previous editions have welcomed everyone from Charli XCX and Olivia Rodrigo to Stormzy and Doechii, while Tame Impala, Caroline Polachek and Kacey Musgraves are among the first names confirmed for 2027. But music is just the tip of the iceberg at this eight-day festival, which transforms the fields outside the Danish city of Roskilde into a temporary community of music lovers, artists and creatives. Sit in on debates, discover contemporary art installations, take part in workshops or simply soak up the atmosphere before heading back to the stages. Roskilde is also one of Europe's largest non-profit music festivals, with proceeds supporting charitable causes, so there's another reason to feel good about attending. Tickets for 2027 are already on sale, with full festival passes and shorter options available. Best for: jazz, soul and lakeside concerts Few music festivals can boast a setting quite as spectacular as Montreux Jazz Festival, which takes over the shores of Lake Geneva each summer, with the Swiss Alps providing a rather impressive backdrop. Founded in 1967, the festival has welcomed some of the biggest names in music over the decades, from Nina Simone and Miles Davis to David Bowie and Prince. And despite its name, jazz is only part of the story. Expect everything from soul and blues to rock, pop and electronic music, with performances taking place in intimate venues and larger concert halls, alongside free concerts and events along the lakefront. Between gigs, there's plenty of time to explore Montreux's waterfront promenade, take a boat trip across the lake or venture into the surrounding mountains. The 2027 line-up and ticket details are yet to be announced. Best for: Salsa, Latin rhythms and dancing You might not expect to find one of Europe's biggest celebrations of Latin and Afro-Cuban music in a small town in southwestern France, but that's exactly what happens in Vic-Fezensac each summer. Since 1994, Tempo Latino has been bringing the sounds of salsa, Cuban son, mambo and Latin jazz to the heart of the Gers countryside, transforming the town into a lively celebration of music and dance. Previous editions have welcomed the likes of Yuri Buenaventura, Spanish Harlem Orchestra, Flavia Coelho and Eliades Ochoa, with concerts taking place in the town's bullring and smaller venues, while street performances and late-night dancing keep the party going well beyond the main stage. And when you're not dancing, there's plenty to explore in this corner of France, from pretty Gascon villages to vineyards and local markets. The 2027 dates and line-up are yet to be announced, but it's one worth keeping on your radar.

item.title: 13 country-ready outdoor and Wellington boots to splatter through puddles in style in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
A crisp autumnal walk in the British countryside is one of life’s little pleasures – until a squelchy patch of track or a sudden downpour threatens to ruin the mood (trudging about in wet socks is surely one of the most unfortunate feelings it’s possible to endure). So a good pair of waterproof boots is a must for all weekend rambles. Fortunately, there are plenty of options out there that turn the humble rainboot into a bona fide part of your outfit, rather than resigning yourself to donning a pair of shapeless green numbers. Hunter remains the undisputed champion for off-duty models and festival-goers, with its coveted slim-fit shape earning cult status with the style set for decades. The runway has fully embraced the outdoorsy look in recent years, too. Burberry outfits its Wellington boots in its signature vintage check, Bottega Veneta’s chunky Puddle boots have sparked a wave of minimalist copycats, while Chloé’s block-heeled Betty rubber boots have become a modern street style staple. Add in Prada’s bright rubber lug soles, and fleece-lined iterations from Loro Piana, and it is clear that wet weather footwear has earned itself a new luxury status. We’ve found the best Wellington boots on the market, from British heritage bootmakers with royal warrants to more contemporary labels reinventing the classic outdoor boot – along with all of our editors’ most loved tried-and-tested pairs. Put on a thick pair of Welly socks, grab your raincoat, and prepare to brave the drizzle. To find the best Wellington and outdoor boots, we put pairs through their paces across varied British landscapes and weather conditions. We evaluate fit and initial comfort straight out of the box, noting whether sizing runs true, if calf openings accommodate different leg shapes, and whether soles provide good arch support on long strolls. We've trudged across waterlogged tracks, muddy paths and wet grass alike, assessing grip on slick surfaces, thermal insulation on cold mornings, and the durability of zips, buckles, and linings. Proper care extends the lifespan of natural rubber, keeps linings fresh, and prevents premature cracking or discolouration. Here’s how to maintain your boots after a muddy outing: - Don’t let heavy mud dry and cake onto natural rubber. Hose or rinse boots down with lukewarm water as soon as you step inside, using a soft sponge or cloth to wipe away stubborn dirt. Avoid stiff bristle brushes to prevent scratching. - For deeper grime, use a gentle detergent or mild dish soap with warm water. Clean both the rubber uppers and the lugged outsoles, where dirt works into the tread. Rinse with clean water. - Air-dry naturally away from heat in a cool, well-ventilated space. Never put rubber boots directly next to radiators, open fires or in direct sunlight, as high heat causes natural rubber to dry, stiffen and split. To maintain the boot’s shape, stuff the interiors with crumpled newspaper or clean hand towels. - Use a conditioner. Natural rubber blooms over time, developing a powdery white film as insoluble minerals rise to the surface. Restore its luster and flexibility by applying a boot spray or conditioner with a microfibre cloth. - Keep boots in a dry, dark place, stored upright to prevent creases. More of our editors’ favourite shoes for travel

item.title: 12 of the best restaurants in Dublin: new-gen homegrown chefs are changing up Dublin's food game
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
There was a time when Dublin’s most notable gift to the culinary world was a spice burger – usually ordered from a chipper on the way home from the pub (Anthony Bourdain even tried one when he visited the city for his TV show No Reservations in the early 2000s). But in recent decades the Irish capital has shed its reputation for sub-par (or, not to malign chippers, let’s say unadventurous) food and gained a newfound swagger, thanks to a young generation of brilliant homegrown chefs. The result is that it now has a restaurant scene to rival any in Europe, and a corresponding generation of foodies to fill its hottest tables – as well as a renewed focus on championing Ireland’s abundant ingredients. As a keen Irish foodie – and someone who regularly ordered spice burgers as a student in the city many years ago – I will now patiently queue at the hole-in-the-wall serving the best pizza in town and build lunch at a buzzed-about spot into my weekend plans. Here’s a pick of the best restaurants in Dublin – from crisply laid two-star tables to the neighbourhood joints we’d all love to have around the corner. Brilliant Brazilian food is not what you expect to find – or look for – in Dublin city centre, but Amai by Viktor has been taking everyone by surprise since it quietly opened in the second half of 2025. The restaurant is set above The Corkscrew off-licence in a beautiful room that was once a shoe shop. Running the kitchen is Brazilian Viktor Silva, whose multi-course tasting menu might include beef pastel with banana ketchup, wood pigeon with blackberry and cachaca jelly with black lime. It’s also open for lunch when you can taste a crunched-down version. Love (amai means “to love” in Brazilian Portuguese) goes into everything here – long may Dubliners enjoy this slice of South American passion and sunshine. Address: Amai by Viktor, 4 Harry Street, Dublin D02 CX24 If you’re the type of person who likes to lock in your foodie adventures in advance, this is the one for you, as gold-dust bookings are best bagged via Instagram a couple of months ahead. Sandwich shop owner Barry Stephens opened a Mexican food truck during lockdown, and this is its evolution, set in a former warehouse in the northside neighbourhood of Clontarf. His wife Jen softened the space by painting it pink, and it now hums with grinning diners tucking into Korean-spiced, six-hour-smoked free-range pork belly, beef birria tacos and charred baby gem in a blue cheese vinaigrette, washed down with cold beers from Dublin brewery Whiplash. The terrace outside is the spot for cocktails on a sunny day and hopping summer dance parties. Address: Chubbys, Rear of 46 Clontarf Road, Clontarf, Dublin D03A5X2 This new arrival in the Liberties neighbourhood is the hot table everyone is talking about. From the team behind Michelin-starred yet uber-casual Variety Jones next door, Mongoose is only open from Sunday to Tuesday – hence the frenzy to bag a seat. The fluorescent cardboard signs on the window and the stripped-back decor belie the high-level cooking going on here. Dishes such as cockles in white wine, Parmesan-topped agnoletti pasta and porchetta with gremolata are hearty and happy-making; and there’s a wodge of sticky toffee pudding with Jersey milk ice cream for dessert. The brilliant value Monday lunch menu has three courses for 32 euros – a great excuse to beat the start-of-the-week blues and treat yourself to a meal out in what can be a very pricey city. Address: Mongoose, 78 Thomas Street, The Liberties, Dublin, D08 F2RN Tucked down a lane off super-central Dawson Street, on the site of a former wine bar, Comet is a European-style bistro that got foodies in the Irish capital all aflutter when it arrived in mid 2025. The pedigree of the team who run it is impressive: chef Kevin O’Donnell cut his teeth at Dublin favourite Bastible before working in starry kitchens in Denmark and returning home to roll out popular supper clubs; along the way he met his wife, Laura Chabal, who now brilliantly runs the front of house at Comet, which they set up with O’Donnell’s old Bastible bosses. Anyone feeling daring can roll the dice on the four-course carte blanche for 78 euros. Otherwise, there could be melon and cucumber salad with cured pork, aged duck and beetroot, and a quail roasted on toast with vin jaune sauce that’s been a menu staple since Comet opened. The brilliant low-intervention wine list is a worthy pairing for the sublime cooking. Address: Comet, 3 Joshua Lane, Dublin D02 C856 Northside enclave Stoneybatter has become a restaurant hotspot in recent years, with classic Italian at Grano and brilliant modern Chinese at Hakkahan. And this neighbourhood café added a zero-waste ethos to the mix. It was founded by Sarah Boland, who trained at Ballymaloe Cookery School in County Cork, and head chef Hannah O’Donnell, formerly of Galway favourite Kai, steers the kitchen. For dinner (Wednesday to Saturday), there could be rabbit croquettes with the sharpness of apple as a “picky bit”, followed by mussels with beet tartare and scallops with chickpea masala. These are flavour combinations you won’t find anywhere else in the city, and they work. A weekend brunch of croissant French toast with whipped dark chocolate and strawberries is as over-the-top and treat-yourself as it sounds. Address: Vada, 30 Brunswick Street North, Stoneybatter, Dublin D07 TP64 Bang originally opened to much buzz in Dublin in the boom years of the late 1990s before fizzling out and being sold a decade later. Now Richie Barrett, the son of that owner, has rejuvenated the space once again, and the buzz is very much back. The focus this time around is on the food of the Iberian Peninsula, which chef Eric Matthews (Barrett’s longtime friend and partner in this new venture) has turned into a menu featuring a gooey tortilla named after the legendary Barcelona tapas spot Cal Pep and piri piri chicken reminiscent of beachside lunches in the Algarve. It’s all served amid interiors as warm as a Valencian sunset – and, proving their commitment to the theme, the decadent chocolate mousse swims in a puddle of caramel made from jamón fat and gets an extra kick of Pedro Ximénez sherry at the table. Address: Bang, 11 Merrion Row, Dublin D02 KW61 One of Dublin’s quintessential neighbourhoods and a must for visitors, Howth is a charming fishing village and well-heeled residential suburb on the north side of Dublin Bay, known for the seafood restaurants lining its small working harbour. Mamó is an affectionate term for grandmother in the Irish language, and this small restaurant feels like a warm embrace as soon as you walk in. The food here is a spin on contemporary Irish fare – even the cod chip from the nibbles section of the menu is a clever culinary nod to the restaurant’s location. Work up an appetite on the panoramic trail around Howth Head before lunch (the ground-floor counter takes walk-ins if you haven’t booked) or look out over the twinkling lights of the harbour at night from the first-floor dining room. Address: Mamó Restaurant, Harbour House, Harbour Road, Howth, Dublin, D13 E9H9 Spain informs the overriding theme of the food at this perennial favourite spot in a long narrow space on Aungier Street. The menu kicks off with tapas-inspired classics such as moreish croquetas, padrón peppers and squid à la plancha and moves on to more substantial starters: beef tartare with pickled Spanish chillies or crab with taramasalata and radish, perhaps. Mains follow the same big-flavored cue – the salt-aged Delmonico steak for two accompanied by béarnaise, beef dripping potatoes and Bordelaise sauce is a menu staple, and there is an extensive list of lesser-known Spanish and Portuguese wines and sherries. Order the modest-sounding flan de queso for dessert even if you think you’re full – honestly. Address: Uno Mas, 6 Aungier Street, Dublin, D02 WN47 For one of Dublin’s more elevated fish-and-chip experiences, perch on a stool at the diminutive spot Fish Shop in Smithfield, which has been serving happy regulars for 10 years. There’s a handful of small plates to start – oysters, prawn croquettes or mussels from County Cork – and the main event is a selection of sustainably sourced species from Irish coastal waters such as hake, haddock and plaice, which can be served without the crisp beer batter if that’s your preference, and hand-cut chunky chips. Accompany it all with a glass of something from the highly selective wine list, which gives a shout-out to the expat Irish winemakers turning out brilliant bottles in vineyards from Slovenia to the South Downs. There’s a side of salad for a crunch of green and a zingy lemon posset for dessert. Also, try its sister wine bar on the other side of the river, Bar Pez, on Kevin Street. Address: Fish Shop, 76 Benburb Street, Smithfield, Dublin, D07 X3PN Most evenings, Note thrums with a pleasing bustle as people drop in for an after-work Negroni at the bar and snacks of lamb kofte topped with Aleppo pepper, or something more substantial from the succinct bistro-style menu served in the wedge-shaped dining room. It might include Connemara oysters with pickled garlic scapes followed by beautifully plated dishes such as smoked beetroot, with milk curd, cherries and dillisk. The wine list features a cherry-picked roster of natural and low-intervention wines and grower Champagnes from small producers, as well as a tight line-up of 10 classic cocktails, including two non-alcoholic options (try the Connemara Sour with peated whiskey). Despite being pretty much in the centre of the city, it still manages to retain a casual neighbourhood feel. It’s also one of the best restaurants in Dublin that opens for dinner on Mondays – worth noting if you are in town for a long weekend. Address: Note, 26 Fenian Street, Dublin D02 FX09 Michelin-starred D’Olier Street is smart and slick – the culmination of three friends’ dream to open a fine-dining restaurant in Dublin. Occupying the striking, stuccoed Victorian D’Olier Chambers opposite Trinity College, the restaurant serves just one option: a leisurely-paced, 13-course tasting menu for 139 euros that ranges from micro bites to more substantial plates, so there is no need to feel daunted. There is also a five-glass wine pairing curated by one of Dublin’s best sommeliers, plus a non-alcoholic cocktail pairing. Australian-born chef James Moore spent time working in the two Michelin-starred kitchens of Manhattan’s Atera, so there are some serious cooking skills on show here – try to bag one of the 10 seats at the chef’s counter and pray that the foie gras custard with pineapple and dinky English muffins is still on the menu. Address: D’Olier Street, D’Olier Chambers, D’Olier Street, Dublin D02 H589 Chef Mickael Viljanen has been the talent behind the stoves of one of Dublin’s best restaurants since 2021, and the culinary creativity he brought with him was rewarded with two Michelin stars the following year. Born in Sweden, raised in Finland and a long-time resident of Ireland, Viljanen combines his Nordic sensibilities with sublime skills and decadent ingredients such as foie gras and hand-dived scallops. His inventive renderings of Irish produce could include dishes such as Donegal lobster glazed with Kari Gosse spices, plus pumpkin, yuzu and mandarin. The three-course lunch is a more affordable way to experience one of Ireland’s most exciting dining rooms – be sure to save space for the dedicated Irish coffee trolley. Address: Chapter One Restaurant, 18-19 Parnell Square North, Rotunda, Dublin D01 T3V8

item.title: 14 best hotels in Budapest 2026, Hungary's historic capital
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
The best hotels in Budapest have been riding high of late thanks to a bevy of international names arriving in the capital, the latest addition being St. Regis in May 2026. Settled by Celtic tribes and developed into a flourishing city of baths and amphitheatres by the Romans, where Emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote part of his Meditations, the city on the majestic Danube that eventually became Budapest (and the capital of one of Europe’s largest and most splendid empires) offers a universe of cultural flavours to charm every palate. From Islamic shrines and Ottoman bathhouses to Art Nouveau, baroque and neo-renaissance palaces, ruin bars, and Michelin-starred restaurants, there's no shortage of things to see and do. The great European artery, the Danube, winds through the city, crossed by ornate bridges that link the genteel villas and medieval streets of the Buda hills with the elegant boulevards of Pest. Compact and eminently walkable, Budapest has world-class museums, galleries, architecture and music venues, and a burgeoning food scene from contemporary street food to destination restaurants, while hidden courtyards reveal artisan bakeries and coffee shops, boutiques of traditional crafts and innovative fashion. And with some of Europe’s most elegant and distinctive luxury hotels, you may want to stay for longer than just the weekend. This is our pick of the best hotels in Budapest. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Budapest What is the best part of Budapest to stay in? While the Buda side of the Danube may be the smartest part of town for wealthy residents looking for peace and quiet, Pest is where the action is and is packed with historical buildings and great places to eat, drink, shop and stroll. While this edit of the best hotels in Budapest, from new openings to heritage classics, concentrates on the central Pest districts (from here, reaching the central landmarks is easy), there are also a couple of carefully selected options on the Buda side that still feel well located for a trip that encompasses all the best things to do in Budapest. How we choose the best hotels in Budapest Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page.

item.title: The 10 best things to do in London this weekend
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
When searching for the best things to do in London this weekend, it’s hard not to end up more confused and indecisive than when you started. While it’s never a bad idea to secure a booking at one of the best restaurants in the capital, spend an evening in one of the latest innovative bars on the scene or even explore an iconic London attraction, we’re always on the lookout for new, exciting pop-ups, openings and events. Each week, we get the inside track on exciting things to do in London for the upcoming weekend to help us discover a new area of the city or explore a new address in a neighbourhood we thought we’d already uncovered. Things to do in London this weekend (16 - 18 October) Pulitzer Prize-winning opera Angel's Bone arrives at the London Coliseum following its UK premiere at Manchester’s Aviva Studio in spring. The run is part of the English National Opera's dual-centre model, bringing opera to audiences in both Greater Manchester and London – with productions shaped by the venues in which they’re performed. Angel’s Bone tells the story of Mr and Mrs X.E., a desperate couple longing for a better life who discover two wounded angels in their garden. However, what begins as an act of compassion takes a darker turn, highlighting human greed and socially relevant issues. Address: London Coliseum, St Martin's Lane, London WC2N 4ES Argentine bakery Madre is the latest business to take residency in King’s Cross – and the treats are well worth making time for. The coffee shop at Fabrica X is part of The Mills Fabrica, a platform that supports innovation across techstyle and agrifood, with a focus on sustainability and social impact. Think small-batch, indulgent bites that pair fabulously well with their usual coffee offering. Address: The Mills Fabrica, 36-40 York Way, London N1 9AB A handful of new drinking dens have opened across the capital recently, just in time for cosy autumn evenings spent nursing a pint (or stronger concoction, should you so choose). The Last Exchange is the city’s newest pub, having opened its doors in Exchange Square, a stone’s throw from Liverpool Street Station. The team is determined to ‘pub properly’, with all the tipples you can imagine and a menu of elevated classics. Sip on a pint of The City Scribbler, the pub’s own house beer, and feel the stresses of city life fizzle away. Elsewhere, Bar Buah has started welcoming thirsty foodies at The White Horse, Peckham. Ex-Oranj chef Elies Salvà Ruiz de Villegas is in charge, so expect dishes such as crab caldereta and oxtail croquetas to go down very well with a glass of wine. Address: The Last Exchange, 11 Exchange Square, Broadgate, London EC2A 2BR; Bar Buah at The White Horse Peckham Website: publicanestate.com; whitehorsepeckham.co.uk 4. Have a laugh at the Leicester Square Theatre Enjoy an evening of laughs as man of many talents – comedian, writer, director and novelist among them – Andy Hamilton takes to the stage at the Leicester Square Theatre this Sunday. Cackle away as he explores the wonders and the weaknesses of human memory, touching on the nights he’ll never forget along the way. Address: Leicester Square Theatre, 6 Leicester Place, London WC2H 7BX BREW//LDN goes Bavarian for its first-ever Oktoberfest celebration this weekend, uniting 18 breweries in the same space for two days of beer-sloshing. More than 35 beers are available on tap at the site, found at Riverside East in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, plus a live oompah band, DJs and street food stalls. Address: Riverside East, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, 5 Thornton St, London E20 2AD 6. Pick up affordable pieces in Battersea Aesthetes and art lovers come together under one roof as the Affordable Art Fair Battersea returns for its autumn edition this week. The fair offers an accessible introduction to collecting with thousands of works priced under £10,000 across multiple spaces – with more than 100 galleries participating. Address: Battersea Evolution, Battersea Park, Queenstown Road, London SW11 4NJ Celebrate six years of Michelin-starred Kol, recognised as one of the best restaurants in the world, as the team throw a one-night-only celebration this Sunday. Chef and founder Santiago Lastra is transforming the restaurant into a dynamic culinary festival as four of the city’s most celebrated chefs, including Margo Henderson and Jeremy Lee, interpret iconic Mexican dishes in their own way. Tickets cost £135 per person and include a glass of biodynamic wine Gut Oggau, five dishes, and a cocktail. Address: KOL, 9 Seymour Street, London W1H 7BA 8. Experience the art of French patisserie Claridge’s Art Café has been one of London’s sleekest addresses for a sweet treat since it opened its doors. However, following a rebranding that sees Thibault Hauchard front and centre of the operation, there’s never been a better time to check out the selection on offer. Think artisan coffees, boiled eggs with truffle cheese soldiers and avo toast in the morning, before heartier lunch dishes and an array of spectacular patisserie options until close. Address: Art Café By Thibault Hauchard, Brook's Mews, London W1K 4HR 9. Find hidden treasure at a vintage market As if its array of viral street food stalls, thrift shops and various secret hideouts weren’t reason enough to visit, Camden Market welcomes a new open-air market on Saturdays this autumn in collaboration with Bootyfull Car Boot. Expect curated stalls filled with vintage fashion, retro accessories, rare vinyl records, original art and jewellery – or sell your own wares by securing a stall for £40. Address: Market Place, Hawley Wharf, NW1 10. Get soulful at Soho’s latest live music series Where better to spend an autumn evening than up high in one of the city’s glitziest rooftop bars? On select midweek nights throughout the rest of October, Flute at Broadwick Soho presents a series of live music events in collaboration with Johnnie Walker. Savour a range of limited-edition cocktails as performers including Madeleine (13 October) and Kianja (21 October) bring the soul above the colourful chaos of Soho. Address: Flute Bar, 7th floor, 20 Broadwick Street, London W1F 8TH

item.title: The jet lag app that frequent fliers (and NASA astronauts) swear by
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Timeshifter was featured on Condé Nast Traveller's Bright Ideas in Travel 2026. What traveller, in their tedious shuffle back to the cramped rear of the plane, hasn’t gazed longingly at the lie-flat seats in business and first class? Surely the jet lag wouldn’t hit so hard if you could recline all the way back and get some proper rest, right? But that assumes jet lag is a sleep deprivation problem when, in fact, it’s not. “Everything that’s shared today publicly about how to address jet lag is wrong,” says Mickey Beyer-Clausen, co-founder and CEO of Timeshifter, a circadian tech company that aims to help travellers and shift workers adjust to new time zones and manage irregular schedules. “The biggest challenge is that circadian science is not publicly very well known.” Timeshifter is working to change that. Understanding circadian science begins with the fact that each of our brains contains a tiny “clock,” a cluster of neurons called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which is smaller than a grain of rice. This clock determines your body’s daily cycle of sleep and alertness – the circadian rhythm. “What we’re talking about is internal time,” explains Martha Merrow, a chronobiologist and visiting professor of circadian medicine at the University of Oxford. “Everybody’s got their own internal time, which is unique to them," she says. Two people who share the same schedule can still have different internal times due to a range of factors, among them a person’s “chronotype,” which describes if you’re an early or late riser. Whenever you cross a few time zones, your internal time can differ from the actual time at your destination. That disagreement is jet lag. Yet much of the conventional advice about jet lag doesn’t address the key mechanism that helps your internal clock adjust. In short, it’s all about light, with sleep playing only a supporting role. “Sleep comes into it in two ways,” Merrow says. “One, if you don’t get enough of it, you really feel horrible. But the other way is that when you sleep, you actually are actively modifying your light environment by closing your eyes. So by sleeping at the ‘right time’ or ‘wrong time,’ you can help the phase shifting that you’re trying to achieve – or you can hinder it.” That exposure to light is “the main thing,” she says, that helps our internal rhythms adjust to wherever we are. That’s why snoozing on a flight doesn’t always help; it might shift your circadian rhythm in the ‘wrong’ direction. “You can sleep for eight hours and feel massively jet-lagged because all your circadian clocks are out of whack,” according to Beyer-Clausen. The solution is getting the timing right for light exposure, darkness, and sleep. “You have to personalise that for each traveller,” he says. That’s why the Timeshifter jet lag app asks for your age, your usual sleep times, your caffeine and melatonin habits, and your chronotype – early bird, night owl, or neither. Then you enter your flight numbers; the app pulls info about your departure and arrival times. With all that info, the app’s algorithm formulates a plan that begins days before you depart. It tells you when to expose yourself to light or avoid it; when to use and avoid caffeine; and when to snooze (and take melatonin, if you like). The protocols behind the app were first developed to support professional travellers who have no margin for error: NASA astronauts. Steven Lockley, Timeshifter’s co-founder and chief scientist, previously worked with NASA when he was an associate professor at Harvard Medical School. “I had been a user of the science through Dr Lockley in preparing for missions,” says Michael López-Alegría, a former NASA astronaut and investor in the app’s 2026 funding round. “Our bodies can naturally shift our circadian clocks about an hour a day, but using recommendations driven by science and provided through the Timeshifter app can accelerate that dramatically.” According to Lockley, following the guidance can help you shift as much as three to four hours a day. What does that look like in practice? I downloaded the app, entered my details for a theoretical trip (flying from my home in London to Tokyo and back), and checked what my Timeshifter plan looked like. Outbound, it told me to go to bed at 1am and 2am on the days before my flight. That’s easy enough for me, a hyperactive night owl. Harder would be the recommendation I avoid caffeine the morning I go to the airport (ouch, the brain fog), then sleep as soon as I board the plane (not going to happen with my nerves). I showed several personalised plans I generated to Merrow, who has no commercial relationship with Timeshifter. She confirmed the app generally aligned with the principles of circadian science. She also observed, as other reviewers of the app have, “it will be difficult to get excellent compliance” due to human behaviour. “For instance, they expect [you to] sleep on much of one flight, but we know that drinks and a meal will be served in addition to the entertainment.” My success would depend on me following along to the plan, which might not always be possible. The Timeshifter app itself acknowledges such limitations. Its guidance explains that even if you can’t exactly sleep when it advises you to get some z’s, you could wear dark glasses to avoid light and still help nudge your internal clock. When you can follow the advice, it’s a game-changer, according to Sem Verbeek, a professional tennis player and 2025 Mixed Doubles Wimbledon Champion. Timeshifter’s user base includes a cohort of professionals like him – athletes, Formula 1 teams, astronauts – who need to be sharp when they land in a new time zone. “The biggest proof of concept for me came during my trip to Australia at the start of last season,” says Verbeek, who explained he would normally need to travel during Christmas to be prepared for the first week of the season. Timeshifter helped him “spend more precious time with my family and adjust more quickly and effectively than before.” Timeshifter gives you your first plan for free; after that, it’s around £7.55 per trip or around £18.89 per year, appealing to frequent long-haul fliers who can control their schedules. And due to partnerships with major travel brands, more of us ordinary travellers are getting free access. United Airlines’ Premier 1K members receive complimentary plans for each flight. In August, InterContinental Hotels expanded its partnership with Timeshifter; travellers staying at the brand’s properties get access with every booking. “The response has been great,” notes Tom Rowntree, vice president of global luxury and lifestyle brands at IHG Hotels & Resorts. “We’re able to support our guests to overcome some of the effects of long-haul travel even before they arrive.” But even pros can’t always follow the guidance perfectly. Verbeek admits his tennis matches can get in the way. “The most difficult part about following a plan is having to work around court times. We don’t always control when we can practice, let alone play our match,” he shares. “But a Timeshifter plan isn’t so strict that you need to follow it 100 per cent.” Which is good news for anyone who, say, demands some espresso before navigating their way to the airport.

item.title: The Orient Express is launching a new route to the French Riviera
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
As someone who travels a lot for work, I have developed a particular dislike for short-haul flights. When budget airlines first started making an appearance, I thought being able to fly to another country in a couple of hours for the price of a London coffee was the best thing ever. Now, I would give anything to swap a flight for a train – even if that means spending eight hours on the rails. Thankfully, we are incredibly spoiled on this side of the world since Europe offers some of the best train holidays in the world. And although I am a big fan of a high-speed Italian train, there's no better way to travel than aboard one of Belmond's gorgeously luxurious trains. The company already offers rail journeys ranging from the Peruvian Andes and Southeast Asia to the Amalfi Coast and the Scottish Highlands, but it has just announced a glamorous new addition to its already impressive collection of journeys. From 10 May 2027, the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express will travel to Monte Carlo for the first time in its history, introducing a new route from Paris to Monaco. The journey, which will become an annual addition to the train's schedule, will take passengers through some of the most spectacular scenery along the French Riviera before arriving in the glamorous principality, which will become a new stop on the train's onward journey to Venice. The experience begins in Paris, where passengers will board the train's distinctive midnight-blue carriages before settling into their accommodation for the night. There are several options to choose from, including the classic Historic Cabins, Suites and Grand Suites, each drawing inspiration from the train's Art Deco heritage. For those looking to really splash out, there's also L'Observatoire, an exclusive carriage created in collaboration with French artist JR. Designed as a private sanctuary on the rails, it comes complete with a bedroom, an en-suite bathroom featuring a freestanding bathtub, a spacious living area, a library and even a secret tearoom. As evening approaches, guests can enjoy dinner in one of the train's two restaurant cars, Étoile du Nord and L'Oriental, before heading to the famous Bar Car 3674 for cocktails and live piano music. But perhaps the most exciting part of the new journey comes the following morning. After waking up to breakfast served in their cabins, passengers will be treated to sweeping views of the Mediterranean as the train makes its way along the Côte d'Azur. The route passes the red cliffs of the Massif de l'Estérel and travels through Saint-Raphaël towards Cannes and Nice. The train will then continue towards Monaco before arriving at Monaco-Monte-Carlo station. Monte Carlo also has a surprising connection to the train's history. In 1977, two original train carriages were purchased at an auction in the principality, helping set in motion the project that would eventually become the luxury train we know today. "Introducing the destination feels like a natural continuation for the Venice-Simplon Orient Express, bringing the romance of luxury rail travel to a locale that has always understood the art of arrival. There's also something rather special about coming back to Monte Carlo, given the role it played in the train's history," said Pascal Deyrolle, Belmond's Europe area managing director for trains. The new journey is part of Belmond's expanding collection of European rail experiences, alongside the second year of its Villeggiatura by Train series, which connects the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express with Belmond hotels in Italy. Of course, a journey this luxurious comes with a price tag to match. Tickets for the new Paris-to-Monte-Carlo route start from €4,870 per person, based on two people sharing a Historic Cabin. The fare includes the overnight journey, all meals with sommelier-selected wines, unlimited soft drinks, transfers and 24-hour steward service.

item.title: A London bar you've probably never heard of just made it onto the world’s 50 Best Bars list
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
New bars appear in London almost every week. Some throw open their doors with loud, glitzy opening parties, and others unlock theirs without so much as a sound. In my experience, each can be met with reactions good and bad â though very few tend to spark the sort of awe that Waltz has done over the last 12 months. When the Japanese-inspired bar opened on Scrutton Street, East London, in April 2025, those who work in the hospitality industry â chefs, bartenders, front of house aficionados and lifestyle writers like myself â spoke about it in the same way in which one might point a friend to a particular good corner at sample sale. In other words, with the sort of hushed excitement that youâd rather strangers didnât see. Last night, though, the game was well and truly up. At the global 2026 edition of The 50 Best Bar awards in Milan, Waltz secured the ranking of 32nd, and the brilliance of the bar was made plain for all to see. This is something of a flex, considering itâs the first fresh bar to enter the list since Scarfes at the Rosewood London hotel, which was finally recognised after a decade of work in 2023. When the news was announced at the ceremony, the room reacted with an appropriately raucous roar of excitement, mostly from the establishmentâs founder, Gento Torigata, his team, and the rest of the London bar scene, including those representing fellow winners Satanâs Whiskers, The Connaught Bar and Scarfes. While the aforementioned other bars share very little DNA, one thing that unites them is the fact that they are both nothing short of a London institution. Whether youâd prefer to enjoy The Connaught Barâs bespoke martinis, Scarfesâs piano sessions or Satanâs Whiskersâs furry taxidermy friends, each promises an indisputably good, fad-free experience that, alongside sublime service, has a timeless appeal. Perhaps that is what some of the 800 anonymous judges who vote to crown The 50 Best recognised in Waltz: the makings of a place with an enduring allure.Â But for me? What makes Waltz one of the capital's best bars is that and plenty else. Tucked behind an understated frontage guarded by a linen curtain, inside is a charming yet sleek cubby hole of warm, lightly polished wood, enveloping shades of blue and the sound of the ownerâs favourite jazz. The centrepiece of the room is a long stretch of elm counter, made from a tree felled in Islingtonâs Gibson Square. Behind it, the pared-back bar is bookmarked by a pair of handsome, chunky speakers, while a vast indigo murmuration of starlings flutters overhead. Apparently, designer David Ross took inspiration for the look from Japanese listening bars, but used British craftspeople and materials to assemble a more tactile vibe designed to feel more at home in London instead. While I havenât heard it from the bartenderâs mouth, word on the street is that Gento, the Tokyo-born man behind it all, borrowed the name from Bill Evansâs Waltz for Debby, the album that nudged him into a love affair with jazz. Having originally trained in French cooking and pastry, he took the scenic route to Scratton Street. Gento learned to shake and stir behind bars in Ginza before going on to work in Sydney and Singapore and, most recently, at bartender favourite Kwant in Mayfair. Waltz is walk-in only, so youâll want to arrive early or late to nab one of the seats at the bar. Bartenders, cool, calm and collected, dapper in navy waistcoats, crisp white shirts and a smile, serve a menu of two halves. The Evergreen section, or Gentoâs signatures, is available all year round, and features a slightly earthy, soul-warming Matcha Old Fashioned that mixes Japanese whisky, the green tea powder and honey, as well as a saline Gibson that swaps out vermouth for smooth sake and promises a fruity kick to boot. The other, In Season, does what it says on tin. Except, itâs slightly more precise than you might expect. If you like something, youâll need to return immediately, because here, Gento follows Japanâs traditional calendar which recognises a gobsmacking 72 micro-seasons throughout the year. That means there are new creations practically every week. When I went, I had a green walnut situation that saw the unripe nuts channelled into a twist on Italian nocino. And guess what? It was delicious. I could say more, but Iâm past my word count. Just know that Waltz doesnât feel like novelty for noveltyâs sake, or sustainability for the same reason. This isnât a place where you go to order something rudimentary and wallow in your woes, itâs a space where youâre practically guaranteed to be completely distracted from them. You can sense Gentoâs passion for produce, experience his discerning palate and understand his love of his native Japan. But drinking at Waltz isnât like going to Japan because this bartender is now a Londoner, and heâs doing what Londoners do best: he has taken a lifetime of experience and created something that is entirely his own.

item.title: I Survived a Massive Everest Avalanche. Here Is the Reality of Facing Death.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
This story is excerpted from Nicole LoBiondo’s debut memoir, Where the Air Grows Thin, which chronicles her quest to climb the Seven Summits while serving as her mother’s primary caregiver through ALS. Blending high-altitude adventure with an intimate story of love, loss, and resilience, the book is available here, or wherever books are sold. I wanted to know how a body feels when it’s dying. Not in some distant, abstract way. I wanted to know in the way you know your own breath on a winter morning—intimately, viscerally, unmistakably yours. I wanted to know what it meant to be a body inside the moment the world collapses. When an avalanche comes, it doesn’t surround you—it consumes you. When it approaches, it sounds like a freight train gone feral, wild on the tracks, its weight bearing down from every direction. But unlike a real freight train, there’s no warning, no brakes screaming before the hit. The terrible weight of white destruction keeps building, rumbling, roaring, until the earth itself moves beneath you. In that moment, all you can do is hope, and wait. I would become good at both—hoping and waiting—in the last years of my mother’s life. But right now, all I wanted was to survive. That morning on Everest, we were camped at a place they call, with cruel irony, the Valley of Silence. There is nothing silent about it. We had just come through the Khumbu Icefall, that broken, heaving maze of blue ice that swallows people whole. Lhotse towered straight above us like a wall meant to keep us out. Nuptse stood off to the right, watching. Everything around us was white and cold and impossibly still, except for the tremble in our breath. Our bodies were lean with years of preparation, hardened on smaller peaks that now felt like playgrounds. Every movement was muscle memory. Every breath was a calculation. We knew the dangers—hypoxia, pulmonary edema, cerebral swelling that could kill you before you even knew you were dying. But none of it felt theoretical. Up here, you are never more alive than when your death is just a moment away. The air thinned until it barely existed, but we pressed on. That’s what you do on Everest. You keep going. There is no glory in the stillness. You climb because it’s the only direction left. I was in the tent with Kara—my climbing partner, my mirror in grit and madness. One second, we were sipping water and talking logistics. The next—the ground shifted. A subtle tilt, then a violent lurch. We looked at each other. We knew. Not with panic—with clarity. The kind that burns into you like a brand. The snow outside disappeared into a thick, fast-moving white. The world had gone quiet in that deceptive way it does just before it screams. We didn’t know about the earthquake yet. Only that something had come unhinged. The tent began to move beneath us, sliding to the right, the avalanche rushing down from the left. Kara and I locked eyes—both of us understanding, without speaking, that this might be it. Her face contorted in terror. I felt the cold rise through my spine like a second skeleton. Then we lifted—just like that—lifted straight into the air and carried with the snow. Our bodies were weightless and useless. We belonged to it now. Blocks of ice. Fist-sized rocks. The splintered heart of the mountain itself came crashing down around us. Not just snow, this was the whole mountain peeling itself apart, taking everything with it. The sound was thunder but deeper, like something ripping loose from the center of the world. Kara—who for a living flies commercial planes through lightning storms without flinching—looked out at the wall of snow coming toward us and said it, her voice jagged and breaking: We’re going to die. She tore open the tent and ran barefoot into the white chaos. I followed. I didn’t think. There was no time to think. Only instinct, only movement, only the bare skin of my feet on the frozen earth. And then—white. Only white. The snow takes me. It doesn’t feel sudden, though it is. One moment I’m upright, a body in motion; the next I’m airborne—flung like a rag doll, spinning through whiteness. My limbs flail without direction. Up becomes down. Down becomes a concept I can no longer trust. Then instinct kicks in. I slam my ice axe into the slope, my whole weight crashing down on top of it. For a second—just one—it holds. And that’s enough. Enough to stop the spinning. Enough to keep me from disappearing entirely. Around me, everything is moving. Snow pours over me like a second skin. It rushes past my ears, fills the corners of my mouth, shoves its cold fingers beneath the collar of my coat. The sound of it is deafening and yet strangely distant, like listening to a scream from underwater. All I can hear—really hear—is my own breath. Fast. Shallow. Frantic. I knew that sound. I’d heard it in the nights beside my mother’s bed—the fragile rhythm of a body deciding whether to stay. Survival sounds different depending on who’s listening. To her it was the wheeze of a machine; to me it was the mountain’s howl asking the same question: Do you still want to be here? And then, out of nowhere, I’m back in my kitchen. January. The snow outside was gentle then, a kind of lullaby against the windows. I remember the soft golden light in that room—the stained glass throwing sapphire and amber and blood-red across the wood floors. The mug in my hands was hot. I was safe. I was warm. I remember looking at the avalanche training materials spread out on the counter beside me. The body-disposal form sat on top, absurd in its finality. Name. Date of birth. Preferred method if they find you—or if they don’t. I had signed it with a pen that clicked too loudly, my signature looping too neatly across the line, as if you could prepare for death with handwriting. If you die on the mountain, your body will be put in a crevasse or buried in a respectful manner by your Expedition team members, unless you specify otherwise, and it is feasible to do otherwise at the discretion of the Expedition Leader. If you die down low, it might be possible to get your body down where it could be cremated by Buddhist monks from the local monastery. This would cost well in excess of several thousand dollars, including the cost of recovery labor, transport, body preparation, wood, and appropriate donations to the local monastery. If you die down low, it might be possible to get your body down for repatriation. If you elect for repatriation of the body, it would be via Kathmandu and would be quite complicated and would cost well in excess of ten thousand dollars and might take several weeks. The words had felt bureaucratic then, almost comically detached. But now, in real time, they pulsed with meaning. I understood their weight in the most human way possible: I might be the body. I thought I understood what it meant to risk everything for a view. I was wrong. Because nothing prepares you for this kind of fear, the intimate kind. The kind that slides inside your body and presses against your lungs from the inside. Sometimes survival doesn’t look like strength. It looks like stillness. Like silence. Like staying exactly where you are when everything around you is begging you to let go. The roar stopped. No more screaming. No more thunder. Just stillness—the kind that isn’t peaceful but final. My body acted before my mind caught up. I rolled to my side and clawed upward, lifting my axe toward light—toward sky, toward breath, toward anything that wasn’t snow. I don’t remember how long it took. I just know that I broke through. I dug myself out of what could have been my grave. Everything hurt. My ribs. My shoulder. My sense of time. The avalanche had scrambled me into something unrecognizable. I didn’t stand—I crawled. Crawled through the wreckage of where our camp used to be, through the cold and chaos, through the cruel quiet that comes when death almost happens but doesn’t. Thirty, maybe forty feet away, impossibly, a Sherpa tent was still standing. From inside, I heard chanting. Not the kind meant to soothe. This was something older. Something more primal. A dirge in a language my body recognized even if my mind didn’t. Low and steady and mournful. A sound that said: We are still here. But we were almost not. I looked around and saw no one. No Kara. For a moment, I was sure she was still under it—under the snow, under the weight of the mountain. Her last words echoing like a curse: We’re going to die. I kept crawling. Toward the tent. Toward the chanting. Toward anything. Halfway there, someone grabbed my arm and pulled me the rest of the way in. I fell into warmth—body heat and breath and the wild, uneven rhythm of people who had seen the edge and come back from it. Faces swam into focus. Sarki. Pemba. Phurba. Fura. Nima. And then—Kara. In the corner, knees pulled to her chest, her lips moving in time with the others. Alive. Trembling. Whispering prayers into the mountain’s throat. She looked at me with eyes so full of shock I could barely hold them. But she was here. We both were. And that felt impossible. The tent was heavy with what we didn’t say. We had survived—but only just. The mountain had come for us and changed its mind at the last minute. That kind of mercy doesn’t come free. Outside, everything had shifted. The terrain was no longer a landscape. It was a threat. We were trapped in a bowl of broken snow and silence, surrounded on three sides by steep walls of ice and rock that loomed like judges. The Lhotse Face above us—unclimbable now. The path back to Base Camp—gone. The Khumbu Icefall, that gnarled, deadly maze we had already crossed once, was worse than ever. Seracs the size of houses stood ready to fall. Crevasses waited beneath the snow like open mouths. We could not go up. We could not go down. We could only sit there, alive and unsure what that even meant anymore. I had sat like that before—at the foot of another mountain, the one called hospice. The same waiting, the same thin air of uncertainty, the same quiet bargain you make with whatever god you still believe in: Just one more breath. There are things you know before you’re told. The silence in a room after an avalanche is one of them. I didn’t need the numbers. I could see it on their faces—the knowing. Not the shock of what just happened but the awareness of what that kind of force leaves behind. The people who won’t crawl out. The bodies that are now part of the mountain. The quiet calculation behind every still breath in that tent: Who didn’t make it? Whose name won’t be spoken aloud again? Some of the Sherpas cried, quietly. No sobbing. No hysteria. Just saltwater tracking down weather-worn faces. These were the kinds of men who didn’t need to speak to be understood. Grief was there, plain and disciplined. They wept with the restraint of people who’ve buried friends before—who’ve carried the weight of death on their backs like packs and kept climbing anyway. I looked for my team. I didn’t see them. No familiar shapes. No bright jackets. No names called out in relief. Just snow. Just prayer. Just the terrible wondering. Maybe they’re gone. Maybe I’m the only one left. When the chanting stopped, it was like the mountain had inhaled and wasn’t sure whether or not to exhale again. No wind. No movement. Just the long pause where you wait to find out if you’ve been spared—or if you’re next. The radios were dead. Not broken, just quiet. No one knew what to say. Maybe no one wanted to be the one to speak into the static and say the wrong thing. Or worse, say the truth. Then a voice broke through. “Is anyone alive at Camp One?” A Sherpa beside me answered. “Yes. I’m in the tent with a few people.” A pause. Then: “Is Nicole alive? We have her brother on the phone with the Seattle office.” That’s the moment it became real. Not the snow or the terror or the breathless clawing toward daylight—but this. My brother was on the phone. Calling Base Camp. Asking if I was alive. He was probably in his office or in a stairwell, or sitting down somewhere because someone told him to. He was hearing the same silence we had just lived through, except for him it came through a line in Seattle, where the mountain is just a word. But still, he knew. That’s the thing about fear—it travels. You think you’re out here alone, doing something brave. But you’re not. You’re tethered to every person who loves you, and when something tries to kill you, it drags them down too. I thought about the nights I stayed up beside my mother’s bed, checking her breathing every few minutes like it might disappear if I didn’t. And now here he was—doing that for me. “Yes,” the Sherpa said. “She’s here with us.” Those words opened something in me. It wasn’t about being safe. I wasn’t safe. None of us were. The snow hadn’t stopped falling, and we were still pinned in by the walls of the Western Cwm, still sitting ducks in a bowl of death. But my name had been spoken. I had been accounted for. And someone I loved had heard it. That would have to be enough. For now. Then Base Camp came back: “That’s good to hear, mate. We’ll communicate back to you when medevac is available.” “We need to get you out of there.” But no one moved. No one reached for their packs or stood to look outside. We knew. There was nowhere to go. Not yet. We had survived one avalanche. We weren’t so sure we’d survive another. Then the next report: “Twelve confirmed dead. More unaccounted for. Checking for the walking wounded.” No one said anything. But we all knew what it meant. On Everest, you always know someone. The climbing community is small. You share tents and stories and routes. You share rope and oxygen. You share fear. I closed my eyes. I thought about who might be gone. Whose face I wouldn’t see again at the next camp. Who I’d laugh with over instant coffee one morning, and by that afternoon, they’d be a body wrapped in nylon, waiting to be flown home. Time folded. I remembered my kitchen again—the form, the signature, the ridiculous neatness of my own handwriting—and I felt an ache so sharp it bordered on reverence. We think we sign our names on paper, but sometimes it’s on the air itself, a quiet contract with the world to keep breathing. The second avalanche came.

item.title: Witches Are Taking Over America’s Waterways on Paddleboards This Halloween
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Witches paddle on the Hudson River in Sleepy Hallow, New York. You might have seen them before, packs of people dressed like Stevie Nicks climbing onto paddleboards and rowing out onto the water like a cast of Hogwarts extras. Witch paddles, as they’re now generally referred to, began like all great unhinged ideas, conjured on a whim. What turned this spectacle into a full-blown spooky-season phenomenon? A few conveniently timed birthdays. Annette Ausseresses, the agreed-upon originator of the concept, had a tradition with her girlfriends of celebrating their Halloween-adjacent birthdays in witchy fashion. “The first year was dressing up as witches and going hiking,” she says. “The next, we had paddleboards, so we said, let’s dress up as witches and go paddling.” It was October 2013, the place was Morro Bay, California, and unbeknownst to them, they’d just unleashed a fury. So how did their little coven become a nationwide Halloween craze? Ausseresses credits two things: a local news story that went global on the Associated Press wire, and a woman in Portland who caught wind of the idea and decided to stir up some trouble of her own. Enter Ginny Kauffman. She saw some pictures of Ausseresses’ event and brought the concept to the Rose City in October 2017, taking to the Willamette River with just a couple of friends. But as word spread, Portland’s sorceresses began multiplying. “People loved it because, well, this is Portland,” she says about a city whose slogan is “Keep Portland Weird.” By 2019, the Halloween gathering had grown to 200 participants (men and kids included), and copycats began materializing elsewhere. Then came COVID, a gloomy timestamp for even the most resilient of enchantresses. When the world finally emerged from isolation, Kauffman says the appeal of dressing like a witch or warlock and doing something gloriously ridiculous was even more powerful to resist. Witch paddles spread even further across the country, proving that Ausseresses had unwittingly tapped into something bigger than a Halloween gag: a desperate desire to play. “For me, the best part is watching the joy that everybody has from it,” Ausseresses says. “I know that sounds super corny, but it really is. People are out there, they’re meeting their friends, they are smiling, they have fun.” Kauffman agrees. “People just want to be silly,” she says. These days, though, Kauffman no longer leads the charge for Witches on the Willamette. What began as a casual paddle eventually became too much of a liability to continue, she shares. Now, she keeps her witchery to private paddles with friends. Alas, no one has yet stepped forward to inherit her broomstick, leaving Portland’s once-mighty coven without a head witch. However, Ausseresses’ event is still going strong down in California, along with plenty of other pointy-hatted armadas of men, women, and children, from mountain lakes to the Southern rivers. Here’s witch paddles across the country where you can get very SUPerstitious this year. Morro Bay Witches and Warlocks paddle is the O.G. of these hex-cellent events, and you can expect to see founder Annette Ausseresses and many of her original crew out on the water once again, getting into double, double toil and trouble. “We don’t require that you have a paddleboard,” Ausseresses says. “You can do it in a canoe, a kayak, an outrigger. The local dragon boat team does it in the dragon boat.” A couple of years ago, even Ausseresses’ 93-year-old mom, who passed away last month, took to the waters. “I rented an electric boat and took her out on that,” she says. Around 500 people are expected for this casual “meet-up” event. Each October, more than 600 costumed participants and curious onlookers descend on the Bridgewater Channel near Lake Havasu’s London Bridge for a wonderfully weird day on the water. What started as a local lark has become a full-blown pageant, with live entertainment, elaborate costumes, and plenty of photo-worthy magic. Register early via WitchPaddleHC.com and come ready to join the spellbound scene. Anna Marie Madai of Littleton, Colorado, held her first Witch Paddle at Chatfield Reservoir on a lark in 2021. “Eighty people showed up,” she recalls. With eerie tree stumps jutting from the water and everyone having a blast, she decided to do it again. The next year, she put the event on Facebook—and got a message from the park. “They said, ‘You have 14,000 people interested in your event. You can’t hold that here.’” Apparently, the spell had worked a little too well. Madai partnered with Sacred Sister Collective, a 501(c)(3), and found a bigger home for her multiplying coven. This year’s October 17 paddle is already sold out with 500 participants, but spectators can join the ghoulish gathering for free. If ever there were a place destined for a witch paddle, it’s Sleepy Hollow, New York, a famous setting for the classic ghost story The Legend of Sleepy Hollow. Tara Scheller, owner of Rivertown SUP and Yoga, launched the Hudson River SUP Witchfest in 2020 after hearing about Witches on the Willamette in Portland, Oregon. “It was COVID, so I just reached out to my small paddle community and asked if they wanted to paddle on the Hudson,” Scheller says. Sixteen people showed up. The next year, 50 did. Then things got appropriately supernatural. After moving to Kingsland Point Park, the event ballooned to more than 100 paddlers, 50 vendors, and 1,200 spectators. “It was madness, but a good learning experience,” Scheller says. These days, the paddle has become a full-blown festival—and Sleepy Hollow’s spooky bona fides are enough to lure witches from well beyond the Hudson Valley. “I’ve met people who have driven in from Ohio, Connecticut, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey,” Scheller says. The Macon Witches Float started with a cause behind the costumes. The event originally raised money for Macon Periods Easier, a nonprofit working to combat period poverty by supplying menstrual products to local schools and agencies while making menstruation a little less taboo. But as more costumed paddlers took to the Ocmulgee River each year, the event outgrew its volunteer roots. Visit Macon and Ocmulgee Outdoor Expeditions stepped in to keep it afloat. “We still offer collection opportunities for products to benefit the event’s original cause,” says Marisa Rodgers, vice president and chief marketing officer of Visit Macon. Today, the float has become one of Macon’s signature October events, joining a whole calendar of spooky-season happenings around the city. Paddleboarders, canoers, and kayakers are all welcome. Florida’s iconic Weeki Wachee Springs State Park may be best known for its dazzling mermaid shows, but on Halloween morning, another magical species takes to the water. The Weeki Wachee Witches Paddle sends a flotilla of pointy-hatted paddlers down the famously clear Weeki Wachee River, with witches trading broomsticks for kayaks and stand-up paddleboards. Breakfast is included, and festivities begin at 8 a.m, sharp. Costumes are strongly encouraged—there’s a best-dressed contest—and every paddler (kids included) earns a medal simply for joining the witching hour. Registration is $40 for those bringing their own kayak or paddleboard and $60 with equipment rental through the park’s kayak outfitter. Reservations can be made through Weeki Wachee Springs State Park or by phone, and space is limited. When the pandemic forced Maari Falsetto to close Inner Alchemy, her West Seattle spiritual practice, paddleboarding became an outlet. It also reinforced something she’d been thinking about during lockdown: “People need people.” Falsetto began organizing socially distanced outdoor gatherings, from sound baths to kundalini yoga. Then she heard about a witch paddle on Orcas Island and decided to conjure one of her own. Today, her annual Witches, Warlocks, and Wizards Paddle on Puget Sound draws about 50 participants, including kids. It’s freewheeling and BYOB—bring your own board. Kinsey Gidick is a travel writer based in Scottsville, Virginia, where she lives in a 282-year-old house with a Civil War general buried in the front yard. Which is to say, she’s no stranger to the supernatural. While reporting this story on the nationwide phenomenon of witch paddles, she tracked down the women responsible for putting covens on the water. She’s unsure whether she’s covering a trend or being recruited into a cult, but she’s already picked out her hat.

item.title: How Much Exercise Do You Need to Protect Your Bones? Science Has an Answer.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
How we reported this story: The author, Danielle Zickl, a health journalist, interviewed two experts, a physical therapist and a sports scientist, who explained why exercise is necessary for bone health. Whether you’re scrambling up a mountainside or shredding uneven singletrack on your bike, outdoor athletes need a sturdy foundation. While the focus is usually on cardiovascular stamina or muscle strength, strong bones matter just as much—and are often overlooked. But recent research in the BMJ journal makes a compelling case for paying attention to your bone health—and how your favorite activities could actually slow down age-related loss of bone mineral density (BMD). BMD measures the amount of minerals in your bone—the more minerals there are, the denser it is, and the less likely it is to break. “Bone is living tissue and responds to stress and load, so regular weight-bearing activity and resistance exercise are important for maintaining bone health as we age,” Lori Diamos, MS, PT, FAFS, told Outside. Diamos is a physical therapist and founder of PT Pearls, a physical therapy practice based in Chicago, Illinois. Here’s what the study found and how you can protect your bones as you age. The study’s researchers examined data from 124 clinical trials involving 18,429 participants aged 40 and older and looked at which types and amounts of exercise best preserve bone density and prevent fractures. Results showed that roughly two to three hours per week—or about 20 to 25 minutes a day—of brisk walking, jogging, or similar moderate-intensity activity helps protect bone health by slowing age-related loss of bone mineral density in people aged 40 and up. For protecting the spine, brisk walking or jogging, as well as combined aerobic and resistance training, were effective. For protecting the thigh bones, brisk walking or jogging and mind-body exercises, such as Tai Chi or yoga, were effective. And for protecting the hip bones, brisk walking or jogging was particularly beneficial. Mind-body exercises were also associated with an approximately 42 percent lower risk of fractures.
