The study authors note that data on race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status “were rarely reported and could not be incorporated,” which they acknowledge is a “limitation for assessing equity in exercise effects on bone health.” Walking and jogging create repetitive ground reaction forces that travel through the bone and stimulate new bone growth, Susie Reiner, PhD, told Outside. Reiner is an assistant professor of exercise and sport science at Seton Hall University and founder of TheoryEx, a sports science consulting firm. Muscle contractions against resistance also put force on tendons, ligaments, and bone, which can help preserve and improve bone mass, she said. Yoga and Tai Chi incorporate body-weight resistance while also challenging mobility, stability, balance, core control, and coordination, Diamos said. The outdoors are unpredictable, she noted. Surfaces, slopes, and footing can change quickly, and you may need to climb, descend, step over something, balance on one leg, or quickly recover from a misstep. Lower bone mineral density can increase susceptibility to stress injuries and fractures, especially when falls are an inherent risk when navigating rocks, roots, unstable, sometimes wet surfaces out on the trails, Reiner added. “Training the body in different positions and directions gives it more movement patterns to draw from when those situations happen in real life,” Diamos said. “Having strong bones will give you the structural foundation to tolerate those repeated stresses and loads.” Ultimately, building strong bones doesn’t have to be extremely strenuous or time-consuming. “One of the biggest barriers I see with busy adults is the belief that exercise only counts if it’s long or intense,” Diamos said. “Around 20 to 25 minutes a day feels much more approachable and realistic.” Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: We Handpicked the 17 Best Ski and Snowboard Deals from Evo’s 25th Anniversary Sale
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy When there’s a ghost in your house, you hit up the Ghostbusters. When we need skis or snowboards, we hit up Evo. It’s just common sense. Jokes aside, the PNW-based gear house is running a massive online anniversary sale that’s overflowing with thousands of jaw-dropping ski and snowboard deals. You can also save big on El Niño-ready outerwear, mountain bikes, skateboards, wetsuits, and more. Now, you can peep the sale in its entirety here. Or, you can keep reading for 17 deals that’ve been handpicked by our team of discerning, discount-loving gear nerds. One thing to keep in mind: the sale runs through October 22nd, so you’ve got plenty of time to shop. However, some of the deepest discounts have limited inventory, so it makes sense to jump on it if you need some fresh gear! First up, to celebrate the 25th anniversary of all things Evo, the PNW outfitter is offering 20 percent off one full-price item. There is a catch, though, as certain brands and gear categories are off-limits. That said, you can check out all of the eligible gear here. Prepping for snowpocalypse 2027? Hell yes. Shop the entirety of Evo’s ski sale here, or keep reading for a few noteworthy picks. Line-lacing ladies who love to tour in pursuit of powder will be amped to see the storied Atomic Backland 108 W on the clearance shelves. A lightweight poplar-and-caruba core and low-swing-weight, early-rise tips make uphill a dream. On the descent, camber underfoot, a 108mm waist width, and an agile sidecut make navigating trophy couloirs and floating through caked glades a cakewalk. And with the 40 percent discount, you can have your cake and eat it, too. Name a more iconic ski from the last 20 years. We’ll wait. Atomic’s Bent 120 is back for more like Oliver Twist. A freeride-focused silhouette and rippable camber-dominant hybrid profile combine with a predictable poplar core to help Bent disciples bring surfy style and freestyle antics to resort ripping and powder playgrounds. The girthiest plank in the Bent lineup, the 120 is designed for the deepest days—and the Evo Anniversary discount is pretty damn deep, too. More versatile than the 120 for hammering hardpack and tossing tricks, the Atomic Bent 110 still delivers more float than the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. And Evo’s still delivering the discounts with 300 bucks off the 2026 version. That combo of versatility and buoyancy makes this a stellar pick for skiers traveling to deep snow hubs like Hokkaido. It’s also a radical option if you’re looking for a touring ski that’s a blast in blower and still capable in less idyllic conditions. Skis aren’t the only deals you’ll find in this massive Anniversary Sale. Accessories like these tester-beloved Smith 4D Mag Goggles are discounted by major margins. The 4D Mag has a unique curvature to the bottom portion of the lens, noticeably increasing peripheral vision. Our favorite aspect of these goggles, however, is simply Smith’s ChromaPop clarity- and contrast-enhancing lens tech. Each goggle comes with a low-light option for low-vis days and a darker tint that protects your peepers in bluebird conditions. Not only that, but we’re huge fans of Smith’s MAG interchangeable lens system, which uses a combination of magnets and a straightforward locking mechanism for secure and quick lens swaps. Honestly, we’re floored by the snowboard selection at Evo right now. We’ve never seen so many tester favorites on sale! Check out the sale in its entirety here or keep reading for a few top options. Sage Kotsenburg’s K2 Sky Pilot blew our testers away at our annual snowboard test. The directional, setback, wide ride has a broad nose that planes through powder like a hovercraft yet gobbles up chundery landings and hectic mogul fields when it’s time to send it thanks to a carbon– reinforced tail and vertical bamboo stringers. The fact that you can pick one up for under $400 right now is also blowing our minds, as is the fact that there’s still a generous size range on offer. If you love old-school camber and need a new daily driver, look no further than Capita’s Aeronaut. The pro model of sidehit savant Arthur Longo, this versatile, poppy, bamboo-backed all-mountain menace can lace the jump line one run and thrash powder stash hikes the next. A confidence-inspiring, ollie-boosting, intuitive camber profile and a carving aficionado-approved progressive sidecut add to the adaptable ride’s do-it-all chops. The opportunity to save a couple hundred bucks on a tester-approved jack-of-all-trades doesn’t come around every day—take advantage! If you’re new to snowboarding or you’re looking for a reliable beginner- or intermediate-friendly deck, we’ve got to point you to the Lotus (women’s) and Pulse (men’s). These tester-stamped Salomon snowboards are our top recommendation for greenhorns. They feature a soft, forgiving flex and traditional camber—a combination that makes learning the ropes easy without encouraging newbies to develop bad habits. They’re also affordable at full retail, so grabbing one for under $300 is a total steal. If you usually rent but have been considering investing in your first snowboard, these have your name on ‘em! We truly love the Salomon Highlander, to the point we might add a fresh pair to our Evo cart since they’re over a Benjamin off right now! An idiosyncratic spin on a traditional all-mountain snowboard binding, the Highlander features a shockingly flexible heel cup that moves with you, giving riders unmatched lateral movement that translates to comfortable bell-to-bell riding and playful, stylish tweaks and butters. But that heelcup is actually reinforced with Kevlar cord, which provides ample stability and edge-to-edge power when freeriding. Additional features like canted footbeds, calf-cradling, adjustable highbacks, and boot-wrapping toe and ankle straps make these some of the comfiest bindings we’ve ever ridden. Our female snowboard testers’ favorite binding multiple years in a row, the Union Trilogy is a top-of-the-line option that’s trusted by pros and average Chloes alike. Foam dampening offers excellent chatter control when you blast off piste. Solid adjustability makes these feel custom-fit once you turn a few screws, and the mid-stiff flex gives ripping women the responsiveness and support they demand. Saving a hundred bucks on these Unions makes them a slam-dunk buy for us! Oyuki, a Hokkaido-based brand behind some of our favorite ski gloves and mitts on the market, got purchased by Evo a few years ago, and Evo’s Anniversary Sale is a sweet time to stock up on Oyuki gear. Check out all of Oyuki’s offerings here, or take a look at a few of our favorite pieces below. Sustainability and style go hand in hand with these Oyuki three-layer shells. Both the men’s Goshiki and women’s Nimi are dripping with monochromatic swagger, while a freeride-friendly fit accommodates layers on chilly days from Jackson to Japow. Not to mention, the nylon shell is crafted from repurposed fishing nets collected along the coastlines of Japan. Even better, they’re currently available at bargain-bin rates during Evo’s Anniversary Sale. A staple of the Oyuki glove lineup, the Sencho features top-tier Gore-Tex inserts for weatherproofing, PrimaLoft Gold insulation for warmth, and meticulously stitched goatskin leather for unrivaled style points, welcome durability, and impressive dexterity. Once you go Oyuki, it’s hard to go back—especially when you save a chunk of change. We’ve admittedly got skiing and boarding on the brain right now, but singletrack season ain’t done yet! As such, we’ve got to make a quick mention of Evo’s bike sale, which is stacked with hundreds of deals on everything from helmets and jerseys to components and frames. In particular, you can save thousands of bucks (ahem, plural) on mountain bike completes from top bike brands like Santa Cruz, Yeti, and more. Surfers have the slimmest pickings during Evo’s Anniversary Sale, but if you do need new neoprene, wetsuits, booties, gloves, and more are currently on sale for 20 percent off. Last but not least, Evo’s skate department is clearing completes, trucks, wheels, and bearings. Same goes for helmets and pads. If you’re in the market, are shopping for the holidays, or have been thinking about dusting off the cobwebs after decades away, this skate-centric slice of Evo’s Anniversary Sale must not be missed!

item.title: Things To Do in Sydney in December: A One-Day Itinerary
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Have one day in Sydney? This itinerary takes you from sunrise at Bondi Beach to dinner on Sydney Harbour, with famous sights, Christmas shopping, and food stops along the way. It's a full day, so choose the stops that interest you most instead of trying to fit everything in. The city grew around its harbor, so the Opera House, The Rocks, the arcades, and the gardens are all close to the waterfront. If you plan well, you spend the day seeing things instead of traveling between them. Sydney in December sweetens the deal. The water is warm, the sun sets late, and the city lights up with decorated trees and market stalls. Christmas party cruises in Sydney put the harbor into the festive mood. Here's a full December itinerary, from sunrise at Bondi Beach to dinner on the harbor, packed with some of the best things to do in Sydney in December. Start where Sydney starts its mornings. Bondi is a wide curve of pale sand about 0.6 miles (1 km) long, facing east, so the sun rises straight over the sea. The water is clear and turquoise, and a Bondi Beach sunrise is worth setting an alarm for. Arrive early for a swim at Bondi Icebergs, a saltwater pool cut into the rock where waves break over the wall. Otherwise, swim between the red and yellow flags, which go out when patrols start around 8 am. Finish with breakfast on Campbell Parade, where cafes open early, and tables face the water. Bondi is about 5 miles (8 km) from the city: 30-45 minutes on the 333 bus from Circular Quay, 20 minutes by taxi. - Best for: ocean sunrise, an early swim and beachfront breakfast - Time needed: 2 to 3 hours, including travel - Cost: free for the beach, $10 for the Icebergs pool - Good to know: Thursdays are normally reserved for cleaning, though summer opening depends on tides. Check current pool hours before visiting. Circular Quay is the harbor's front door, where ferries, trains, and city streets meet. Two of Circular Quay's best-known attractions sit side by side a few minutes away. Ten minutes east of the Quay, the Royal Botanic Garden Sydney stretches along the water's edge: lawns, old fig trees, more than 27,000 plants, and curving paths with the harbor peeking through. Entry is free; it opens at 7 am, and the paths are flat. Follow the path around the point to Mrs Macquarie's Chair, a bench convicts carved into sandstone in 1810 for Elizabeth Macquarie, the governor's wife. From there, the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge line up in one frame, making it a well-liked spot to visit. - Best for: free harbor views, shade, and the best photo spot in the city - Good to know: the Chair sits at the far end of the point, so allow for the walk The garden path leads straight to it. You have seen the Sydney Opera House a thousand times in photos, and it still surprises up close: the white shells are far bigger than they look, and the surface is covered in small tiles that shift color with the light. It opened in 1973 and now carries UNESCO World Heritage status. You can walk around the forecourt and wide steps outside, and guided tours take you inside the concert halls. Walk around to the back toward the ferry wharves for a stunning view of the Harbour Bridge. - Best for: close-up views of the sails and a free harbor walk - Time needed: 30 minutes outside, 1 hour with a tour - Good to know: book the tour ahead, as popular slots go early A ten-minute walk back around the Quay takes you from the oldest part of Sydney to the middle of the modern city. The Rocks is where the city began; Martin Place is where it keeps Christmas. Between them sit lunch and the first sign of the season. Walk a few minutes west of the Quay and the streets narrow fast. The Rocks is a cluster of sandstone lanes, stairways, and courtyards below the Harbour Bridge, now filled with pubs, cafes, and galleries. The First Fleet landed here in 1788, so European settlement in Australia started on this shoreline. Of all the things to do in The Rocks Sydney, lunch in one of the country's oldest pubs comes first. Several sit within ten minutes of each other and still argue over which came first. On weekends, markets fill the streets with food and craft stalls. - Best for: colonial history, old pubs and lanes worth getting lost in - Time needed: 1.5 to 2 hours with lunch - Good to know: markets run only on weekends, so weekdays are quieter with fewer stalls. Ten minutes from The Rocks on foot, Martin Place is a long pedestrian square lined with banks, offices, and old stone buildings. In December, it becomes Sydney's Christmas centerpiece. The tree here is the tallest in New South Wales, lit by more than 110,000 lights, and the Martin Place Christmas markets fill the square below it with food, drinks and handmade gifts. - Best for: Christmas shopping, street food and the biggest tree in the state - Cost: free to walk through, stalls priced individually - Good to know: In 2026, markets run November 28 to December 24 on selected days, generally Wednesday to Saturday, with daily trading in the final week. Check the schedule before visiting. The tree lights up after dark. Afternoon - Shopping Arcades and Gardens If you still have energy, choose the Queen Victoria Building for shopping and architecture or the Chinese Garden of Friendship for a quieter break. Alternatively, return to your hotel to rest and change before taking a dinner cruise. Locals call it the QVB. Opened in 1898, the Queen Victoria Building fills a city block on George Street and features five floors of stained glass, iron railings, and a central dome under a glass ceiling. It's now a shopping center, with boutiques, jewelers, and cafes on every level, so come for the building as much as the shops. In December, an enormous Christmas tree hangs through the atrium. - Best for: shopping, Victorian architecture, and a cool break from the heat - Good to know: the upper galleries give the best view of the dome and tree. A ten-minute walk south from the QVB takes you to the southern end of Darling Harbour where a high wall hides one of the city's quietest places. The Chinese Garden of Friendship opened in 1988 and is modeled on private gardens from southern China. Inside, you'll find lakes with koi carp, waterfalls, and pavilions, while the walls block much of the traffic noise. A teahouse serves tea and dim sum. - Best for: quiet, shade, and photos unlike anything else that day - Good to know: open daily 10 am to 5 pm, with free 35-minute tours twice daily. Closed on Christmas Day. Darling Harbour is the waterfront on the city's western side. In December, the whole precinct lights up with a Christmas tree floating on Cockle Bay. For things to do in Darling Harbour at night, start with the light tunnel, then board a dinner cruise. A few minutes from the water, Darling Square sets up a light tunnel each December, lit every night until Christmas. The lights arch over the path so you can walk the whole length and stop for photos. More than 50 places to eat and drink line it, making it a great spot as the sun drops toward the horizon. - Best for: Christmas lights, waterfront bars and a sunset walk - Good to know: time it for dusk, when the tunnel shows up best End the day aboard one of the Sydney dinner cruises, departing from King Street Wharf a few minutes from Darling Square. This is the signature Sydney way to wrap up an evening: dinner and a live show on a boat cruising Sydney Harbour. Christmas versions run through December and are ideal for groups. - Best for: a signature Sydney dinner cruise with live cabaret - Time needed: around 3 hours on the water - Cost: ticketed, with dinner and the show included - Good to know: book ahead, as December evenings fill early That's a full day in Sydney, from first light at Bondi to an evening on the harbor. Skip a stop or two for a slower pace, and leave enough time to reach King Street Wharf before your cruise's boarding time. This article was published in partnership with Sydney Showboats.

item.title: 10 Pieces of Gear Our Editors Think Deserve More Praise
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy As Backpacker editors, we’re gearheads. We test a lot of gear, and we still salivate over the shiniest, newest, lightest pieces of backpacking equipment as much as the next hiker. More often than not, it’s the big and flashy items that get the most attention: backpacks, tents, sleeping bags, pads. Those foundations to a backpacking kit are surely important, but on the trail, smaller, oft-forgotten items can make all the difference in comfort and enjoyment. The following gear might not be as sexy as an ultralightweight shelter or newfangled pack, but we think it deserves some recognition. For Editor-in-Chief Adam Roy, the Nomadix Bandana Towel mixes style and function. The microsuede is more absorbent than a traditional cotton bandana, and with a UPF 50+ rating, offers some sun protection when worn around the neck. More packable than a full-sized towel, it offers versatile function with a minimal weight penalty. Waterproof shells and packable insulation get all the hype, but the smallest garment on your body can do the most for your comfort on trail. The best backpacking underwear (I prefer wool or a wool blend like Branwyn’s Essential Bikini or Ibex’s Natural Bikini) is moisture-wicking, odor-resistant, and provides comfort for all-day walking. When packing for a hike, my underwear choice is never an afterthought. Fire bans span much of the backpacking season across the west, but you can still achieve a cozy vibe in camp with this item that weighs almost nothing. “It’s a mini, personal alternative to a campfire,” says Associate Editor Will Brendza. The flame may not be powerful enough for roasting marshmallows, but it will bring a romantic glow to your campsite without the need to scavenge for dry wood. “Tiny flip-top cosmetics cases or contacts cases are good for storing just a couple days worth of toothpaste or medication,” says Roy. Plus, you can buy 100 of them for just $14. Electronics are a must for modern backpackers, and keeping them all charged on a long trip can be a pain. A 3-in-1 cable allows me to pack a single charging system for my phone, e-reader, and headlamp, even though they all have different charging ports. A tiny, weightless adapter for my Garmin watch rounds out the system, so I can pack a single cable instead of four. A good night’s sleep can make or break a trip, which is why Senior Gear Editor Benjamin Tepler loves this Kitsch Satin Sleep Mask. “I use it when I need to nap during the day, go to bed extra early, or want to sleep in on-trail,” he says. “This particular eye mask is wrap-around rather than a strap-style, which lets me side-sleep without being harassed by the adjustment clips found on other eye masks.” A water bowl made from high-end ultralight materials migh seem unnecessary, but the Lifetime Bowl from Atlas Pet Company has become one of the most unsung treasures in my gear collection. It doesn’t leak, and I can stick it in my pants pocket, dog’s pack, or clip it to the leash or my backpack so it’s always at the ready. The material is featherweight and tough, which is great, since the bowl accompanies me and my pup on every adventure from afternoon bike rides to long-distance backpacking trips. Multitools are great, but for many trips, they’re overkill. Roy makes do with miniature scissors, especially when traveling long distances for a backpacking trip. “They can do most tasks a knife can do but are also allowed on planes,” he says. With this simple item, you can turn your headlamp into a lantern, leveling up evening camp activities like card games or dominoes (“as fun as cards, but less likely to get wet,” says Roy). By the time they reach camp, most hikers are so hungry they’ll eat with a stick. But a proper utensil can make the freeze-dried dinner experience seamless. Brendza loves the GSI Outdoors Essential Backpacking Spoon, which is long-handled to reach the bottom of a pouch, and features spatula-like silicone edges for scraping up every morsel. “I always thought a spoon was just a spoon, but this little number with the rubber edge changed everything,” he says. “Now I can squeegee my dehydrated meal bag to scoop up every last drop of nutrients.”

item.title: 5 New Thru-Hiking Routes To Start Planning In Alaska, India, Japan, and Beyond
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Imagine spending weeks walking across remote mountain ranges, following ancient paths between villages, or trekking through wilderness so vast that you can go for days without seeing another hiker. For those willing to trade modern convenience for a chance to sleep under the stars, a new generation of long-distance trails around the world offers plenty of reasons to lace up and go farther. From the rugged peaks of India’s Western Ghats to Alaska’s wild backcountry and Romania’s historic villages, these trails offer a mix of challenge, cultural discovery, and sense of accomplishment found after hundreds of miles in the dirt. Some of these routes are new for the 2027 hiking season, so you could be among the first hikers to complete them. Others are still being mapped or expanded, creating a bucket-list for hiking and backpacking sweat-jetters who relish traveling halfway around the world for a challenge. Alaska already has a reputation for big wilderness. The new Alaska Long Trail (ALT) could give hikers a new way to experience it all. This 500-mile route is split into five sections. It’s currently being developed to connect Seward with Fairbanks, following roughly 120 miles of the historic Iditarod National Historic Trail through the Chugach National Forest. About 75 percent is already complete with new connector trail segments, bridges, and public-use cabins. “The National Forest Foundation is working with the Forest Service to build these new links, so that one day you’ll be able to walk from Seward to Girdwood the way mail carriers and mushers did a century ago,” says Annie Eggert, Chugach Program Coordinator for the NFF. Sections of the ALT are expected to open in stages throughout 2027. Accommodation: Inns, alpine huts, and wild camping If your ideal European vacation involves crossing six countries on foot, then the new Wolf Trail is a must-do. This 2,170-mile route begins in Germany and travels through Poland, Austria, Switzerland, Italy, and Slovenia. The outdoor brand Jack Wolfskin initiated its development in 2026. A handful of international thru-hikers, like Canadian backpacker Lauren Roerick, walked the Wolf Trail this season to help refine it ahead of spring 2027. “What makes the Wolf Trail particularly appealing is the sheer variety packed into one route,” says Roerick. “Rather than committing to a single mountain range or country, you move through a patchwork of European landscapes with the trail itself being the connector.” The trail is divided into seven sections. Roerick’s favorites include hiking toward Oberstdorf along the German-Austrian border and Slovenia’s Julian Alps. Updated GPX maps for the trail are expected to be published in 2026 via Jack Wolfskin. Type: Village homestays and wild camping India’s Western Ghats are home to some of the country’s most dramatic landscapes. However, until recently, they lacked any official hiking trail. The Epic Sahyadri Trail (EST), a 1,056-mile village-to-village route through the Sahyadri mountains, is the first continuously mapped trek in this region. The trail is divided into 40 stages across 11 sections. Walking through this landscape offers a very different way to experience India away from its famous cities and well-known monuments. As a local from the area, I am most excited that the EST passes through villages like Bhoirwadi and Karjat rather than simply connecting wilderness areas, making communities along the way an integral part of the experience. Hikers can access homestays, hostels, home-cooked meals, forests, and landscapes which rarely appear on a conventional India itinerary. All stages have been documented, and GPX maps are available via HikeX, an Indian online community for hikers. Location: Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan The Caucasus may not be on the average American hiker’s bucket list. That’s precisely why the Transcaucasian Trail is interesting, as it connects two distinct cultures—Europe and Asia. This 1,865-mile trail connects Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan. It passes through mountains, remote villages, forests, and historic landscapes. It also links communities that have traditionally been experienced as separate destinations. In some places like Georgia’s Svaneti region, hikers experience mountain scenery with medieval-type villages and tower houses. “When you hike from Mestia to Ushguli, you stay overnight in family-run guesthouses that are still very much people’s homes,” says Merab Mchedliani, an Intrepid tour leader in Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan. Tourism here also helps revive once-struggling communities due to their geographical isolation. “It’s not only bringing travelers into the mountains but also gets local people to move back home. And that gives them a lot of hope,” adds Mchedliani. GPX route maps for hikeable sections are currently available, while some sections in Azerbaijan are expected to be completed in mid-2027. Type: Village homestays, hotels, guesthouses, and campgrounds While not completely new, the Via Transilvanica received official recognition as a national hiking trail in Romania in 2026. Now, it’s gaining popularity among the international hiking community. The nearly 1,000-mile trail crosses Romania from northeast to southwest, passing through mountains, forests, villages, and farmland. Rather than being designed as a wilderness challenge, the route emphasizes the Romanian cultural landscape and the communities along the way. “The trail takes you through some of the most beautiful parts of Romania and gives you the chance to discover the culture, history, and traditions that make each region unique,” says Zsolt-Barna Kocsis, a tour leader and certified mountain guide. “Hikers might visit a painted monastery in Bucovina to learn about its ancient frescoes, then spend the evening around a campfire with a local shepherd family, sharing stories and eating mămăligă with fresh milk.” The full route is a serious undertaking. However, GPX hiking maps break it down by section for dayhikes, multi-day adventures, or longer expeditions. Location: Northern Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan Type: Village homestays, hotels, and campgrounds The Hitachi Province Long Trail officially opened on September 19, 2026, though it was first announced in 2019. The trail traverses the northern Ibaraki Prefecture, just outside of Tokyo. The full route connects many walking trails with hiking routes, and older, previously abandoned, and recently restored paths. Parts of the route traverse mountain areas and can get steep, while other sections are mellow and even paved. The trail’s official website states: “The Hitachi Province Long Trail is not just a long-distance trail that involves traversing mountainous terrain for extended periods; it’s a ‘rural, regional, and environmental’ trail that takes you on a journey through diverse terrains, landscapes, and historical sites, repeatedly visiting both rural areas and mountains. The easily accessible circular route allows you to start your journey through northern Ibaraki Prefecture from anywhere, and you can freely plan how far you’ll walk.”

item.title: Is Your Sodium Intake Impacting Your Hiking Performance? A Dietician Explains Why It Matters.
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Take a look at the nutrition label on a freeze-dried backpacking meal, and you might be surprised by how much sodium it contains. Some meals pack more than 1,500 mg into a single pouch, roughly two-thirds of the recommended daily limit of 2,300 mg for most adults. That’s a lot for one dinner, but when you’re spending hours sweating your way up steep climbs, you’re also losing sodium along with water. Sodium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal nerve and muscle function. Yet there’s a contradiction in how you might think about it on the trail: You question the sodium in your freeze-dried dinner while adding electrolyte powder to your water bottle and snacking on pretzels, jerky, and cheese. So, are you consuming too much sodium or not enough? The answer depends on what’s already in your food, how much you’re sweating, and how you’re replacing fluids. You can pack nearly identical amounts of food and end up with dramatically different sodium intakes. I compared two realistic days of backpacking food, each containing commercial meals, protein bars, snacks, and other familiar trail staples. Both provide roughly 3,150 calories and weigh about 23 ounces dry, yet one contains 5,465 mg of sodium while the other contains just 1,975 mg. That’s nearly 3,500 mg of difference before you add a single electrolyte packet. Some of the variation comes down to individual products: Mountain House Beef Lasagna contains 1,180 mg of sodium, compared with 340 mg in Good To-Go Pad Thai. Even switching pretzel flavors or protein bar brands can make a noticeable difference. Neither food bag is automatically better, but the comparison shows why it’s worth checking what you’re already carrying before deciding to supplement. Health experts recommend limiting sodium for a reason. Consistently consuming more than your body needs can raise blood pressure, increasing your risk of heart disease and stroke over time. A particularly salty meal can also leave you thirsty or temporarily bloated as your body regulates its fluid balance. If you’ve been advised to limit sodium because of high blood pressure, kidney disease, or another medical condition, those recommendations still matter when you’re backpacking. But eating a high-sodium diet day after day isn’t necessarily the same as eating salty meals during a strenuous backpacking trip. When you’re sweating heavily, you lose sodium you wouldn’t lose while sitting at a desk. That doesn’t mean every milligram of sodium in your food is necessary, or that you should add electrolytes without thinking about what you’re already eating. It simply means your activity and conditions matter when interpreting those numbers on the label. Even if you’re hiking alongside someone on the same trail, you may be losing very different amounts of sodium. Sweat losses depend on two things: how much you sweat and how concentrated that sweat is. Research has found sweat sodium concentrations ranging from roughly 230 to 1,600 mg per liter. Temperature, exertion, clothing, heat acclimatization, and individual physiology all affect your losses, which means mileage alone tells you very little about how much sodium you’ve lost. Here’s another wrinkle: Losing 800 mg of sodium through sweat doesn’t automatically mean you need to consume 800 mg to replace it. Your body regulates sodium and water balance, and research suggests targeted sodium replacement matters more under certain combinations of prolonged exercise, substantial sweat losses, and fluid replacement. That’s why taking an electrolyte packet every hour isn’t necessarily appropriate. A packet doesn’t account for how much you’re sweating, how much you’re drinking, or how much sodium you’re getting from food. Sodium doesn’t have to come from an electrolyte supplement to count. Salty snacks, meals, and electrolyte drinks all contribute to your intake, although when you consume that sodium can matter during long, sweaty days. Imagine spending 10 hours hiking in warm weather, sweating heavily and drinking water but eating very little. At camp, you prepare a freeze-dried dinner containing 1,500 mg of sodium. That sodium helps replace losses and retain fluids during recovery, but it wasn’t available during the preceding hours of hiking. Eating salty snacks throughout a prolonged, sweaty hike provides some sodium along the way instead of waiting until dinner. That doesn’t mean you need electrolyte powder in every water bottle. If you’re regularly eating pretzels, cheese, jerky, or other salty foods, you’re already consuming sodium during the day. On the other hand, if your trail menu contains relatively little sodium or you struggle to eat while hiking, an electrolyte drink may be a convenient alternative. What matters isn’t whether the sodium comes from a packet or a snack, but whether you’re adding something your food isn’t already providing. It’s easy to assume that replacing the sodium you lose through sweat will protect you from exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH), a potentially dangerous drop in blood sodium. But according to the Wilderness Medical Society, most cases occur primarily because you drink too much fluid relative to your losses, often combined with your body’s tendency to retain water during prolonged exercise. Sweat sodium losses can contribute under some circumstances, but taking electrolyte supplements won’t prevent hyponatremia if you’re overdrinking. The guidelines recommend avoiding overdrinking, generally by drinking according to thirst or using fluid needs you’ve estimated from experience in similar conditions. They also recommend having salty foods or drinks available during long, hot activities. Headaches, fatigue, nausea, and muscle cramps aren’t reliable indicators that you need more sodium because they can have several causes. If you or a hiking partner develops worsening confusion, repeated vomiting, seizures, or collapses during or after prolonged exertion, seek urgent medical help rather than assuming more water or electrolytes will solve the problem. So how much sodium do you actually need? There’s no simple answer. Your sweat losses vary with the conditions and your individual physiology. Even knowing exactly how much sodium you lose wouldn’t tell you how much to replace. For context, 1,500 mg per day is considered an adequate intake for most adults under ordinary conditions, while 2,300 mg is the general recommended daily limit. Neither is a backpacking-specific target. A food bag containing 5,465 mg isn’t automatically excessive for a strenuous hiking day, just as one containing 1,975 mg isn’t necessarily inadequate. And since research hasn’t consistently shown that extra sodium improves endurance performance, there’s little reason to chase a precise replacement target. The bottom line? Hike your own hike. If you’re curious about your sodium intake, track what you eat and drink, the conditions you’re hiking in, and how you feel during and afterward. You might notice patterns that help you plan future trips, without getting caught up in replacing every milligram of sodium you sweat out.

item.title: Free the Hips, Ruin the Shoulders?
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
In 2016, on the last few hundred miles of my first Pacific Crest Trail thru-hike, I got my hands on a very early Pa’lante Packs prototype: It was hipbelt-free, frameless, and approximately the size of a peanut. This new wave of minimalism instantly hooked me; losing the hipbelt felt like the relief of unbuttoning tight jeans after Christmas dinner. I reluctantly handed the pack back and flew home to New Zealand. Then, I did what any level-headed person swept up in the free-the-hips movement would do: I took a pair of scissors to my Hyperlite Windrider and hacked the belt clean off. I felt weightless and, far more importantly, incredibly cool. The concept of removing the hipbelt from an ultralight pack isn’t new, but it went mainstream in stages. The GoLite Breeze brought frameless, beltless packs to a wider audience back in the late ‘90s; cottage packs like the Mountain Laurel Designs Burn carried the idea further into ultralight consciousness, and by around 2017, Pa’lante had helped it go viral. For years, I treated my Pa’lante’s stowable hipbelt like a guilty secret. But by my 2025 Continental Divide Trail thru-hike, I switched packs and added a detachable webbing belt. When I misplaced it before this year’s Pacific Crest Trail hike, my left shoulder ached through the desert water carries. The ache turned into a tingle right down my arm, then numbness. A padded replacement belt helped, but the nerve irritation still lingers. As I watched hikers around me with hipbelt-less packs develop nagging shoulder and back issues of their own, I realized I wasn’t the only one having problems; the movement that felt so liberating was taking a toll on our bodies. To understand what carrying a pack entirely on your shoulders does to the body, and why designers build packs this way, I spoke with two physical therapists: Morgan Brosnihan, PT, DPT, of Blaze Physio and Matthew Shafter, PT, DPT, a thru-hiker with an enviable 7-pound base weight. I also spoke to Chris Pickering, a pack designer who joined Nashville Pack and Equipment Company when it was just getting started. Brosnihan explains that sustained pressure from pack straps compresses the muscles, ribs, and nerves. Hikers with a stiffer upper back or weaker supporting muscles tend to hit their limit sooner. For some, that compression can aggravate an underlying anatomical issue they didn’t know they had. As Brosnihan puts it, carrying everything on your shoulders is “working harder, not smarter.” Online, going beltless is often presented as a matter of toughing it out or something anyone can do with a low enough base weight, but individual bodies are more complicated. Like with minimalist trail shoes, Shafter says adaptation comes from gradually exposing your body to a load over time. His test is simple: hike all day with the belt off, carrying your heaviest food and water. “If pain comes in, even in the final hour of a hike, then that’s your answer … your shoulders are not adapted enough to handle the force,” he says. “Listen to your body and only cut the hipbelt when it says it’s ready.” That can take months or even years. Designers face a different problem. Pickering says the Cutaway, Nashville Pack’s flagship pack, was designed with wide, running-vest-style shoulder straps to keep it comfortable without a belt, provided loads stay under 20 pounds. But hikers’ loads fluctuate wildly between resupplies, meaning a pack built for the light end of that range only covers part of the trip. For that reason, Pickering now sees hipbelts as an essential option in modern ultralight design. A pack that carries well but weighs 4 to 5 ounces more, he says, “is always going to be a better bag for any hiker in the long term.” I’m still a believer in going light, and so is Shafter: He says lighter packs let you see more and go easier on your joints, as long as it’s done on your own terms. So has the movement gone too far? I can only speak for myself: I cared more about how a beltless pack looked than what it might do to my body. The tingling was the wake-up call I needed. Turns out I’d rather keep walking than keep looking cool. True ultralight design shouldn’t be about elitism or dogma. Look for gear that gives you options, like a removable hipbelt. Clip it on for the five-day food carry and the bone-dry desert stretch. Free your hips when you can, and put the belt back on before your shoulders finally force your regretful tingling hand.

item.title: I Hiked Through a Preserve Built for Predators to Reach This Brutal Jungle Summit
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
I nearly slid down another steep, mud-slick slope, laughing and clutching the walking stick my guide had cut from a small tree. “I thought you said this was the dry season,” I called to him over the steady patter of rain. He just shrugged and smiled back. Not that I minded the rain. It took the edge off the suffocating humidity and distracted me from the constant brutal ups and downs that were straining every muscle in my legs. It was mid-April, and my husband and I were in the middle of hiking the three-day, 35-mile Victoria Peak Route in Cockscomb Basin Wildlife Sanctuary (CWBS) and Jaguar Preserve, a trek only accessible during the short dry season. CBWS is the world’s first jaguar preserve and home to a variety of other big cats including pumas, ocelots, margays, and jaguarundis, though the animals are rarely spotted by hikers. We’d just summited the infamous Victoria Peak, one of Belize’s most challenging trails. That evening, we’d spend the second night in a hammock in the jungle with no other humans in sight. Despite the fire in my legs, I was on cloud nine. This was an adventure worth traveling for. The three-day backpacking trip started with a shuttle ride from our comfortable hotel room overlooking the beach at Jaguar Reef. It was 5:30 a.m., and to the west, a thin haze of fog hovered in the negative space between tall grasses and the languid tips of palm fronds. Arriving at Cockscomb Basin Wildlife Sanctuary and Jaguar Preserve, we met our guides for the trek: Macario Cucul and Alex Mes. All treks in the sanctuary require two guides because the final push to the summit of Victoria Peak requires roped climbing and two experienced belayers. And not just any guides will do. The Belize Audubon Society, which manages the Victoria Peak Trail, requires a special certification and route-specific training before guides can lead expeditions here. The trail is only hikeable during the dry season between March and May. The rest of the year, the route turns into creeks or waterfalls, and the way is impassable. All of that, plus a restriction that only allows one group at a time to overnight in the backcountry, means only around 150 people complete the trek each year. That guarantees seclusion while also protecting wildlife within the sanctuary. So as the four of us embarked on day one, it didn’t take long to feel like we were in true wilderness. The jungle was thick—with both vegetation and moisture. As we hiked, we were serenaded by birdsong and the harmonious hum of grasshoppers as long as my hand. The heavy canopy shielded us from direct sun, but it was already sweltering in mid-April. We huffed uphill, avoiding ant highways and stopping at frequent creek crossings to filter water. The humidity felt like hiking in a wet sleeping bag (especially for a desert rat like me). I was 4,000 feet closer to sea level than I am at home, but still it felt harder to breathe with that much moisture in the air. My clothes clung onerously to my body. It’s a long 12.5 miles to the first camp. Along the way, our guides stopped to point out macaws in the trees, tarantulas in logs, or to identify plants, of which they had intimate knowledge. At night we camped in a simple, open-air shelter with a roof and beams on which we slung our camping hammocks—tents aren’t recommended. There are two camps along the route, located at kilometers 12 and 19. However, we overnighted at the same one—at 19 km—both nights. As the sun set, our guides lit a fire and boiled water in an oversized pot, and we rehydrated our individual meals. Travelers must bring all their own food. That didn’t stop us from gathering around the picnic table and dining together. We swapped stories, inspected each other’s dinner options, and learned about one another’s cultures. By hiker midnight (9:00 p.m.), we were already curled in our ultralight sleeping bags, nestled inside bug nets. Ahead of us was our final test: Our push to the summit of Victoria Peak and back. In the morning, chipper birdsong started like clockwork just before sunrise. As we mounted headlamps on our foreheads, I couldn’t tell whether the specks of light gleaming back were the reflection of water droplets from last night’s rain or a hundred tiny spider eyes. As the sun rose, more relentless ups and downs on the 5 miles to the nation’s second-highest mountain clawed at not only my muscles, but my resolve. Victoria Peak tops out at just 3,675 feet—a modest height by many hikers’ standards. However, the cumulative gain over the three-day hike is closer to 9,500 feet. Paired with slopes that were often steeper than 45 degrees, it made for slow going (and muddy behinds). The final vertical push to the peak was a delightfully divergent challenge. Wearing harnesses and helmets, we scrambled up sheer rock faces using ropes and side-stepped along precarious cliffs, pulling ourselves upward. Expansive views of the jungle, Maya mountains, and sea to the east glowed below us, a fresh perspective that promised the peak was near. By the time I reached the top, my arms were burning as much as my legs. We took celebratory selfies and signed the trail register. Then, we inhaled calorie-dense snacks before storm clouds rolled in. It started raining as we prepared to descend. At several intervals, the only things that kept me from sliding down a tumble of rock-turned-waterfall were my own arms clinging to my rope and one toe planted on a hold half the size of a deck of cards. I smiled nearly the whole wet, rolling route back to camp. By the time we returned to Cockscomb Basin on day three, soggy feet and all, I reveled in a deep and exhaustion-ringed cloud of wonder and pride. I was thrilled an expedition like this exists: a singular, wild, wonderful, uncrowded adventure open for exploration during such a small window each year. That it supports local guides and wildlife preservation is a cherry on top. It was the most difficult journey I’d completed in a while. If I were to do it again, I would cram more snacks and extra socks into my pack and spend more time training on steep slopes. But despite the challenge, I’m already scheming a return trip—just as soon as the sharper corners of my memory soften, of course. When to go: March to May, give or take a few weeks before or after (dry season) How to book: Visit https://belizeaudubon.org/vpnm/ and email info@belizeaudubon.org Cost: About $550 to $650 USD per person; fees include two guides and wildlife sanctuary day-use fees that go directly to protecting and supporting the park.

item.title: Forget Energy Bars—These “Walking Tamales” Are My New Favorite Trail Snack
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Of all the ideas that I’ve seen in 20 years of covering the outdoors, the savory energy bar is the one that won’t die. Every few years, a company decides it’s going to buck the trend of sweet protein bars and energy gels and release an oat bar flavored with rosemary and sea salt or a nut-and-soy-crisp-based bar with curry and pepper. I’ve found them to be universally bad, and based on the fact that almost all of them disappear within a year or two of launch, I think most of the hiking public agrees. If the success of Fillo’s Walking Tamales is any indication, maybe those innovators should have been thinking more traditionally. Since launching in 2022, these ready-to-eat tamales have gone from being a culinary curiosity to a hiker favorite. Last April, I named the $2 bars one of my personal favorite pieces of gear of the year; on Reddit and in blog posts, Pacific Crest and Appalachian Trail hikers have called them lifesavers. On a recent Editors’ Choice trip to Wisconsin’s Ice Age Trail, I kept two in my fanny pack at all times Part of the genius of Fillo’s is in their design. Unlike a traditional tamal, which wraps corn masa around a protein like shredded pork or chicken, Fillo’s mixes their vegan fillings right into the dough and flattens it into a thin bar. The result is both slim enough to slip into a pants pocket and basically indestructible: I think you could beat them with a rock and they’d be more or less the same afterward. The flavors are a welcome change from peanut butter tortillas and sweet snacks. The Bean Salsa Roja and Bean Salsa Verde varieties are the easiest to find, and mix mayocoba beans and chickpeas with spices, olive oil, and either tomatillo and serrano pepper (Verde) or guajillo and chile de arbol (Roja). It’s not a totally conventional flavor profile for a tamal, but it works, with the peppers adding a hint of spice to the creamy beans. (Other flavors are less successful: The Elotes style is fine at best, and I haven’t been brave enough to try the sweet Mexican Chocolate Almond or Peanut Butter Piloncillo yet.) Unusually for a gas station meal, they’re vegan, and all the ingredients are recognizable things you might find in your kitchen. The tamales are good hot or cold. I’ve heard of people boiling them over a canister stove right in the wrapper, but I usually eat them cold, straight out of the packaging. Once you get past the weirdly smooth outside—a consequence of being packed in plastic instead of a corn husk—it’s a little like eating leftover Mexican takeout out of the fridge. Two of them plus a handful of whatever snack I’ve been munching on usually makes a solid lunch for me. There are a few downsides, the main one being weight: At 4 ounces and 250 calories each, they’re a lower calorie-density food than peanut butter tortillas, Clif Bars, or a host of other common hiking lunches. I wouldn’t necessarily pack a week’s worth of them for a trip. But for a long weekend or the first few days after a resupply, they’re the easiest and most consistently satisfying midday meal I’ve found. They’re less sugary than bars, less messy than cold-soaked noodles in a jar, and unlike putting cheese or PB&J on a tortilla, I don’t have to stop to eat them. Plus, when it comes to keeping yourself moving, the intangibles matter too: It’s a lot easier to keep putting one foot in front of the other when you know that you have a good lunch waiting down the line. Expect me to keep raiding gas station shelves for these babies for a long time to come.

item.title: 9 Weird Hiking Hacks That Actually Make a Difference
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy The concept of “cool” goes out the window as soon as you hit the trail. It’s one of the most liberating things about hiking and backpacking—you can get as weird as you want, and no one’s going to judge you. Well, maybe they will. But who cares? Not us and not Mother Nature. So go ahead: Hike backwards with your hands in the air, wear a hardhat and a speedo, and cuddle a bottle of your pee at nighttime. Believe it or not, there are actually good reasons why hikers might do all of those things. Hiking hacks come in many forms, but sometimes the weirdest ones offer the most function. And since anything goes when you’re on the trail, we figured we’d arm you with the most bizarre, most potentially useful hiking hacks we’ve ever come across. Some of these are personal tricks from the editors at Backpacker. Others are tips we’ve gotten from friends, things we’ve personally witnessed on the trail, or read about in our research. Try one or two, or give them all a shot at once—you’ll surely start some conversations along the way. We’d never recommend hiking the entire Appalachian or Pacific Crest Trail backwards, but if you did, you probably wouldn’t have much back pain. According to research, walking backwards can help reduce lower back pain by increasing back extensors and activating deep stabilizing muscles. If you suffer from lumbar discomfort, this exercise could help. And the best part? You don’t have to do it for that long. Doctors and physical therapists recommend starting with sessions of one to two minutes and working your way up to 10 minutes. Choose a smooth, straight section of trail, and if you plan on making this a daily part of your hiking ritual, consider getting a clip-on rearview mirror to maximize personal safety (and style). Many hikers suffer from “Sausage Finger Syndrome” (AKA hands that swell while you’re hiking). As your hands swing at your sides, fluid collects in your extremities, which makes them swell. It happens to me every single time. Sometimes my fingers are so distended I can barely close my hands. The fastest fix? Hiking with my hands held above my head. Sure, your arms might get tired, and your hands may eventually fall asleep—but at least they won’t look like catcher’s mitts. I’ve found that a few minutes of hiking with my hands up can do wonders. Check out Backpacker’s other tips for reducing finger swelling on the trail. If you’ve ever broken a spoon trying to scoop cold peanut butter or Nutella out of a jar, you aren’t alone. Few things will break a hiker’s spirit faster at breakfast or lunchtime than a solidified spread. There is a solution, though—it just requires a little patience and a warm… crotch. That’s right: Stick that jar or packet of solidified food down near your nether regions and use your body heat to warm it up. Your groin is close to your core, making it a great source of body heat. The method is called the “crotch thaw,” and it’s Backpacker editorial staff-approved. Some nights are colder than others, and if your sleeping bag’s rating is close to or higher than the low, you might get chilly when temps really take a plunge. If you’re already wearing all your layers, what are you supposed to do? Well, one age-old trick is to put warm water in a water bottle and keep it in your sleeping bag. But let’s say you can’t heat water up on the stove; let’s say for argument’s sake that it’s so cold that you don’t even want to get out of your tent to relieve yourself. If you have a water bottle you don’t mind dedicating to it, you can use your urine for warmth. Pee into the bottle, and snuggle it tight in your sleeping bag. (Backpacker Editor-in-Chief Adam Roy notes that there seems generational gap when it comes to the pee bottle: On a snowy springtime trip to Banff National Park, his older partners nodded at his bottle, while the younger ones blanched.) Placing it under your shirt on your stomach will warm your core up fastest. Just make sure that lid is screwed on tight: If you spring a leak, things will inevitably go from bad to worse. Dog owners will understand the struggle of returning to a trailhead with a bag full of poop, only to discover there’s no garbage can to dispose of it in. And no one likes bringing poop into their car, especially on a hot day. Luckily, every vehicle comes with an exterior compartment that’s perfect for storing those bags. Open your gas door and tuck the stinky cargo in beside the gas cap. Then, simply throw it out as soon as you find a gas station. “If only it were big enough for WAG bags,” laments Backpacker Senior Editor Zoe Gates. Recently, Backpacker’s editors hiked a section of Wisconsin’s Ice Age Trail together. One of our trail snacks was a box of individual-sized chip bags. I wasn’t sure what to do with them until Editor-in-Chief Adam Roy demonstrated the “chip drink” hack. The technique, made famous by this post from Semi-Rad’s Brendan Leonard, is simple: You simply smash the chips in their bag, and viola! Suddenly you have a more packable form of chips that you can pour into your mouth like a beverage—a very salty, crunchy beverage. (Tip: Get the air out of the bag by poking a hole in it with a pin, deflating, and covering the pinprick with tape.) OK, hear us out: We’ve only seen this hack discussed in obscure Reddit threads, and yes, it sounds outlandish. But people make some decent arguments for it. Hardhats actually ventilate very well because of the internal suspension systems. They’re waterproof. At camp, if you take out the mesh liners, they can double as wash basins, seats, or foraging baskets. Is that a stretch? Yeah, we’ll admit that it is. But we’re here to talk about the weird stuff. And anyway, wearing a hardhat comes with the bonus of offering at least some protection from falling tree branches, rocks, or whatever else the universe might throw at you. When rehydrating a backpacking meal, there’s a fine line between undercooking your food and waiting so long it gets cold. Well, you don’t have to choose. Duct insulation is a cheap, easy-to-obtain material sold at most hardware stores. It makes an excellent “food koozie.” Stitch or tape together a pocket shaped like your dehydrated meal, and pop the entire pouch inside after you’ve added your hot water. It insulates the bag, keeping the food hot much longer and allowing it to rehydrate entirely. It also keeps it warm while you eat. You’ve heard of beverage koozies; why not have one for your food as well? Bonus: Duct insulation is squishy and makes great sitting pads, so your food koozie can pull double duty as a seat. This tip comes from our friends over at Outside who wrote about it in 2019. Wes Siler explains how he got the idea from Guantanamo Bay, where soldiers risked their freedom to smuggle in Speedos for the prisoners to wear instead of underwear. The damp, unsanitary prison conditions described at Guantanamo reminded Siler of his backpacking trips. So, he decided to try it for himself. Turns out, according to Siler, Speedos make a very effective pair of hiking briefs. They’re stretchy, breathe relatively well, and dry out quickly. It also gives you the freedom to strip down and go swimming at a moment’s notice. The experience left such an impression on him that Speedos became his go-to backpacking underwear for more than a decade.

item.title: Let This Dinner Menu Take You to Sicily, No Passport Needed
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine
I’m dreaming of Sicily: the land, the sea, the food, the history. The olive trees, the grapevines, the wheat fields. The wild fennel and artichokes. The market stalls piled high with just-picked cauliflower, shiny fat eggplant and cucuzzi, the yard-long summer squash that’s grown on trellises. The fish on view at the lively pescheria: swordfish, tuna and branzino, sardines, cuttlefish and urchins. This dream is making me hungry. On a recent visit to Sicily, friends from Catania took us to a small seaside restaurant with an all-fish menu. At the entrance was a small display of the day’s offerings on ice. You choose your fish before heading outside, where well-weathered, sun-bleached tables and chairs sit right on the docks. For the main course, your chosen fish is roasted whole in a wood-burning oven and then deboned. It can be served plain, with olive oil and lemon. Or it can be tossed with pasta and a quickly made sauce — that was my favorite. Recipe: Sicilian-Style Pasta With Fish Ragù The pasta was paccheri, the sturdy, pleasantly chewy shape known for its sauce-clinging nature. (You could substitute similarly hearty rigatoni, calamarata or pappardelle, if preferred.) The sauce was revelatory. It was essentially a deft ragù di pesce, a rapid sauté of onions and red peppers in olive oil, with chopped tomato and a splash of white wine. The boneless roasted fish pieces were then added. The simple combination was perfectly delicious, just saucy enough to dress the pasta. I fantasized about making it in my own kitchen. In Sicily, it was made with orata, sea bream. Back home in the States, we tried it with cod and with halibut and were more than happy with both. But nearly any firm-fleshed fish could stand in — rockfish, sea bass, corvina — whatever is spanking fresh. Instead of sitting down for the first course, we stood, nibbling on crostini topped with savory caponata, enjoyed with a bottle of crisp white Grillo. Recipe: Zucchini-Eggplant Caponata Toasts Traditional caponata is made with eggplant fried in olive oil and then simmered in a sweet-sour sauce that includes tomatoes, vinegar and sugar, along with capers, green olives, celery and sometimes raisins. There are other versions of caponata, too, made with artichokes or other seasonal vegetables, the agrodolce sauce being the through line. I made mine with zucchini and eggplant; both looked good at the market. My version is light on tomato, possibly because that’s the way I first knew it, when we used to buy it in those flat glass jars at the Italian deli. Though you can eat it right away, of course, caponata is best when it’s allowed to meld its flavors for a day or two. And since it keeps well, it’s nice to have a batch on hand in the fridge, ready at any moment to serve with drinks or as a midnight snack. Lately, for dessert, I have been enamored with roasted fruit, so I continued the theme for this meal, this time with pears, flavored with a little powdered fennel seed. They were anointed with a creamy zabaglione, kissed with Marsala, the fortified sweet wine. Sicilian zabaglione is nothing more than Marsala, egg yolks and sugar, heated and whipped into a frothy custard. In restaurants, they make a show of it, the chef in plain sight, beating the mixture vigorously by hand in a copper pan. Be warned: When making it at home, you’ll need a strong arm (or a volunteer) for all that whisking, but, for a sauce this good, it’s worth the workout.

item.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Rome, According to a Best-Selling Local Cookbook Author
item.description:
Source: Eater
Roman cuisine is a reflection of the city itself — layered, deeply rooted in tradition, and full of contrasts. After years of eating my way through Rome, I’ve found the best meals are shaped as much by history as the hands that prepare them. Family-run trattorias have served the city’s defining dishes for generations: cacio e pepe, carbonara, roasted lamb, and offal-based specialties, many of which trace their origins to Rome’s historic slaughterhouse economy. While these places remain essential, a wave of neo-trattorias constantly reinterprets the classics, and the broader dining scene continues to shift too. The influence of Rome’s immigrant communities and cuisines, from Ethiopian to Venezuelan, is stronger than ever. The 38 Best Restaurants in Rome, According to a Best-Selling Local Cookbook Author Where to eat in Rome, including the best pizza, pasta, wine bars, and more Rome in February and March can feel like a damp intermission which pivots quickly toward spring. One day you’re ducking into bars to escape the downpour and the next you’re scanning patios for a table in the sun. If recent years are any indication, high season now revs up well before Holy Week, and by late March the city is already moving at full tilt. This is the narrow stretch to lean into artichokes simmered with the first peas, favas, and lettuce into vignarola, Rome’s definitive spring stew. Blink and you’ll miss it. Eating and drinking well in Rome isn’t just about knowing where to go; it’s about knowing how to navigate the city’s idiosyncratic dining culture. Travelers often book tables months in advance, making last-minute reservations tough. While online booking is becoming more common, many places still rely on the phone, and it’s best to call at the very start or very end of service, when the staff actually has time to pick up. Plan ahead — but leave some room for spontaneity too. We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing dining scene in Rome. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30. New to the map in October 2026: In San Giovanni, Beppe e I Suoi Formaggi has moved beyond its former Ghetto shop, with a larger space where Beppe Giovale’s selection of Italian and French cheeses shares the table with dishes like tajarin with alpine butter. Near the Pyramid of Gaius Cestius, third-generation family-run Taverna Cestia serves Roman classics, seafood, and wood-fired pizza alongside a thoughtful wine list. In Prati-adjacent Della Vittoria, Vetro pairs natural wines with small plates that borrow freely from Roman and wider European traditions, making it as appealing for dinner as for a drink. Katie Parla is a Rome-based food and beverage journalist, culinary guide, and New York Times best-selling cookbook author. Her latest cookbook, Rome, is available now. Vetro’s sidewalk crowd can look like the cigarette-rolling Olympics, with drinkers claiming improvised seats and lingering over glasses of wine and beer. Inside, high-tops and tables offer a more settled way to explore a menu whose ingredients often speak Roman, while its sensibility ranges across Europe. Gildas and eggs with mayonnaise join tongue with sweet potatoes and piquillo peppers, while baccalà mantecato goes by brandade and comes with marinated zucchini and isot pepper. Order a few snacks and small plates, and suddenly staying for dinner becomes an appealing proposition. Set in a former alimentari on Viale Carso, the bar pairs its neighborhood hangout atmosphere with a thoughtful natural wine selection spanning Italy, Spain, and southern France, including wines served sfuso (on tap). Vibe check: Stay outside for the people-watching; claim a table inside to work your way through the food menu. Colombian chef Roy Caceres is a veteran of Roman fine dining. His landmark, Michelin-starred restaurant, Metamorfosi, didn’t survive the pandemic, but his signature dishes have found a place at Orma (an anagram of Roma) just a few blocks southeast of the Galleria Borghese. Orma is home to a number of distinct concepts: The bistrot is a power-lunch spot set on a shaded terrace, the cocktail bar specializes in tropical fruit- and herb-forward drinks, and the restaurant offers tasting menus and a la carte dishes that blend Caceres’s Colombian heritage with Italian flavors and ingredients. Fans of the chef’s Uovo 65° Carbonara (a soft-cooked egg floating in Parmigiano-Reggiano foam, served with a side of puffed pasta and tender strips of guanciale) will find it in the bistrot, while the restaurant serves his renowned lacquered eel with pickled onions. Best for: The business lunch is a great deal for anyone into fine dining but not keen to linger. A short walk from the Trevi Fountain, this friendly trattoria has been serving satisfying dishes from Emilia-Romagna, a region in northeastern Italy, since 1931; the current owners took the helm in 1967. The menu is rich in egg-based house-made pastas like tortelli di zucca (pumpkin pasta with butter and sage) and tagliatelle alla bolognese (long strands of fresh, egg-based pasta dressed with a rich meat sauce). Save room for meaty mains including bollito misto (assorted simmered meats) and fried liver. Must-try dishes: Tortellini in brodo and the bollito misto. Just 100 feet from Rome’s most intact ancient monument, Armando al Pantheon champions local food traditions. For more than five decades, the Gargioli family has been dutifully producing Roman classics like fettuccine con le rigaglie di pollo (fettuccine with chicken innards) and coda alla vaccinara (oxtail braised in tomato and celery). Among the seasonal side dishes, look for puntarelle (Catalonian chicory) with anchovy sauce and carciofi alla romana (simmered artichokes) in the cooler months. Save room for the torta antica Roma, a ricotta and strawberry jam pie. The lovingly curated wine list gets better every year. Know before you go: Book online exactly one month ahead to secure a spot — it fills up fast. Moriondo e Gariglio is a time capsule with a cocoa perfume. Founded in Turin by cousins Agostino Moriondo and Francesco Gariglio, former chocolatiers to the Savoy royal household, the chocolate shop followed the court to Rome in the late 19th century and eventually settled on Via del Piè di Marmo, a couple of minutes from the Pantheon. Glass counters hold more than 80 chocolates and bonbons, all made by hand. In autumn, locals stock up on the shop’s cult marrons glacés, sold whole or blended into a paste, while spring brings elaborately engineered Easter eggs with surprises hidden inside. A small box is an easy souvenir. A kilo feels like joining a noble Roman ritual. Know before you go: Chocolate production winds down in the warm months, which see the arrival of pâte de fruits in their place. After Settimio al Pellegrino, a cult favorite featured on Anthony Bourdain’s Parts Unknown, shuttered in 2022, Leonardo Vignoli and Maria Pia Cicconi (of Cesare al Casaletto fame) resurrected the restaurant. They’ve retained the institution’s signature tiled floors, midcentury furniture, and infamous doorbell required for customers to gain access. The trattoria near Campo dei Fiori serves a succinct menu, including minestra con broccoli e arzilla (romanesco and skate soup) and former chef-owner Teresa Zazza’s legendary pan-fried meatballs. Best for: A dinner (or weekend lunch) when you’re ready to drink from the incredibly affordable wine list. If Roman restaurants have become known for brusque, no-nonsense service, Hosteria Grappolo d’Oro did not get the message. Affable servers circulate through the dining rooms beneath exposed wooden beams, delivering pure versions of cucina romana classics like toothsome tonnarelli cacio e pepe and tender roasted suckling lamb. Best for: The 36 euro, four-course Roman tasting menu is one of Rome’s best deals. Open for: All dayPrice range: $In the southwest corner of one of Rome’s most touristy squares, Forno Campo de’ Fiori bakes sweet and savory Roman specialties like jam tarts and flatbreads. Look for pizza alla pala (long slabs baked directly in a deep electric deck oven), which is sold in slices by weight; the unctuous toppings and crispy bases make a surprisingly balanced pair. An annex across the alley on Vicolo del Gallo stays open during the main bakery’s afternoon break, from 2:30 to 4:45 p.m. Must-try dish: The pizza con mortadella is one of the best bites in town. Culinary power couple Francesca Barreca and Marco Baccannelli reopened their landmark restaurant Mazzo after a five year hiatus, and this time around, a relatively central location in San Lorenzo makes it considerably more accessible to many residents. The dining room has also grown from a single 12-seat communal table to full-fledged restaurant seating complete with a massive porthole peering into the brightly lit kitchen. Just like the original, the new Mazzo plays with nostalgic forms in dishes like wagon wheel pasta with braised beef and onions, which joins Barreca and Baccannelli’s classics like fried tripe with grated pecorino Romano in a pool of tomato sauce, a retooling of Rome’s signature offal dish, trippa alla romana. Must-try dishes: The fried tripe, and the wagon wheels with an oniony braised beef sauce. The Camerucci family’s well-loved trattoria is not actually in Monti, but rather the adjacent multicultural Esquilino district near Stazione Termini. The cuisine is heavily Marchigiano — from the Italian region of Le Marche — so expect lots of game like braised rabbit and roasted duck, meat-filled fried olives, and fresh pasta like the legendary raviolo filled with a runny egg yolk and dressed with butter and sage. Must-try dish: The runny-yolk raviolo is not to be missed. Founded in the Historic Center in 2004 by Rome’s premier baking family, Salumeria Roscioli does triple duty as a deli, wine bar, and restaurant. Though the menu is extensive, the real stars are the cheeses (burrata with semi-dried tomatoes is spectacular), cured meats (Culaccia and mortadella with Parmigiano-Reggiano are both stellar), and pasta classics (get the gricia, cacio e pepe, amatriciana, or carbonara). If you dine at lunch or on the early side at dinner, the bread basket will include warm bread from nearby Antico Forno Roscioli. The wine list is wide-ranging, and don’t miss the distilled spirits before closing out the meal. Vibe check: Request a table upstairs or outside to avoid getting seated in the basement. For two centuries, Rome’s Jewish community was confined to a walled ghetto along the Tiber River. The squalid buildings are long gone, but a historic ghetto-era bakery survives on what has become the transformed neighborhood’s main thoroughfare. The pizza ebraica — a sort of fruit cake studded with nuts, raisins, and candied fruits — is an easy specialty to eat on the go, but it’s worth seeking out a bench to get messy with a slice of ricotta and sour cherry tart. Also try the amaretti and biscotti made with heaps of cinnamon and a generous smattering of whole almonds. Must-try dish: The ricotta and sour-cherry tart — grab it before it sells out. Via Prenestina has been a hub for Ethiopian and Eritrean community and cuisine in Rome for decades, and Mrgda, situated on this wide avenue at the edge of Pigneto, is a standout example. Partake of the free-flowing tej, a heady, honey-fermented wine that pairs perfectly with dishes like richly spiced legumes, aromatic vegetables, tender braised chicken, and deeply seasoned raw beef. Each bite is scooped up with Mrgda’s ethereal, naturally leavened injera, which has a balanced tang. Know before you go: There is a vegan restaurant from the same owners, Mrgda Vegano, just a few blocks away. Routinely named among the best places to drink in Europe, this long-established craft beer pub in Trastevere pours around a dozen draft beers from Italy, the U.S., Belgium, Germany, and the U.K., in addition to a small but well-curated assortment of bottles. The staff is passionate and knowledgeable, and can guide you to the right choice for your palate. It’s worth waiting for the few tables on the street outside, set up during the pandemic, which offer a front row seat to Trastevere’s lively nightlife. Best for: Drinking vintage sour beers from Italy and beyond, 365 days a year (it’s even open on holidays). Open for: Dinner, with lunch Wednesday to Sunday L’Elementare has multiple locations around Rome, but the Trastevere outpost is the one that stands out service-wise. The focus is Roman pizza tonda: thin, nearly rimless, crisp and chewy at the edges. It’s baked longer than a Neapolitan pie, lending structural integrity that prevents slices from collapsing under disappointing tip sag. Start with molten supplì ar telefono, fried bricks of lasagna, and fried parcels of tonnarelli cacio e pepe. Know before you go: There are several locations, so double check you are booking the Trastevere address, and be warned that although they post all day hours Wednesday to Sunday, the kitchen actually does close from 3:30ish to around 6:45. Trapizzino is a small street food chain with locations throughout Italy (and an outpost in New York). The concept is based on the trapizzino, a combination of the popular triangular tramezzino sandwich with long, slowly leavened pizza dough, invented by pizzaiolo Stefano Callegari in 2008. Callegari fills his tricornered creations with Roman classics like oxtail simmered with tomato and celery, chicken cacciatore, and tripe cooked with tomato, each going for just 5 euros. Know before you go: Visit the Trastevere branch for table service and a full bar with Lazio wines. The cool, windowless inner sanctum at number 10 on Via del Moro in Trastevere only has a handful of tables lining two walls, and they fill up quickly with 90-minute reservation slots beginning at 6 p.m. The interior design evokes the Orient Express with wooden accents and overhead racks above the seating, and the bartenders’ wardrobe and glassware are a throwback to the last century too. The menu of bottled classic cocktails, Champagne, and non-alcoholic drinks provides an oasis of refinement in the heart of Rome’s rowdy nightlife district. Know before you go: Reservations are essential — book online for this hidden cocktail bar experience. Latteria Trastevere is a wine bar and bistro in Rome’s nightlife epicenter focused on natural vino, cheeses, and cured meats culled from tiny, sought-after producers across Italy. There are some hot dishes too, and Sardinian owner Antonio Cossu brings in island specialties like sa fregola (pearl couscous) with crab and bottles from Barbagia, one of Sardinia’s most delicious wine regions. As a bonus, Latteria is open nearly every day of the year. Must-try pairing: The Sardinian prosciutto and wines from small producers from the Barbagia. Few restaurants in Rome are as deeply tied to the city’s culinary identity as Sora Lella. Founded in 1959 by Elena Fabrizi — actor, cook, and icon — this trattoria in a medieval tower on the Tiber Island has long been a standard bearer for the hearty cucina romana. While there was a period when the restaurant seemed to coast on its reputation, the third generation has brought it back to top form. Today, Sora Lella is once again a satisfying place to experience traditional Roman dishes executed with care. The wine list leans local, highlighting Lazio’s underappreciated labels. With its rustic wood-paneled dining rooms and medieval tower setting, Sora Lella is a nostalgic but enduring pillar of Roman dining. Must-try dish: Go in spring for the coratella d’abbacchio (sauteed sucking lamb offal) with artichokes, or try the coda alla vaccinara (oxtail stewed in a rich tomato and celery sauce).
