L’Antidoto sits on a cobbled Trastevere side street, far from the crowds queuing outside tourist-packed trattorie. What started as a simple natural wine bar in 2020 has evolved into one of the most compelling dining experiences in the city with the arrival of chef Mirko Pelosi in 2024. Pelosi’s training in France, Norway, and Scotland gives him a worldly sensibility, which he puts to work aging fish, fermenting vegetables, and sourcing spices from across continents. Each dish is rooted in ingredients, driven by technique, and free from ego. The menu changes constantly, but expect dishes like mahi mahi confit, chard, tendons, and grapes. In a Roman dining landscape crowded with derivative plates and copycat concepts, Pelosi’s food is a revelation. Know before you go: Two hungry people definitely can — and should — order everything on the menu. A short walk from the Colosseum, Tempio di Iside is an elegant fish restaurant known for its crudi (raw dishes) like fish carpaccio, sea urchin roe, langoustines, and oysters. The pasta with sweet red shrimp, cherry tomatoes, and fresh pecorino is excellent (and proof there are valid exceptions to the “no cheese with seafood” rule), as are the spaghetti with clams, whole roasted fish, and pasta with spiny lobster. Book ahead, especially to secure an outdoor table for dinner in the summer, and expect to pay a premium for access to some of the freshest fish around. Know before you go: Book ahead for a coveted outdoor table in summer. Located in the sprawling Centocelle district in eastern Rome, Menabò Vino e Cucina offers a veritable tour of Italian regional comfort food. Rigatoni is served with oniony braised beef in the style of Naples, while pasta with chickpeas and mussels evoke the coastal south. Meanwhile, unctuous local classics like pasta alla gricia get punched up with fresh, seasonal twists such as grapes or figs. As the name promises, wine shares the stage with the kitchen’s creations, and the list is populated primarily by naturally and traditionally made wines. Know before you go: The menu is always changing and the wine list is consistently outstanding. After a career working in Roman gourmet temples like Salumeria Roscioli, Pasquale Borriello struck out on his own in 2022. His small shop in Trastevere near the church of San Francesco a Ripa has a few high-top tables where you can sip natural wine or craft beer alongside Italy’s greatest cheeses. All the big names are on the menu — Parmigiano-Reggiano, gorgonzola, and mozzarella di bufala among them — but Borriello favors the smallest and most artisanal producers of these famous styles. In addition to formaggio, Forme sells cured meats, sandwiches, and pantry items like jars of obscure marinated vegetables. Best for: Sit at a high-top table and try blue cheese from celebrated affineur Andrea Magi. Marco Radicioni trained with Rome’s gelato maestro Claudio Torcè, embracing his sensibility of all-natural flavors, meticulous sourcing, and restrained sweetness. Since launching his own gelateria, Radicioni has grown into a maestro in his own right, churning some of the most exquisite gelato in Italy. His newest location in Monteverde Vecchio serves more than just Otaleg’s rich and creamy gelato made from the world’s best pistachios and chocolates. There are specialty coffee and artisanal pastries, too, which have transformed Otaleg into a point of reference for third-wave coffee drinkers. Know before you go: Try the Monteverde location for gelato and coffee; Trastevere for pure gelato bliss. A few minutes from the Circo Massimo, Pizzarium alum and Bonci protégé Alessandro Ruver runs a tiny laboratorio where pizza in teglia gets the kind of focus usually reserved for restaurant menus. The daily lineup of trays features long-fermented dough that bakes up light, crisp, and audibly crunchy. Pizzas get named with a sense of humor, and topped with ingredients from small farms in central Italy. The Ragùver is loaded with slow-cooked meat sauce and Parmigiano-Reggiano, reminiscent of Sunday sauce. Know before you go: Like most Roman slice joints, you eat standing at a few outdoor high tops, so don’t wear yourself out too much wandering the nearby Colosseum and Forum before stopping by. Santo Palato is chef Sarah Cicolini’s neotrattoria in Rome’s Appio Latino district, a residential area just beyond the city walls near San Giovanni in Laterano. When it first opened in 2017, the trattoria quickly became a pilgrimage spot for those craving a bold, updated take on Roman cooking. The new, larger location, which opened in the spring, stays true to that original spirit, serving deeply satisfying dishes like tender trippa, an ethereal chicken gizzard frittata, and the yolkiest carbonara around. With a bigger kitchen, Cicolini now has the space to turn out fresh pasta and a wider range of braised, grilled, and smoked meats. Diners can watch it all unfold through large windows that separate the kitchen from the dining room, bringing the action right into view. Know before you go: The communal table near the entrance is available for walk-ins. Book well in advance if you’d rather sit anywhere else. After nearly two decades in Rome’s historic Ghetto, cheesemaker Beppe Giovale closed his original shop at the end of 2025 and resurfaced in San Giovanni with a brighter, roomier version. The Via Gallia location still revolves around a refrigerated counter filled with more than 100 mostly raw-milk cheeses, including selections from Giovale’s family dairy in Piedmont and small producers throughout Italy and France. But there is now a real kitchen and around 20 seats, allowing the menu to venture beyond cheese and butter tastings into dishes like tajarin with alpine butter and tongue with bell peppers and salsa verde. For shopping only, Giovale maintains a small stall at boxes 227 and 228 in the Mercato Trionfale; the Ghetto location has closed. Must-try dishes: A selection of cheeses made by Beppe and his family, accompanied by the smoked salted butter. Located in Testaccio, Rome’s undisputed offal capital, Piatto Romano focuses on classics like rigatoni con la pajata (pasta with milk-fed veal intestines cooked in tomato sauce) and fettuccine con le rigaglie di pollo (fettuccine with chicken innards). There are plenty of pescatarian options as well, like the outstanding cod baked with onions, pine nuts, apricots, and prunes, and pan-fried anchovies spiked with vinegar and chile pepper, and the vegetable dishes are incredible. Must-try dishes: Vegetable sides like the braised zucchini greens and foraged greens salad are showstoppers. Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and some Friday evenings The Testaccio neighborhood market is the best place in central Rome to shop for seasonal produce, meat, fish, and baked goods all in one place. Get there in the morning to see it in full swing (it’s open Monday through Saturday until 2 p.m. and occasional evenings). Visit Da Artenio (Box 90) for takeaway pizza slices and pizzette, little pizzas topped with tomato sauce, potatoes, or onions. Don’t miss the essential Mordi e Vai (Box 15), where the Esposito family prepares sandwiches filled with offal and meat based on generations-old recipes, including disappearing historic dishes like alesso di scottona (simmered brisket). Nearby Da Corrado (Box 18) sells natural wines, artisan cheeses, and a handful of hot dishes — including incredible soups — while Casa Manco (Box 22) serves naturally leavened pizza by weight and Sicché (Box 37) specializes in Tuscany-inspired soups, sandwiches, and salads. Must-try shops: Hit Mordi e Vai for offal sandwiches and Da Corrado for cheese, soup, and wine. Founded in 1967 by Amatrice native Gioacchino Salvi, Taverna Cestia sits across from the ancient pyramidal tomb of Gaius Cestius that gives the restaurant its name. Now run by third-generation restaurateur and sommelier Valerio Salvi, the trattoria covers a lot of ground without losing focus. Roman staples like tonnarelli cacio e pepe and grilled abbacchio share the menu with locally caught seafood, seasonal vegetables, and thin, crisp Roman pizzas from the wood-fired oven. The sprawling dining room and outdoor tables attract families and large groups, while the unusually thoughtful wine list favors small producers and natural wines. Must-try dishes: This very Roman trattoria serves a very Neapolitan dessert: babà. The rum-soaked pastry can be cloying and sodden elsewhere; here, it’s spectacular, with just the right balance of booze, sweetness, and airy crumb. The sign teetering on the roof might read “Cafè Du Parc” in the most appealing mid-century font ever, but this kiosk at the nexus of the Aventino, Ostiense, and Testaccio districts now has new ownership and a new name, Mostro. It opens early for specialty coffee, cruises through the afternoon with restrained momentum, then pivots into low key drinking with draft cocktails and natural wines that attract locals who aren’t phased by the flurry of trams and buses that careen over the adjacent cobblestones. The vibe stays casual and the soundtrack vacillates between staff playlists and vinyl on the turntables by the bar. Know before you go: This is largely an outdoor stop, so dress for the weather, and aim for earlier hours if you want a calmer moment with your drink before the aperitivo crowd clocks in. Following careers in fine dining in Italy and abroad, Leonardo Vignoli and Maria Pia Cicconi went back to basics with Cesare al Casaletto, a straightforward trattoria the husband-and-wife duo took over in 2009. The menu features Roman classics with a few restrained twists, like fried gnocchi served on a pool of cacio e pepe sauce. The pasta alla gricia has achieved cult status, the suckling lamb mains are exceptional, and the beverage list spotlights stunningly affordable natural wines from Italy, France, and Slovenia. If you take public transit: Take tram 8 for easy access, and stroll back to the center through Villa Pamphili park after lunch. Pizzaiolo Sami El Sabawy first made a name in the Roman pizza world at the iconic slice joint Pizzarium (also on this list). But it’s the thin crust, wood-fired personal pizzas he makes today that attract diners to Torpignattara in eastern Rome. Named after the Roman phrase meaning “to do something continuously,” A Rota lives up to its name; once you try the impeccably crisp pizza and golden fritti, like supplì and battered squash blossoms, you’ll keep coming back for more. El Sabawy specializes in a hyper-thin, low-hydration dough that he rolls out with a pin before baking at a lower temperature for longer than its Neapolitan counterpart. The result is a shatteringly crisp base, sturdy enough to support both classic and creative toppings without losing its integrity. The traditional margherita is a lesson in balance, with bright tomato sauce, fior di latte, and fragrant basil, but don’t skip Sami’s specials, like April’s stuffed pizza filled with chard, potato, Parmigiano-Reggiano, and ham. Must-try dish: Try the classic margherita to understand Sami’s style, then go for the seasonal special. Located a short distance from Stazione Trastevere, C’è Pasta… e Pasta (translation: “There’s pasta… and pasta”) serves delicious kosher meals to eat in or take away. Order at the counter and don’t miss Roman Jewish classics like carciofi alla giudia (fried artichokes), filetti di baccala (battered fried cod), aliciotti con l’indivia (layered anchovy and frisee casserole), and concia (fried and marinated zucchini). As the name promises, they also serve pasta dishes and sell fresh pasta to cook at home. Must-try dishes: The Roman Jewish concia and baccala are particularly special. Bruno Persiani, an Umbrian transplant to the Italian capital, opened this homey trattoria in southern Trastevere in 1968 to serve a mix of dishes from Umbria and Rome. Tavernaccia is now run by Persiani’s daughters and Sardinian son-in-law, who throws in a few of his own regional specialties like suckling pig cooked in the wood-fired oven. The fresh pastas are excellent (especially Sunday’s lasagna, which sells out fast), and the wood oven-roasted brisket is otherworldly. Organic and natural wines from Italy and Slovenia round out the wine list. The service is patient and unbelievably kind — far from the norm in the Italian capital, so don’t get used to it. Must-try dishes: Order whatever was made in the wood fired oven that day, whether it’s brisket, lasagna, or eggplant parm. Open for: Dinner, with lunch on weekends Nearly a decade in, Trattoria Pennestri is still one of Rome’s smartest answers to the question “where do I eat Roman food near the center but away from the tourists?” The room is relaxed and the cooking is grounded in the classics, but the kitchen knows exactly when a twist is worth making, like rigatoni con la pajata brightened with a measured hit of collatura (anchovy elixir) that elevates the sweetly lactic, milk-filled calf intestines with a savory note. The accessibly-priced wine list leans heavily toward small producers, with a strong showing from Lazio and central Italy. Know before you go: Book ahead, especially on weekends, and ask the staff to steer you through the wine list. Stecca is the Roman debut of Abruzzese chef Franco Franciosi of Mammaròssa in Avezzano, in partnership with Flavio De Maio of Rome’s Flavio al Velavevodetto. In a low-lit Garbatella space fitted with austere, Nordic-inspired design, the two turn the dining room into a kind of multisensory stage where Abruzzo’s mountain flavors meet Roman cooking. The menu shifts constantly and leans comforting: rigatoni with meat roll sauce; perfectly roasted lamb chops with puntarelle; a creamy soup of chickpeas, chestnuts, and dried figs. It’s all paired with excellent naturally leavened bread and a serious central Italy-leaning wine list Know before you go: There are a handful of bar seats, ideal for solo diners. After nearly 30 years at the helm of Rome’s first Thai restaurant, Beijing-born chef Ge Jing Hua opened Sinosteria in 2020 to serve a blend of Chinese regional cuisines featuring dishes like Beijing-style tripe with chile oil and cilantro, and Shandong-inspired squid with peppers, ginger, and bamboo. There are also signature creations like basmati rice with coconut milk, shrimp, capers, and oregano from Pantelleria. The front of house is expertly managed by Ge’s gregarious sommelier son Jun, whose natural wine list and coffee menu are outstanding. Must-try pairing: Ask Jun to recommend a natural wine or tea. Trecca is, for lack of a better term, a neo-trattoria. It delivers everything a Roman trattoria should: an informal setting, rigorously seasonal comfort food, and an offal-forward menu. But there’s also a natural wine list, an Instagram page, and two young brothers at the helm. Manuel and Nicolò Trecastelli lean into Rome’s powerful flavors and rich ingredients. Their carbonara and amatriciana are as loaded with pepper-spiked guanciale as any in the city, and tomato and vinegar are employed in the meaty mains to offset their unctuousness. Must-try dish: Try the pajata in any and every way the restaurant serves it. At Da Michele, two generations of the Pignotta family have perfected an incredibly high-level wine and seafood experience, presented without pretense. Since opening in the residential San Paolo district in 1991, this spot has become a neighborhood institution, drawing back regulars with its consistently fresh catch from local fish markets in Fiumicino and Anzio, and attracting wine connoisseurs from across the city eager to taste through the exceptional cellar. Pair mineral-driven white wines from across Europe — including older vintages — with al dente linguine with telline (wedge clams) and fried or roasted fish. Must-try pairing: Pair linguine with telline or roasted fish with older vintage white Burgundy from the cellar. Pizza Nader in the Roma 70 neighborhood — an area in the southern part of town once home to emperor Nerva’s grain reserves — is worth the detour. This unassuming shop might look like your standard Roman pizza al taglio joint, but step inside and you’ll find a level of care and precision that sets it apart. Sacks of stone milled flour from Le Marche, Campania, and Sicily crowd the entrance, where I ate a delightful supplì on a visit last month while waiting for a slice of pizza adorned with pecorino, black pepper, and guanciale. Owner Nader Abdelkader praises the dedication of the farmers and millers that make the flour for his deeply flavored pizzas and the dozen types of naturally leavened pane that he bakes. Must-try dish: Don’t miss the legendary kebab, a favorite of regulars.

item.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Tokyo, According to a Local Expert
item.description:
Source: Eater
Restaurants in Tokyo are known for shokunin, the people who focus on a single skill to the point of obsession. These chefs dedicate their lives to the smallest details of a cuisine: the optimal temperature for the oil when frying tempura, the perfect texture for sushi rice, the ideal sear on grilled unagi. This long-term commitment separates Tokyo from the other great dining cities in the world, and it has fostered a lot of continuity in the restaurant scene; some of the earliest restaurants in Tokyo also served sushi, tempura, and unagi, along with soba, sukiyaki, and other specialties still represented in restaurants today. Though Tokyo is infamous for a few highly regarded spots that are impossible to get into without an introduction by a regular, visitors will find more than enough to love across the massive dining metropolis. The 38 Best Restaurants in Tokyo, According to a Local Expert Where to eat in Tokyo, including sushi, ramen, and yakitori, as recommended by a local food writer and shochu advisor. We update this list quarterly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing Tokyo dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in yen), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30. New to the map in October 2026: The tea master at Chokeikyo offers traditional, modern, and even cocktail options. The handroll sushi bar reaches new heights thanks to legendary nori from the revered shop Yamamoto Noriten. The baton has been passed to a new chef at Sezanne and it continues to shine. Finally, yet another pizza spot at Bulgari Bar for a metropolis spoiled with top pizzerias. Yukari Sakamoto is the author of Food Sake Tokyo and offers guided tours to markets in Tokyo. She is a graduate of the French Culinary Institute, a sommelier, and a shochu advisor. This spacious warehouse is a sister shop to the original Koffee Mameya Kakeru, a popular boutique in Omotesando. The cafe specializes in flights of coffee, which might include a pour over, an espresso, a latte, and one or more mocktails, all showcasing different expressions of the same bean. You can also order drinks a la carte, including spiked coffee cocktails in the evening. The interior is sleek, with contrasting wooden chairs and a U-shaped limestone counter, and the knowledgeable staff wear white lab coats and bowties — though they’re perfectly friendly. Know before you go: Reservations are required. Former New York City architect Shinji Mizutani opened Tanikoretani in the Kiyosumi Shirakawa neighborhood with his brother, Tomoji. Vegetables shine at this hipster izakaya, including in dishes like mizu nasu eggplant sashimi, mountain vegetable tempura, and wafu ratatouille. There are also classic sake-friendly plates like seasonal sashimi, karaage fried chicken, and potato salad. The best plan is probably to opt for the omakase, and leave it to the brothers to create a menu for you. Best for: An early dinner following a late afternoon visit to Kiyosumi Teien, one of Tokyo’s traditional gardens, just a short walk from the restaurant. Yamariki in Morishita, an older part of Tokyo, is a shinise restaurant, meaning that it dates back one-hundred years. The signature dish, nikomi offal stew, is simmered in Hatcho miso, zarame sugar, red wine, and bouquet garni; Yamariki’s version is said to be one of the top three nikomi in Tokyo. There is also a colorful selection of vegetable dishes including tsukemono pickles, rainbow crudite with miso for dipping, and a hearty salad with an anchovy dressing. Be sure to inquire into any seasonal dishes like tempura of spring mountain vegetables. Sake, beer, and shochu are all on the menu, but Yamariki is also known for a short list of wines that pairs well with its cuisine. Know before you go: Yamariki also serves yakiton, grilled pork skewers with interesting cuts like tongue, heart, liver, stomach, and harami skirt steak. You’ll find dozens of shops lining this street in the Tsukishima neighborhood all serving monjayaki, a local dish similar to Osaka’s okonomiyaki. The setup at every shop is essentially the same: Diners select fillings such as mentaiko (spicy pollack roe), mochi, and cheese, and cook the monja themselves on a large iron plate set into each table with the help of a tiny spatula. The trick is to spread the mixture out thin and wait for it to crisp up (the staff will gladly show first timers the proper technique). Paired with an icy mug of beer, it’s a fun meal. Know before you go: The street is blocked off at night for pedestrians, letting visitors peruse the shops and giving the whole scene a festive atmosphere. In Juzo Itami’s movie Tampopo, there’s a scene in which a cook surreptitiously makes omurice, a soft omelet over ketchup-stained rice, for Tampopo’s son Tabo. Diners can experience the version of the dish that was specifically developed for the movie at Taimeiken in the historic Nihonbashi district, a short walk from Tokyo Station. The third-generation chef, Hiroshi Modegi, now helms the kitchen at this iconic restaurant, which also serves other kinds of yoshoku (Western dishes adapted to the Japanese palate) like katsu. The first floor is walk-in only and quite popular, while the second floor is more formal and takes reservations. Must-try dish: At lunchtime on the first floor, order the small portions of borscht soup and coleslaw for only 100 yen each. Manhattan has more handroll bars than Tokyo. But the nori specialty shop Yamamoto Noriten, in business since 1849, has started to close that gap, recently opening an imported concept worth your attention: a counter for temaki, DIY hand rolls. Iron Chef Kimio Nonaga has curated a dozen fillings including tuna sashimi, soy sauce-marinated egg yolk, grilled eel, and caviar. A small brick of roasting charcoal warms the nori that is presented in a wooden box. Know before you go: The casual counter is behind a large noren curtain in the retail shop. On the 40th floor of the Bvlgari Hotel Tokyo, Il Ristorante - Niko Romito’s long dining room, decorated in carnelian orange and boasting a vaulted ceiling, feels like a chapel to haute cuisine. Chef Mauro Aloisio’s modern Italian takes advantage of seasonal seafood like amberjack sashimi or the collagen-rich kue longtooth grouper steamed and smoked with sakura chips, while the wagyu beef tongue is braised until it falls apart under a beetroot sauce. Know before you go: Niko Romito is in a hotel so it’s open all-year long, including on holidays (it was a lifesaver for me over the New Year holidays when most of Tokyo was closed). For a shorter meal, head up to the Bulgari Bar on the 45th floor for pizza by Pier Daniel Seu, each paired with a bespoke cocktail. Chef Steve Lancaster is the new chef at Sézanne, formerly the number one restaurant in the world. Though he is new to Japan, Lancaster worked with Japanese seafood for seven years while cooking at Poise in Singapore. Glass shrimp, uni, monkfish liver, and scallops are highlights on his menu at the Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Marunouchi. Many components in the dishes are fermented or include Japanese pantry staples like mirin, soy sauce, or koji on the French menu. The sommelier’s thoughtful pairings of wine and unique sakes, including a sweet kijoshu sake, are a highlight. Know before you go: Substitutions are not accommodated for allergies, so do check when making a reservation. Part of the ritual of riding a shinkansen (bullet train) is enjoying a bento and green tea (or sake if you like), while taking in the view. Located inside of Tokyo Station, Ekibenya Matsuri offers about 170 regional ekiben (“eki” for station and “ben” short for bento box) brought in from throughout Japan, an excellent chance to enjoy a range of regional Japanese flavors. The colorful selection includes rice topped with sashimi, wagyu beef, or yakitori grilled chicken skewers, and there is even a gyutan beef tongue bento that contains a warming device activated by a pull-string, allowing you to enjoy a hot meal on your journey. Know before you go: The shop opens at 5:30 a.m. for anyone catching an early train. Shabusen’s simple menu is sukiyaki or shabu shabu with thin slices of marbled wagyu beef, sliced by staff into thin sheets, or pork with vegetables. Seated at a casual counter, each diner gets their own hot pot to cook their own meal — think New York diner meets high-end hot pot. Once cooked, the meat and vegetables are dipped into a nutty sesame dressing, tart ponzu, or, in the case of sukiyaki, a raw egg. Aficionados of mingei, or traditional folk crafts, will cherish the tableware and noren curtain at the entryway. Best for: Top-quality sukiyaki and shabu shabu, but in a quicker and more accessible format. Torigin Honten, sandwiched between two buildings on a dark narrow pedestrian alley in the heart of Ginza, specializes in yakitori and kamameshi rice cooked with ingredients like ground chicken, bamboo shoots, salmon, shrimp, or sansai mountain vegetables in a personal-size rice pot. There are also chicken and vegetable skewers, grilled over Kishu bincho charcoal. Know before you go: Across the alley there’s a restaurant called New Torigin that serves a similar menu; it’s not quite as good, but can be a serviceable backup if lines at Torigin Honten get long. For his contemporary French cuisine, chef Guillaume Bracaval sources 95 percent of his ingredients locally. Set in the Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Otemachi, Michelin-starred Est features a variety of tasting menus, including items such as monkfish with house-made yuzu kosho, kombu-cured flounder, corn flan gazpacho, and pickled zucchini with tomato paste and nasturtiums. Wine aficionados will want to explore the Japanese bottle list, which is a study on unique grapes like muscat bailey A and fruity koshu, though the sommeliers can also include sake as beverage pairings. The meal finishes with sweets by pastry chef Michele Abbatemarco, including friandises utilizing honeys from various regions of Japan. Best for: Est offers a fabulous vegetable-focused menu, a great primer on Japan’s wide variety of produce. Tori paitan (creamy chicken broth for ramen) is rich and comforting, like grandma’s chicken soup. The broth clings to the thin straight noodles as one slurps. At Kagari, seasonal and colorful vegetables such as watermelon radish, snap peas, and kabocha squash top the dish and rotate throughout the year. Use the side dish of grated ginger and fried garlic, along with a bottle of vinegar from the counter, to brighten up and adjust the umami-rich soup to your liking. Know before you go: The main Ginza shop is on a quiet pedestrian back street, but the sister shop at the Roppongi Hills complex isn’t as crowded. Music and cocktails intersect at Bar Meijiu, where Keisuke Matsumoto crafts bespoke cocktails to suit each customer’s whims. After a quick conversation about flavors and vibes — Are you in the mood for something fruity or sparkling? Or perhaps something caffeinated made with house-roasted beans? — Matsumoto works like an alchemist in a compact booth at the heart of the space to concoct the ideal beverage. The non-alcoholic drinks are also worth a try. Vibe check: While serving customers, Matsumoto also spins items from his record collection, which includes a variety of genres but mainly jazz. Apartment and retail complex Azabudai Hills opened in the heart of the city in 2023 with more than 100 food shops and restaurants, along with the Teamlab Borderless museum. There’s a meal here for everyone, including two-Michelin-starred Florilège and a second location of Sushi Saito, giving diners a chance at a seat despite the fierce competition for reservations at the original. Other standouts include Arabica Kyoto for coffee, Kawamura for tonkatsu, Pelican Café for ham katsu sandos, Sembikiya fruit parlor for over-the-top parfaits, Shogun Burger for wagyu burgers, and Sobamae Yamato for soba and sake-friendly small plates. Best for: Finding something for everyone, at any time during the day. At Tenko, vegetables and seasonal seafood from Tokyo Bay are battered and fried into tempura, a specialty of Tokyo. The restaurant is on the quiet backstreets of Kagurazaka in a former geisha teahouse. Second-generation chef Hitoshi Arai is a master at creating delicate and lacy tempura, serving each one as it comes out of the oil, and it’s worth trying some of the tempura with salt instead of dipping sauce to preserve the crispy covering. Vibe check: Part of the experience is listening to the tempura as it bubbles in the hot oil. Open for: Dinner, with the addition of lunch of Saturdays The former geisha district of Kagurazaka is worth exploring at any time, but especially as evening falls on the atmospheric narrow alleys. Even more so if you’ve booked yourself into Ishikawa for an extended, multicourse kaiseki dinner. Hideki Ishikawa’s impeccable cuisine, superb quality ingredients, and gracious welcome have won him three well-deserved Michelin stars and a host of admirers around the world. Know before you go: Chef Ishikawa used to work at a tableware company so dining here is a delight for the palate and the eyes. Owner Kentaro Nakahara sources the finest wagyu and knows all the best cuts to grill over the charcoal burners set into your tabletop at Sumibiyakiniku Nakahara. Besides his seven-item yakiniku (grilled meat) tasting menu, don’t miss the beef “prosciutto,” the tartare, or his self-styled legendary grilled tongue. Yakiniku is always fun, but it’s rarely as chic, clean, and smoke-free — both from cigarettes and the grills — as it is here. Know before you go: If you want to try that legendary grilled tongue, you must reserve it in advance. Kaiseki, Japan’s ineffable, hyper-seasonal traditional cuisine, always tastes best in its hometown, Kyoto. This can be attributed to the water, which is softer than in Tokyo. Chef Yoshihiro Murata gets around this by shipping water from the ancient capital to the Akasaka branch of his renowned Kikunoi to ensure his dashi soup stock is always perfect. In this tranquil, secluded setting, it’s almost possible to imagine you have left the metropolis far behind. Know before you go: Lunch is more affordable than dinner, and the menu includes several seasonal dishes served on beautiful dishware. The historic Japanese confectionery shop has been making wagashi sweets for the Imperial court since the early 16th century. The flagship Akasaka shop is a glorious sanctuary with a cafe, retail shop, and museum, all designed by celebrated architect Hiroshi Naito. Capturing the fleeting moments of the season is at the heart of wagashi, so the menu changes monthly; in summertime the kakigori shaved ice is topped with sake, apricots, or matcha. Know before you go: The gallery exhibition in the basement always offers something informative, such as hand-drawn prints of Toraya’s wagashi over the centuries. Chef Daisuke Nomura serves modern shojin ryori — vegetarian Buddhist cuisine — strategically locating his restaurant Sougo in the Roppongi district to appeal to the younger, international crowd who live and work in the neighborhood. The menu includes a myriad of vegetables from land and sea, along with traditional shojin ingredients like fu (wheat gluten) and yuba (soy milk skin). Diners wanting to learn more about Japanese food can take classes at Tokyo Cook, a cooking school located within the restaurant. Must-try dish: The signature sesame tofu, fried or grilled to bring out a silky texture. Second-generation chef Daisuke Shimazaki serves traditional Edomae sushi at Sushi Yuu, located in a quiet residential area not far from the busy Roppongi district. While some high-end sushiya can feel stiflingly formal, more like a library or a church than a convivial restaurant, chef Shimazaki puts all of his customers at ease (in English, Russian, or Italian, as well as Japanese). The meal starts off with small seasonal bites such as grilled Pacific mackerel and simmered yellowtail before the parade of nigirizushi. Best for: Sushi Yuu is particularly famous for tuna, which Shimazaki sources from one of Toyosu Market’s top tuna vendors. Sake aficionados flock to Marie Chiba’s Eureka sake bar. The impressive sake list includes labels like Senkin, Aramasa, and Raifuku. Pair a glass with sake-friendly small plates like a smoked jammy egg covered in squid ink mayonnaise, blue cheese ham katsu, and crab cream croquettes. As a sake sommelier, Chiba can expertly recommend pairings, and will warm up some sake to draw out different expressions. Know before you go: There are only a dozen counter seats so be sure to book in advance, or walk in and hope to get a tachinomi (spot for standing and drinking). Yoshihiro Narisawa worked under Paul Bocuse, Frédy Girardet, and Joël Robuchon. But at his namesake restaurant, he fuses French haute cuisine with a profound understanding of Japanese ingredients that has resulted in a style uniquely his own. Serving brilliant left-field dishes such as soil soup (yes, really) and Okinawan sea snake broth, alongside superb langoustine and wagyu beef, he more than merits his two Michelin stars and spot on the Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants list. Know before you go: Chef Narisawa and his team are flexible to accommodate dietary restrictions. Butagumi, serving tonkatsu (breaded deep-fried pork), is set in a romantic 60-year-old, two-story, freestanding traditional house. Here, you dine on premium cutlets — made from your choice of a couple dozen regional heirloom breeds from around Japan — cooked a beautiful golden-brown and served with a pyramid of finely slivered cabbage and thick, house-made Worcestershire-style sauce. Know before you go: Butagumi has a second shop in the nearby Roppongi Hills complex in the Metro Hat level basement two. Nao Motohashi is one of only a handful of female chefs in Japan listed in both the Michelin and Gault & Millau guides. She and her sommelier husband, Ken, are warm hosts at their Aoyama restaurant, which is located in a former house. Diners enjoy an aperitif and appetizers on the first-floor lounge before moving upstairs to the main dining room overlooking an open kitchen. Highlights on the vegetable-forward menu include pickled tomatoes in a rose and hibiscus sauce, scallops with butterbur, and duck with slightly bitter spring mountain vegetables. The signature cheesecake ice cream pairs wonderfully with a warm sake. Must-try drinks: The non-alcoholic program is exciting, with house-made beverages such as grilled mandarin oranges with jasmine; burnt honey juice; and an apple, whey, and pomegranate drink. Grillmaster Takashi Imai’s namesake yakitoriya is large, sleek, and contemporary. All the seats look in on his spacious open kitchen, so you can watch him in action over the main charcoal pit. Besides his excellent chicken skewers, Imai usually offers a list of premium meats, such as French pigeon, and a serious selection of grilled vegetables from his second grill. Know before you go: There’s also a substantial list of natural wine to pair with your skewers. Chef Zaiyu Hasegawa’s decision to move Den from its iconic Jimbocho address has paid off in spades. At the new location, the chef can see each diner’s face and may adjust service or the size of dishes accordingly. The cooking remains innovative and satisfying, incorporating audacious, humorous ideas into Japan’s highly formalized kaiseki tradition. Expect foie gras in your appetizer and unique personalized front of house service from the chef’s wife, Emi, and her team. Must-try dish: The signature Dentucky Fried Chicken. Chef Yuki Motokura left a traditional Japanese kitchen to open Pizza Marumo. Motokura defines his pies as neither Neapolitan nor Roman, but as Tokyo-style. The charred pizza dough has the texture of freshly grilled mochi rice cakes, a comfort food for many Japanese diners. The extensive menu includes wagyu carpaccio, oven-roasted vegetables, and a long list of pizzas. The restaurant covers classic pizzas, as well as unique Japanese-style renditions incorporating umami-rich ingredients like katsuobushi (smoked skipjack tuna flakes), shaved kombu (kelp), shiitake mushrooms, or almost cheesy, soy-marinated tofu. Know before you go: Marumo is popular, so be sure to book a reservation via the restaurant’s website. Fresh, house-made tofu is the specialty at Tofu Shokudo, a temple to soy. Try set meals like a spicy Korean-style soup of soy milk, soft oboro tofu, and pork, or the tofu gozen set featuring nine types of soybean and tofu dishes. The bare bones wooden interior feels like a busy cafeteria packed with diners enjoying the many expressions including cheesy, fluffy, soft, firm, and spongey when deep-fried. Know before you go: Diners start queuing before the doors open for lunch. The take-away window offerings include doughnuts made from okara tofu lees, fresh and fried tofu, and silky soymilk skin called yuba. There’s no shortage of soba specialists in Tokyo, but few manage to create noodles quite as flavorful and satisfying as those at Tamawarai. Each batch is made from scratch — the dough mixed, rolled, and cut by hand — and much of it with buckwheat the restaurant helps to grow. The side dishes, such as soba miso and the wonderfully creamy yuba (soy milk skin), are prepared with equal care. Know before you go: Tamawarai doesn’t accept reservations, so expect to stand in line for up to an hour. No visit to Tokyo is complete without exploring a depachiku — the food halls found on the basement levels of major department stores. Isetan in Shinjuku can’t be beat for gourmet glamor, with local wagashi (Japanese confections) arranged alongside the patisseries of Sadaharu Aoki, Jean-Paul Hévin, and Pierre Hermé. Know before you go: Take a bento or light meal up to the rooftop garden. Just minutes from Shinjuku Station, L’ambre, which opened in 1950, allows customers to step back in time to an old-school kissaten. The cafe sports a high ceiling, red velvet seats, and classical music, providing the perfect atmosphere for enjoying coffee drinks, pizza toast, tuna and egg sandos, and a selection of cakes. Retro menu items include coffee jelly topped with ice cream and whipped cream, as well as a bright-green melon soda float. Best for: A casual throwback lunch. Diners sit around a C-shaped counter in this basement eatery to watch as Mai Nagamatsu shaves smoked and dried katsuo filets into delicate flakes called katsuobushi, and serves them over a bowl of rice. Katsuobushi is rich in natural umami, and sits at the heart of Japanese cuisine, so it’s a rare and precious opportunity to try it shaved a la minute. The set menu uses the skipjack tuna (also called bonito) flakes in each component from miso soup to a garnish made with chili oil. Know before you go: Be sure to make a reservation through Katsuo Shokudo’s website and bypass the queue of diners hoping to get a coveted counter seat. The serene Tea Bar Chokeikyo by Sakurai exalts the tea experience. Umami-rich gyokuro is steeped three times, the last time with thin slices of fresh peach. Star anise, cardamom, cloves, and cinnamon are freshly ground and warmed up in a Turkish ibrik over hot sand before being whisked into matcha. Come later in the day for tea cocktails like hojicha mojito or white tea with shiso gin fizz. Know before you go: It’s easier to get seats here in Daikanyama than at the popular Sakurai Tea Japanese Experience in Aoyama. Chokeikyo is down the street from the hip Tsutaya bookstore. Udatsu is the rare high-end sushiya that can accommodate vegetarians with a special menu. Both courses, vegetable and seafood, are satisfying: Chef Hisashi Udatsu incorporates texture and umami for the delicate vegetable sushi, frying some vegetables and simmering others in kombu kelp dashi. The seafood neta include two types of uni served over fried nori, five types of tuna in a large futomaki roll, and classics like kohada, vinegared gizzard shad. Know before you go: The vegetarian sushi course must be reserved two days in advance. The restaurant has branches in Los Angeles and Hong Kong also offering vegetarian sushi. Blossom Afternoon Tea at the Park Hyatt Tokyo’s Peak Lounge & Bar is a parade of savory and sweet bites. Seared yellowtail, snow crab, and smoked duck are followed by chef Julien Perrinet’s whimsical pastries, where seasonal fruits like chestnuts, pears, strawberries, mandarins, and yuzu shine. For the finale, a trolley laden with small bites including madeleines and canelés is rolled up tableside. There is also a wide selection of British and Japanese teas, hojicha and matcha lattes, and more to sip while taking in the view from the glass atrium 41 floors above Tokyo. Know before you go: Afternoon teas at luxury hotels in Tokyo are popular with locals. Be sure to book in advance.

item.title: 3 Excellent Hot Chocolate Mixes, According to Our Taste Test
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
A good instant hot chocolate mix should deliver everything you want from homemade hot chocolateâdeep chocolate flavor, creamy consistencyâbut, you know, instantly. No chopping chocolate or careful melting required. Just add hot water or milk, stir, and sip. But cocoa mixes vary wildly: Some are milky and sweet; others dark and verging on bitter; and some are closer to thick, velvety drinking chocolate than the stuff you guzzled at that budget ski lodge when you were 10. To find the best hot chocolate mixes, we sampled 15 supermarket and specialty varieties, including Swiss Miss, Starbucks, Ghirardelli, Guittard, Dandelion Chocolate, Jacques Torres, and Valrhona. We prepared each according to its package directions and judged it on chocolate flavor, sweetness, and texture. Our favorites cover three distinct cravings: Starbucks Classic for quintessential hot cocoa, Guittard for a richer, more luxurious sip, and Dandelion Chocolateâs house mix for complex, splurge-worthy chocolate flavor. The best classic hot chocolate: Starbucks Starbucks Classic Hot Cocoa scratched the nostalgia center of our collective brains, tasting like the hot chocolate we remember drinking at ice rinks or after a snow day spent sledding. Why it won us over: Tasters immediately recognized this as âclassic cocoa,â as senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman put it. Starbucksâ instant hot chocolate mix delivered satisfying milk-chocolate flavor and silky texture, even when prepared with waterâthough we recommend using milk or your favorite non-dairy alternative for an even creamier cup. It wasnât the most complex cocoa we tasted, but its balanced sweetness and familiar chocolate profile made it an easy favorite. Richer and more chocolate-forward than Starbucksâ offering, Guittardâs Grand Cacao Drinking Chocolate is the hot cocoa mix to reach for when you want something a little more indulgent. Why it won us over: Guittard makes some of our favorite chocolate chips and the Bon AppÃ©tit Test Kitchenâs go-to cocoa powder, so we had high hopes for its hot cocoa. It delivered deep chocolate flavor and flawlessly smooth texture. While some premium contenders skewed too bitter, Guittard struck an ideal bittersweet balance with âjust enough sweetness to get away with it,â according to food director Chris Morocco. Made with single-origin chocolate, Dandelion Chocolateâs House Hot Chocolate Mix produced something closer to drinking chocolate than the hot cocoa packets we grew up with. It was fruity, intensely chocolaty, and slightly bitter, with a thick, velvety consistency. Why it won us over: Dandelion stood apart from the first sip. While most hot chocolate mixes leaned sweet and milky, this one, as Kelsey put it, tasted like a âmelted bar of dark chocolate.â Tasters picked up notes of red berries buried in the deep chocolate flavorâa reminder, per senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk, that cacao is indeed a fruit. Restrained sweetness allowed the intriguingly complex flavors to shine, ultimately luring tasters back for a second (and third, and fourth) sip. At more than $2 an ounce, this isnât the hot chocolate weâd reach for when a dozen kids come in from sledding. Itâs the one to savor on a cold evening when youâre in the mood for something closer to dessert than an everyday cup of cocoa. We prepared each mix according to its package instructions, using hot water or milk as directed, then portioned the hot chocolate into individual tasting cups and served it warm. Tasters sampled the mixes without knowing which brands they were drinking and evaluated each for flavor and texture. It sounds silly to say hot chocolate should taste chocolaty, but not all contenders met this basic criterion. We wanted rich cocoa flavor with enough sweetness to balance its natural bitterness, but not so much that sugar overwhelmed the cup. Texture mattered too. Our favorites were creamy and silky, without the chalkiness, grittiness, or powderiness that knocked other contenders down the rankings. - Abuelita Mexican-Style Instant Hot Chocolate Mix: Its distinctive cinnamon flavor was pleasant, but set it too far apart from the unspiced mixes our tasters preferred. - Cadbury Hot Chocolate: An overpowering sweetness muddied any true chocolate flavor. - Ghirardelli Classic Hot Cocoa Mix: Ghirardelliâs Hot Cocoa Mix with Semi-Sweet Chocolate Chips took the top spot in 2022. Tasters were just as impressed by this versionâs creamy texture, but ultimately found it too sweet. - Great Value Milk Chocolate Flavor Hot Cocoa Mix: An off-putting waxy aroma and tart flavor kept this one out of the running. - Jacques Torres Classic Hot Chocolate: Rich texture, but a caramelized vanilla flavor distracted from the chocolate. - Lake Champlain Chocolates Traditional Organic Hot Chocolate: Too milky, without enough of a chocolate backbone. - NestlÃ© Rich Milk Chocolate Flavor Hot Cocoa Mix: An aggressive vanilla flavor and cloying sweetness took this one out of the running. - Raaka Double Dark Hot Chocolate: Deep chocolate flavor, but its pronounced bitterness and acidity kept it out of the top. - Sillycow Farms Hot Chocolate: Overly sweet and too mild in flavor for our tastersâ palates. - Swiss Miss Milk Chocolate Flavor Hot Cocoa Mix: Our tasters detected an unpleasant saltiness. - Swiss Miss Rich Chocolate Flavor Hot Cocoa Mix: Unbalanced sweetness and not enough chocolate flavor. - Trader Joeâs Organic Hot Cocoa Mix: This one was far too sugary, with an unnaturally thick texture tasters compared to canned soup. - Valrhona Dark Hot Chocolate Mix: Pleasantly chocolaty, but too sweet. - Vosges La Parisienne Drinking Chocolate: Rich chocolate taste, but with an overt milky sweetness that put it out of balance. - Whole Foods Organic Hot Cocoa Rich Chocolate Flavor Mix: This one was mellow and milky, but overall not quite chocolaty enough and a touch too sweet for us. Editorâs note: This story was originally published in 2022. For this update, we conducted a new taste test of 15 products. The tasting notes for Great Value, Trader Joeâs, and Whole Foods are from our original test; we evaluated the remaining products in 2026.

item.title: The DIY Descaling Solution I Use All Over My Kitchen
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
If you have an espresso machine, ice maker, combi oven, or other small appliance that requires water to do its thing, youâre likely familiar with descaling. And if you arenât it means the insides of those small appliances probably look pretty gross. The process uses an acidic solution to remove mineral buildup in order to stop buildup and keep everything running smoothly. But there are a few less obvious spots in your kitchen that would also benefit from regular descalingâand you donât need to buy a pricey descaling solution to do it. What is descaling solution and how does it work? Descaling solution is an acidic liquid that reacts withâand therefore breaks downâalkaline mineral build ups that happen over time wherever tap water sits or flows. Beyond the inside of tubes and pipes, chalky, crusty alkaline deposits often form around the base of faucets, the outer rims of refrigerator water dispensers, and on the bottom of tea kettles. This kind of buildup is especially prevalent where the municipal water source has a high mineral content (a.k.a hard water), especially if you donât have a whole-house water filtration system. If you arenât sure about the status of your water, you can start with this map from the U.S. Geological Survey and get a water test from your local big box store. Can you make a DIY descaling solution? You sure can. Now, making your own cleaning products can sometimes be risky business, but descaling solution isnât really a product you have to worry about. In fact, if youâre buying a bottled version of descaler, youâre wasting your money. You only need two things: acid and water. For the acid, you can choose either distilled white vinegar or crystallized citric acid. I much prefer citric acid for this because itâs a dry, food-safe powder (takes up less space when bought in bulk) and the comparably faint smell is far more pleasant than vinegar. And while itâs not a true sanitizer or disinfectant, it does have some antibacterial properties. Tap water is totally fine to use in your DIY descaling solution (I do it in a pinch), but distilled water is an even better option because it doesnât contain any minerals. The ratio of acid to water depends on what acid you choose, but since Iâm recommending you use citric acid here, Iâll give you that recipe: If you accidentally add a little more, itâs no big deal, it will just be a more powerful solution. Then, just stir until the crystals are dissolved and voila!: cheap, homemade descaling solution you can use in your small appliances according to the manufacturerâs instructions. In addition to using your DIY descaling solution for small appliance maintenance, you can use it to remove the chalky film from the bottom of your tea kettle and water bottles. And remember that white buildup around the base of your faucet? You can descale that away, too. For fairly fresh mineral deposits, simply pour a little of your homemade solution directly onto the problem area (or soak a paper towel with it and lay it on top), let it sit for a few minutes, then wipe it away with a microfiber towel. If youâre dealing with more of a stalagmite situation, you might need to use more solution, more time, and more elbow grease, but I promise I will budge eventually. Just be sure to wear dish gloves, because while citric acid is food safe, it can irritate sensitive skin, especially when mixed with water. If the base of your faucet has buildup, thereâs a very good chance the other end does too. If itâs easy to remove the sprayer head or aerator, you can soak them in your DIY solution. Mine doesnât detach easily, so I soak the sprayer head of my pull-down faucet by clamping the hose when itâs fully extended, then submerging it in a bowl of descaling solution in the sink. If none of those options work for you, fill a sandwich bag about halfway with the solution and affix it to the sink with a rubber band or twist ties and let it soak for a few hours or overnight; youâll be amazed at what ends up in the bottom of that bag! You can use this same technique to descale the spout of a refrigerator water dispenser. If you find descaling as satisfying as I do (and it is so satisfying), youâll soon be seeking out new spots to clean. Next stop: the dishwasher.
